s: Identify stakeholders and plan interviews
Conduct anchor-customer interviews - two accounts, six sessions
Analyze market, analyst, and segment data
Consolidate and prioritize product requirements
Resolve conflicts and set priorities- must-have, should-have, nice-to-have
Link product requirements to KPIs and PPA targets
Review and baseline product requirements
p: Customer needs and feedback by account
Market outlook and target segment sizing
Product requirements- ID, owner, priority, and acceptance criteria
Priority decisions and deferred requirements log
r: Product requirements document (PRD). The requirements list built here becomes the body of the PRD. This activity does not contribute to the PRD—it produces its content.

Target specification—PPA and KPI table. Each ranked requirement becomes a KPI line that DEF-03 converts into a number. A target that cannot be traced back to a requirement is a target no customer asked for.
Product cost and margin model. Provides the volume, segment and ASP assumptions the cost model is built on.
Feasibility report. DEF-07 assesses feasibility against this specific requirement set. A feasibility study run against a different or older set does not tell the program anything useful.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate review checks the signoff sheet. If the requirements are not signed, the program does not pass the gate.
pu: Turn customer and market needs into a single prioritized set of products requirements that serves as the baseline for the the entire program

These product requirements drive PPA, cost, feasibility, and architecture decisions. Until they are baselined and approved, downstream work remains provisional. Late changes can significantly increase cost and delay the program.
en: Program charter drafted and funded to study
ex: Each product requirement has an owner, priority, and acceptance criteria
Requirement conflicts are resolved or assigned to a clear decision owner
Product requirements are baselined and approved by product, engineering, and sales
rk: Product requirements not approved by all key stakeholders
New customer requirements introduced after baseline
Requirements that prescribe solutions instead of defining needs
Requirements without clear acceptance criteria
Requirements driven too heavily by a single customer
DEF-01.dn: Nothing upstream — this is the program's first activity. What it needs is bought, licensed or asked for, not produced by anything before it.
DEF-01.fn: The seven steps total 5.5 weeks of work inside a 4-week window because steps 3 and 6 run in parallel with the main sequence. This is why the activity TAT does not equal the sum of its step durations. If either parallel step has to move onto the critical path, the activity takes 1.5 weeks longer.

s: Define key use cases from product requirements
Capture workload traces for LLM, vision, and recommendation
Run workloads on previous-generation silicon for baseline
Define KPIs — TOPS, TOPS/W, tokens/s, TTFT, batch scaling
Define precision and quantization policy — INT8, FP8, mixed
Analyze KPI sensitivity to architecture choices
Package workload suite and hand off to architecture
p: Prioritized use cases with expected workloads mix
Representative workload traces for each use case
KPI targets and measurement conditions for each workload
Models, traces, and execution harness ready for architecture modeling
r: Target specification—PPA and KPI table. This activity derives the KPI half of the deliverable; DEF-03 derives the PPA half. The two are published as a single table.
Product requirements document. The use-case list and the deployment mix are written back into the PRD as the context the requirements are based on.
Feasibility report. Feasibility is assessed against these KPI numbers rather than against the requirement text.
pu: The product requirements define what customers expect. This activity translates those requirements into representative workloads and measurable KPI targets for the silicon.

These workloads guide the architecture optimization in ARCH-01. If they don not represent real customer usage, the architecture may be optimized for the wrong use cases. Verification may not catch this because it validates design correctness, not workload selection.
en: Requirement register at v0.9 or better
Lab access to the previous-generation platform
NDA coverage for any customer-supplied model
ex: Each KPI is linked to a defined workload and test conditions
Workload suite runs end to end on the reference platform
The architecture team confirms the workloads are ready for modeling.
rk: Workload traces that do not represent real customer usage
Limited access to customer models due to NDA restriction
Workload mix based on estimates rather than measured data
Undefined precision and quantization policy
KPIs without Cleary defined operating conditions
DEF-02.fn: The main sequence fills the 5-week window exactly. Steps 3 and 5 run in parallel: the reference runs need lab time rather than analyst time, and the precision policy can be settled while traces are still being captured.

s: Define frequency target from KPIs and expected IPC
Break down the power envelope - board, package, die, and domain level
Allocate die area based on block list and IP reuse
Defince initial operating voltage and multi-Vt strategy
Evaluate PPA sensitivity across candidate nodes
Allocate PPA budgets to each block and assign owners
Review PPA targets with architecture and physical design
p: Frequency target with the IPC assumption
Power budget from board to domain level
Approved PPA targets and review record
r: Target specification—PPA and KPI table. This activity defines the PPA target. DEF-02 defines the KPI targets, and both are combined into a single target specification.
Feasibility report. These are the numbers DEF-07 asks each candidate process node to support.
Product cost and margin model. The die area budget is the single largest input to the cost model.
pu: Translate the KPI targets into clear frequency, power and die-area budgets, and allocate them to each block

Program-level targets only become actionable when they are assigned to specific owners. For example, a 75 W board power target should be broken down into die, domain, and block-level budgets. This makes budget overruns visible early, when the design can still be adjusted without impacting performance or requiring a respin.
en: Block list stable enough to allocate against
At least two candidate nodes characterized by TECH-03
ex: Frequency, power and area targets include clearly defined assumptions
Each block has an allocated PPA budget and a clear owner
Architecture and physical design approve the PPA targets.
rk: PPA targets that exceed realistic process capability
Power budgets without sufficient margin
Area budgets that do not account for IP reuse
PPA budgets without clear owners
PPA targets finalized before the DEF-07 feasibility assessment
DEF-03.fn: Allocation is the step that matters, and it sits late in the sequence because it cannot begin until the block list is stable. Steps 4 and 5 run in parallel with the budget work; both feed the review rather than the budgets themselves.

s: Estimate die area from the block list and IP reuse plan
Calculate wafer cost and gross die per wafer for each candidate node
Estimate yield using defect density for each candidate node
Estimate package and substrate cost - interposer, substrate, and HBM
Estimate wafer sort and final test
Calculate unit cost and margin at a forecast volume
Analyze sensitivities to the three largest cost drivers
p: Die area estimate with expected range
Wafer cost and gross die per wafer by node
Yield model and expected yield by node
Test cost with its test-time assumption
Product cost model and margin at the forecast volume
Margin roll-up at the forecast volume
Cost ceiling statement for the design
r: Product cost and margin model. This activity produces the product cost and margin model with all key assumptions, allowing downstream teams to update and re-run the model as inputs change.
Feasibility report. A process node that meets the PPA targets but breaks the cost ceiling is recorded as infeasible, and this model is the basis for that finding.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The funding decision is a margin decision. If the cost model does not close, the program does not pass the gate.
pu: Estimate the product cost before committing to development. Combine wafer, mask, package, test, and yield assumptions to determine the expected unit cost and product margin at volume.

The cost model is also a key feasibility check. A product that meets its KPI targets but exceeds the cost target may not be commercially viable. Identifying this early allows the team to adjust die size, packaging, or cost drivers before the design is finalized.
en: Die area budget available from DEF-03
Wafer and mask quotations received from TECH-04
ex: Unit cost and margin targets are met at the forecast volume
Each cost assumption has a clear source and date
Sensitivities analysis identifies the top three cost drivers and their impact range.
rk: Yield assumptions based on mature-node data
Package costs underestimated in the overall cost model
Test costs without clear test-time assumptions
ASP based on a single-point estimate
Die area estimates without sufficient margin
DEF-04.fn: The sensitivity analysis in step 7 is not optional. On a 2.5D product, cost is dominated by yield, interposer supply and HBM pricing, and at this point in the program all three are assumptions rather than quoted prices.

s: Determine bandwidth demand from DEF-02 workloads
Size the memory hierarchy - on-die SRAM, HBM capacity, stacks, and channels.
Size the host interface - PCIe/CXL generation and lane count
Define Die-to-die interface requirement for chiplet option
Translate interface requirements into pin and bump budgets
Review requirements with architecture and package teams
p: Bandwidth requirements by workload and memory hierarchy level
Memory configuration — capacity, stacks, and channels
Host interface configuration — generation and lane count
Approved memory, interface and bump requirements
r: Product requirements document. Bandwidth and capacity enter the PRD as numbered requirements rather than as qualitative statements.
Target specification. The bandwidth figures become KPI lines, and the bump budget becomes an area constraint on the PPA half of the table.
pu: Define the memory and interface bandwidth required by the target workloads, and translate those requirements into the interface configuration needed by the package and Floorplan.

Bandwidth decisions directly affect the physical design and product cost. For example, using two HBM stacks instead of one impacts the interposer, substrate, power delivery, and package cost. Defining these requirements early reduces the risk of costly changes later in the program.
en: Requirement register carries capacity and latency requirements
HBM and interface roadmaps available under NDA
ex: Sustained bandwidth requirements are defined for each workload and operating condition
Memory configuration and interface counts are defined with clear rationale.
Package team confirms the bump budget is physically feasible
rk: Bandwidth requirements based on peak rather than sustained demand
Capacity and bandwidth treated as the same requirement
<b>Interface standard still under revision.
Interface requirements defined without a pin and bump budget.
Chiplet decision deferred without clear assumptions
DEF-05.fn: Step 5 is the step that creates the commitment. A bandwidth figure stated in GB/s does not constrain any downstream team. The same figure expressed as a bump count constrains the floorplan, the package design and the cost model at the same time.

s: Identify target competitor and expected launch timing
Collect public benchmarks, specifications, and public product information
Normalize benchmark data and comparison conditions
Project competitor capabilities to our target launch window
Compare our product targets against expected competitors
Review gaps with product and sales teams
p: Target competitor list with expected launch timing
Comparable benchmark data with clearly defined conditions
Expected competitor performance and capabilities at launch
Competitive gaps to feed into DEF-01 product requirements
r: Product requirements document. The capability gaps identified here become requirements. A gap that is not written into the requirement set is not addressed by the design.
Product cost and margin model. Competitive position is the basis on which the ASP assumption is defended.
pu: Benchmark the product against competitors expected to be available at the target launch date, not just products available today.

Current-generation comparisons do not reflect the competitive landscape at launch. Since the product is expected to reach the market in about thirty months, competitor performance should be projected for the same timeframe using public roadmaps, technology trends, and expected product cycles.
en: Product concept defined well enough to name a competitor set
Access to analyst material and benchmark submissions
Launch-window assumption from the program schedule
ex: Competitor comparisons use consistent and clearly defined conditions
Competitive performance is projected to the target launch window
Key competitive gaps are identified and fed back to DEF-01 as candidate product requirements.
rk: Comparing only against products available today
Using competitor performance data without consistent comparison conditions
Competitive gaps without clear owners or follow-up actions
Positioning based on a single performance metric
Competitor launch dates treated as fixed.
DEF-06.fn: Normalization runs in parallel because it is time-consuming and independent of data collection. Vendors quote TOPS at different precisions, batch sizes and power points, and none of the published figures are comparable until they have been restated on a common basis.

s: Confirm candidate process nodes with the technology team
Evaluate PPA feasibility for each node - density, frequency, and leakage
Assess IP availability and readiness for each node
Re-run the product cost model for each node
Evaluate package and thermal feasibility at target power
Identify required tradeoffs and their impact for each node
Determine feasibility and recommend a path forward
p: Product cost and margin by node
Package and thermal feasibility by node
Required tradeoffs and impact by node
r: The feasibility report includes the feasibility decision, assessment matrix, and required tradeoffs, providing the basis for the Go / No-Go decision.

Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. A No-Go recommendation from this activity is the only mechanism in the stage that can stop the program, and it has to reach the decision review without being edited.
pu: Evaluate the product requirements, PPA targets, and cost model against candidate process nodes to determine whether the product is feasible as defined or requires specific tradeoffs.

This assessment provides an early Go / No-Go input before the process node and development budget are committed. If major feasibility gaps are identified, the team can adjust requirements, PPA targets, cost assumptions, or node selection before committing to development.
en: At least two nodes characterized by TECH-03
ex: Each key target is assessed for feasibility on every candidate node
Required tradeoffs and their cost or impact are clearly identified.
Feasibility decision and recommended path forward are documented.
rk: Feasibility assessed after the node has been selected.
Optimistic assessment at the boundary.
IP availability taken from the vendor roadmap.
Thermal feasibility checked at typical rather than maximum power.
Required tradeoffs identified without their impact being quantified
DEF-07.fn: The concession list is the part of the deliverable that actually gets used. A binary verdict gives the decision review nothing to act on. A list stating "this node, at 200 MHz below target, with the PHY licensed rather than developed internally" gives the review a decision it can make.

s: Select the program profile and set the kickoff date
Adjust stage baseline for the program scope
Estimate engineering effort by stage and discipline
Compare staffing needs against available capacity
Add external lead times — substrate, probe card, IP, and shuttle
Identify the critical path and define schedule buffers
Review and commit the program schedule
p: Program profile with committed kickoff date
Program schedule with stage boundaries and milestones
Engineering effort by stage and discipline
Staffing plan with identified resource gaps
External lead times and required order dates
Approved program schedule and resource plan
r: The program charter combines the execution schedule, staffing plan, and resource requirements into a single baseline for program execution.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate approves both a schedule and a headcount. A plan with no resources committed against it does not pass the gate.
ef: Effort roll-up by stage and discipline
pu: Translate the program milestones into a detailed schedule and determine the engineering resources required to execute it. Compare those needs against the resources actually available.

The schedule is only achievable if the required resources are available at the right time. Identifying resource gaps early allows the team to adjust staffing, priorities, or the schedule before the program is committed.
en: Scope stable enough to adjust baselines against
ex: Program schedule is based on a committed kickoff date
Required staffing is matched against available capacity, with resource gaps identified
Critical path and schedule buffers are defined for key milestones
rk: Staffing needs that exceed available engineering capacity
Program baselines used without adjusting for actual scope
Supplier lead times not included in the program schedule
Schedule buffers concentrated only at the end of the program
Critical path not derived from actual task dependencies
DEF-08.fn: The supplier lead-time overlay runs in parallel and changes more dates than the internal plan does. A probe card and an advanced substrate each carry roughly twenty weeks of lead time, they are ordered against dates this activity sets, and once ordered they are outside the program's control.

s: Build the financial model - NRE, operating cost, revenue, and breakeven
Evaluate expected, downside, and upside scenarios
Summary key program risks and mitigation plans
Define recommendation and required funding
Prepare executive review package
Conduct the Go / No-Go review and record the decision
p: Financial model and expected product economics
Go / No-Go decision, conditions, and action owners
r: Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. This activity records the final Go / No-Go decision, including approval conditions, required follow-up actions, and any unresolved concerns.
Program charter, staffing and budget plan. The charter is only funded once this decision is made, and the approved figure is written back into it.
pu: Bring together the feasibility assessment, product cost model, and program plan into a clear business case for the funding decision. Provide a recommendation supported by both the expected outcome and downside scenarios.

This activity consolidates the analysis completed during product definition rather than creating new analysis. The business case should clearly show the expected return, required investment, key risks, and downside impact so decision-makers can make an informed Go / No-Go decision.
ex: Business case includes both expected and downside scenarios
Go / No-Go decision, approval conditions, and action owners are documented
Approved funding is reflected in the program charter
rk: Business case based only on the expected scenario
Approval conditions not formally documented
Unresolved concerns or dissenting views not recorded
<b>Feasibility tradeoffs or risks understated during the funding review</b
Go / No-Go decision authority not clearly defined
DEF-09.fn: The decision meeting takes a quarter of a week and the preparation takes three weeks, which is the correct ratio. A gate decision argued in the room rather than resolved before it produces an outcome that depends on who attended.

ARCH-01.t: System-level performance modeling and workload simulation
s: Define the performance model scope, detail level, and key assumptions
Build the baseline system model — compute, memory, and interconnect
Integrate the DEF-02 workload suite
Correlate the model with previous-generation silicon
Explore architecture options — compute clusters, SRAM capacity, HBM channels
Evaluate interconnect and NoC topology options
Integrate power estimates and evaluate performance efficiency
Identify system bottlenecks and performance limits
Evaluate sensitivity and model confidence
Package the model and regression environment for reuse
p: Performance model scope and modeling assumptions
Workloads integrated into the performance model
Model correlation results and error range
Sensitivity results and model confidence range
Performance model, source, and regression environment
r: Performance model and workload analysis report. The deliverable includes the performance model, workload analysis, correlation results, and model confidence used to evaluate architecture performance and tradeoffs.
Architecture specification. Every quantitative claim in the specification traces back to a sweep in this model, or it does not belong in the specification.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. The sweeps are what decide cluster count and SRAM capacity before ARCH-02 draws the boundaries.
pu: Build a system-level performance model to evaluate architecture decisions against the workloads and KPI targets defined in DEF-02. Use simulation to guide partitioning, sizing, and interface decisions before implementation begins.

The model provides a common basis for architecture decisions and tradeoffs. Validating these decisions early allows the team to identify performance gaps and evaluate alternatives before they become costly to change in RTL or silicon.
en: Workload suite delivered and runnable from DEF-02
ex: Performance model is correlated to measured silicon data with a defined error range
Key architecture decisions are supported by simulation and sensitivity analysis
Regression environment is ready for reuse in later stages
rk: Performance model not correlated with measured silicon data
Model detail level not matched to the decisions being evaluated
Architecture analysis based on unrepresentative workloads
Power estimates integrated too late in the modeling process
Model accuracy and confidence range not clearly defined
ARCH-01.fn: Correlation sits early on purpose. A model that has never been checked against silicon produces numbers, not answers, and every sweep run before correlation has to be re-run afterwards.

s: Define functional blocks and system hierarchy
Check die size against reticle and process constraints
Develop monolithic and chiplet architecture options
Compare yield and cost across architecture options using DEF-04 model
Evaluate Die-to-die interface requirements for chiplet options
Define partition boundaries and what crosses each boundary
Evaluate known-good-die and test implications
Select and document the system and die partitioning
p: Yield and cost comparison by option
Die-to-die bandwidth, latency, and interface requirements
Partition boundaries with signals, bandwidth, and latency requirements
r: Block partitioning and PPA budget table. The deliverable defines the block boundaries and die assignments. ARCH-06 adds the PPA budgets for each block.
Architecture specification. The partition and its boundaries are the specification's structural spine—every other section is written against them.
Chip-level block diagram with pin and bump budget. ARCH-08 draws what this activity decides.
pu: Define how compute, memory, and interconnect functions are partitioned across the system, including whether the product uses a monolithic or chiplet architecture.

The partitioning decision has major impact on package design, die-to-die interfaces, yield, test strategy, and product cost. Making this decision before Architecture Freeze avoids major redesign of the die, package, and test solution later in the program.
en: First design-space results available from ARCH-01
Cost model usable for candidate comparison
Reticle and node constraints confirmed by TECH
ex: System and die partitioning is selected with key alternatives evaluated
Each partition boundary has defined bandwidth and latency requirements
Test, yield, and cost impacts are evaluated for the selected partitioning
rk: Chiplet architecture selected without a clear product-level benefit
Partition boundaries defined without bandwidth and latency requirements
Die size feasibility checked without sufficient growth margin
Test and known-good-die implications evaluated too late
Partitioning decision documented without clear decision rationale
ARCH-02.fn: Boundary definition takes three of the eight weeks because it is the part that gets skipped. Deciding "two dies" is quick; deciding exactly which signals cross at what bandwidth and latency is the work that makes the decision real.

s: Define the dataflow for each workload class based on data reuse and movement - weight-stationary, output-stationary, or hybrid.
Size on-die SRAM based on workload data reuse
Define SRAM banking, ports, and bandwidth
Define HBM channels and address interleaving
Define cache and scratchpad usage
Define prefetch and data-movement requirements
Validate the memory hierarchy using the ARCH-01 performance model
Finalize the memory hierarchy and handoff requirements
p: SRAM capacity requirements with workload-based justification
HBM channel configuration and interleaving scheme
Memory hierarchy performance and bottleneck analysis
Memory hierarchy section of ARCH-D1 and memory requirements for downstream teams
r: Architecture specification. This activity defines the dataflow and memory hierarchy section of ARCH-D1, including SRAM organization and HBM configuration. ARCH-09 integrates it into the final architecture specification.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. SRAM capacity is the largest single area line in the budget, and it is decided here.
Performance model and workload analysis report. The hierarchy sweeps are run in the ARCH-01 model and reported with it.
pu: Define how data moves through the system and how the memory hierarchy is organized for the target workloads, including on-die SRAM capacity, data reuse, and HBM configuration.

Memory architecture has a direct impact on compute utilization and system performance. Matching the dataflow and memory hierarchy to workload access and reuse patterns helps keep compute resources utilized while minimizing unnecessary data movement.
en: Reuse analysis available from the DEF-02 traces
Memory compiler capability indicated by PDK-04
ex: Memory capacity and bandwidth are validated against target workloads through simulation
Dataflow is defined for each workload class with key tradeoffs documented
Memory requirements are defined and handed off to PDK and AMS teams
rk: SRAM capacity based on average rather than workload-specific data reuse
SRAM capacity defined without considering banking and bandwidth requirements
Memory architecture based on unverified memory compiler capabilities
A single dataflow applied across all workload classes
HBM address interleaving defined too late in the design process
ARCH-03.fn: Sizing precedes simulation and simulation revises sizing—the two weeks in step 7 include at least one full turn back through step 2. A hierarchy accepted on its first simulation has almost certainly not been swept.

s: Consolidate interface requirements from DEF-05
Review protocol version maturity and expected finalization timing
Select host interfaces — PCIe generation and CXL profile
Select HBM generation and define controller requirements
Select the die-to-die interface for chiplet architectures (if the chipset option is survived.)
Define compliance and interoperability requirements
Define controller and PHY requirements for IP selection and sourcing
Finalize and review the interface definition
p: Host interface selection and protocol versions
ARCH-D4 Interface and Protocol Definition Document
r: Interface and protocol definition document. The deliverable defines the selected interfaces, protocol versions, and the controller and PHY requirements derived from each selection.
Architecture specification. The interface chapter is imported from the definition document rather than restated, so the two cannot drift.
Chip-level block diagram with pin and bump budget. Lane counts and PHY footprints are what ARCH-08 allocates bumps against.
pu: Select the external interfaces and protocol versions required by the product, including PCIe, CXL, HBM, and die-to-die interfaces where applicable. Translate each selection into clear controller and PHY requirements for IP planning and sourcing.

Interface decisions depend on both standards readiness and IP availability. Selecting a protocol version before the specification and supporting IP are sufficiently mature can introduce schedule and integration risks later in the program.
en: Vendor PHY roadmaps accessible under NDA
ex: Each interface is mapped to a specific protocol version with sufficient standards maturity
Controller and PHY requirements are defined for IP selection and sourcing
Compliance requirements and their hardware implications are clearly identified
rk: Protocol version selected before the standard is sufficiently mature
PHY availability on the target process node not confirmed
Compliance and interoperability requirements defined too late
Lane count determined by bandwidth alone without considering system and package constraints
Die-to-die interface selection delayed after the chiplet architecture is defined
ARCH-04.fn: The handoff in step 7 is what makes this activity urgent rather than merely important. IPR-04 cannot evaluate a PHY vendor against a generation nobody has chosen, and PHY license lead times run to a quarter.

s: Define power domains based on the system partitioning
Define voltage rails and regulator architecture
Define DVFS operating points and control policy
Define clock domains and clock-domain crossings
Define reset architecture and sequencing
Define power management controller requirements
Create and validate the initial UPF intent
Review the architecture with physical design and verification
p: Power domain definitions and boundary map
DVFS operating points and control policy
Clock domain architecture and CDC requirements
Initial UPF intent validated in target tools
Approved power, clock, and reset architecture
r: Power / clock / reset architecture and UPF intent. The deliverable defines the power domains, clock and reset structure, DVFS operating points, and initial UPF intent used by implementation and verification tools.
Architecture specification. The power and clock chapter, and the constraint every block owner designs against.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. Power domains are the unit the power budget is allocated in.
pu: Define the power and clock architecture for the product, including power and clock domains, voltage rails, DVFS operating points, clock-domain crossings, and reset structure. Capture the initial power intent in UPF for implementation and verification.

These decisions directly affect both physical implementation and verification. Defining power-domain boundaries and power intent early ensures that isolation, level shifting, clock/reset crossings, and verification requirements are handled consistently across downstream teams.
en: Power budget per domain available from DEF-03
Library and IO low-power capability confirmed by PDK-03
ex: Every clock-domain crossing has a defined synchronization strategy
Initial UPF intent is validated in the target implementation and verification tools
Power, clock, and reset architecture is reviewed and accepted by physical design and verification teams
rk: Power domains defined without clear power-management requirements
Clock-domain crossings not fully identified
DVFS operating points defined without performance and power validation
UPF intent created after RTL implementation has already started
Reset sequencing not defined before implementation and verification
ARCH-05.fn: The crossing inventory in step 4 is the artifact RTL-06 closes CDC against. An inventory that is incomplete at Architecture Freeze becomes a CDC finding in week 40, when the fix is an RTL change under change control.

s: Reconcile DEF-03 PPA targets with the finalized ARCH-02 block list
Allocate die area to each block using the floorplan intent
Allocate power by block and power domain
Define frequency and timing budgets by block and clock domain
Reserve margin for implementation growth and ECOs
Assign owners and obtain budget acceptance
Publish the PPA budgets and change-control rules
p: Reconciliation note against the DEF-03 targets
Per-block area, power and timing budget
r: This activity defines the PPA budget portion of ARCH-D3 against the blocks established in ARCH-02.
Architecture specification. The budget table is referenced by the specification rather than copied, so a budget change does not need a specification revision.
Architecture Freeze review package. A block without an accepted budget is an open item at the freeze gate.
pu: Allocate the program-level PPA targets to individual blocks based on the finalized system partitioning, memory hierarchy, and power architecture.
Block-level budgets provide a measurable reference for RTL, synthesis, and physical design. They also make area, power, and timing overruns visible early enough to manage them.
ex: Each block has accepted area, power, and timing budgets
Implementation margin is explicitly reserved
Budget change-control rules are defined and agreed
rk: PPA budgets allocated without implementation margin
Block budgets not accepted by their owners
Budget changes without formal change control
Block-level totals not reconciled to DEF-03 targets
Timing budgets defined too broadly to expose block-level closure risk
ARCH-06.fn: Step 6 is acceptance, not notification. A budget a block owner has not agreed to is a budget that will be exceeded and disputed, and the dispute happens at PD-09 when there is no time for it.

s: Define and document threat model and asset inventory
Define secure boot chain and immutable ROM
Select root of trust and key storage
Define fuse map, chip identity and lifecycle state
Debug and test access lockdown policy, with DFT
Define and document cryptographic accelerator requirement
Review and approve the security architecture
p: Root of trust and key storage architecture
Fuse map and lifecycle state definition
Security architecture note and review record
r: This activity defines the security architecture section of ARCH-D1, including boot, lifecycle, key-management, and debug-control requirements.
Power / clock / reset architecture. Secure boot constrains the reset sequence: the root of trust must run before anything else is released from reset.
ef: Boot chain and root of trust
pu: Define the security and safety architecture, including secure boot, root of trust, key storage, lifecycle states, fuse usage, and production debug controls.
These controls must be designed into the architecture because they affect boot flow, reset, DFT access, key handling, and implementation requirements.
en: Security requirements present in the product requirements
eFuse and OTP capability confirmed by PDK-02
ex: Threat model is reviewed and each protected asset is mapped to a security control
Lifecycle states, transitions, and validation requirements are defined
Production debug controls are agreed with DFT and bring-up teams
rk: Security architecture defined after system partitioning is frozen
Production debug access not fully controlled
Fuse map defined without lifecycle-state requirements
Root-of-trust implementation selected without validating security needs
No clear security owner through implementation and qualification
ARCH-07.fn: Step 5 is a negotiation, not a decision taken alone. DFT-04 needs JTAG and trace access for silicon debug, and every path it opens is a path this activity has to close in production lifecycle states.

s: Place block intent from the partitioning and the hierarchy
Place iO ring and PHY plan
Define bump field — pitch, count, power-to-signal ratio
Allocate signal bump per interface
Define and document power delivery bump budget against the power envelope
Define package feasibility check with package design
Define and document block diagram and bump budget publication
p: Chip-level block diagram with placement intent
IO ring and PHY placement plan
Published block diagram and bump budget
r: The deliverable defines the chip-level block placement intent and pin/bump budget used by physical design and package teams.
Architecture specification. The physical view chapter—the first place the specification stops being a block diagram and becomes a die.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. Placement intent is what ARCH-06 allocates die area against.
pu: Define the initial chip-level physical architecture, including block placement intent, PHY locations, I/O planning, and the pin and bump budget.
The floorplan and bump budget connect architecture decisions to package and physical-design constraints. Early validation reduces the risk of late interface, power-delivery, or package changes.
en: Interface lane counts available from ARCH-04
Package architecture candidates known from PKGD-01
ex: Bump field and power-to-signal allocation are defined
Each interface has an allocated bump count accepted by the package team
Physical design confirms that the placement intent is feasible
rk: Interface lane counts finalized before bump feasibility is checked
Power-delivery bump requirements underestimated
Placement intent defined without routing feasibility
Package feasibility based on generic rather than selected technology assumptions
HBM PHY placement left unresolved
ARCH-08.fn: The power-to-signal ratio in step 3 is the number that decides the argument. On a part at this power envelope most of the bump field is power delivery, and the signal budget is what is left over rather than what was asked for.

s: Define structure and section ownership assignment
Define and document section authoring across the architecture team
Define and document consistency pass — every number traced to its source activity
Define and document open-issue register and disposition
Review internal technical , two rounds
Review downstream readiness with RTL, DV, DFT and physical design
Define and document freeze package assembly
Define and document architecture Freeze gate
p: Open-issue register with disposition per item
Internal technical review findings, two rounds
Architecture Freeze package and decision record
r: This activity integrates and closes ARCH-D1. Sections authored by earlier ARCH activities are reviewed for consistency and assembled into the final specification.
The deliverable combines the final architecture specification, open-issue disposition, and downstream readiness findings for the Architecture Freeze decision.
Performance model and workload analysis report. Published alongside the specification, because the specification's numbers are only defensible with it.
pu: Finalize the architecture specification and complete the review required for Architecture Freeze.
This activity integrates architecture sections, checks consistency and traceability, resolves open issues, and confirms that downstream teams have enough information to begin implementation.
en: All architectural decisions taken, or explicitly listed as open
PPA budget accepted by block owners in ARCH-06
Downstream leads available to review before the gate
ex: All open issues are closed, assigned for follow-up, or explicitly accepted as risk
RTL, DV, DFT, and physical design complete the readiness review
Architecture Freeze decision and any approval conditions are documented
rk: Architecture Freeze with unresolved issues and no disposition
Specification consistency and traceability checks skipped
Downstream readiness review performed after the freeze decision
Architecture specification lacks implementable interfaces and constraints
Architecture Freeze based on schedule rather than readiness
ARCH-09.fn: The downstream readiness review in step 6 is the one that predicts the program. Architecture reviewing its own specification confirms it is coherent; RTL, DV and DFT reviewing it confirms it is implementable, and those are different questions.

s: Define block template and review cadence
Define and document block owner assignment and kickoff
Define pipeline and datapath per block
Define block interface and protocol against the NoC
Define and document control, configuration and register map, first pass
Verify hook and observability requirement, with DV
Review microarchitecture , first round
Implement handoff to RTL
p: Block owner assignment and kickoff record
Register map first pass, per block
r: Block microarchitecture specifications refine the block definitions in ARCH-D1 and must remain consistent with the frozen architecture.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. Microarchitecture is where a block owner first tests whether the allocated budget is achievable.
Architecture Freeze review package. A block with no microarchitecture owner is an open item at the gate—the specification cannot be implemented by nobody.
pu: Define the microarchitecture for each block, including pipeline structure, interfaces, control behavior, register-map requirements, and verification hooks.
Starting this work during architecture gives RTL owners an implementable reference and exposes interface or budget conflicts before block implementation begins.
en: Architecture specification chapters stable enough to refine
PPA budget accepted per block in ARCH-06
ex: Each block has a microarchitecture specification and named owner
Shared interfaces are agreed by both sides of each boundary
RTL leads confirm that the specifications are ready for implementation
rk: Blocks entering RTL implementation without clear specification owners
Shared interfaces defined independently by each block owner
Register-map definition deferred until RTL implementation
Verification and observability requirements added after implementation
Microarchitecture defined without checking the allocated PPA budget
ARCH-10.fn: Step 4 runs in parallel and is where the interesting failures live. Two block owners each writing their side of a shared interface will disagree, and finding that here costs a meeting rather than an integration debug at RTL-04.

s: Define evaluation criteria from product, PPA, cost, and schedule requirements
Build the initial list of candidate foundries and process nodes
Screen candidates for basic technical and schedule feasibility
Compare PPA, maturity, cost, capacity, and ecosystem readiness
Review key risks and dependencies for each shortlisted option
Select the preferred foundry and process node
Review and approve the technology selection
p: Risk and dependency assessment by option
Approved foundry and process node selection
r: Technology selection report and decision record. This activity defines the deliverable; TECH-03 supplies the technical evidence it rests on.
Node risk assessment. The supply-continuity and geopolitical screen is one of the risk assessment's inputs, and it is gathered here.
pu: Narrow the field of foundries and nodes to a short-list the program can evaluate, and record why the others were dropped.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Product requirements and PPA targets available at draft quality
Volume forecast good enough to discuss with a foundry
Legal cover in place for preliminary discussion
ex: Candidate foundries and process nodes are compared using consistent criteria
Key PPA, cost, capacity, schedule, and IP risks are identified for each option
Preferred foundry and process node are selected with clear decision rationale
rk: Node selected mainly from roadmap preference rather than product fit
Foundry comparisons based on inconsistent assumptions or conditions
Capacity and schedule constraints evaluated too late
IP and design-enablement readiness assumed rather than verified
Selection made without a documented alternative and decision rationale
TECH-01.fn: Step 3 is the pacing item and almost none of it is our work—information requests sit with the foundry's technical marketing team, and the response time is theirs. Starting the engagement in week one is the only lever the program has over it.

s: Review available process options and device flavors
Map product PPA and architecture needs to available options
Evaluate performance, leakage, density, and cost tradeoffs
Assess optional features such as backside PDN, RF, or HV where applicable
Confirm library, IP, rule, and EDA support for the preferred configuration
Select the process configuration for the program
p: Selected process option and flavor set
r: Process option / flavor sheet agreed with foundry. The deliverable it is contractual rather than advisory.
Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet. Every option on the sheet carries a price adder, so the flavor decides a meaningful part of the wafer cost.
Technology selection report. The selection is only complete when the flavor is named—a node without a flavor sheet is not a selection anyone can build on.
pu: Choose the flavor of the node, not just the node—performance or density library, the multi-Vt menu, the metal stack, backside power delivery, and any analog or high-voltage adders the product needs.

A node name is not a specification. Two programs on the same node with different flavor sheets get different density, different leakage and different routing resource, and the difference is larger than most architectural decisions.
en: Early DTCO results available from TECH-03
ex: Required process options and device flavors are selected for the product
PPA and cost impacts of optional features are understood
Selected options are confirmed to be supported by the foundry and design ecosystem
rk: Process options selected without quantified PPA benefit
Optional features added without accounting for cost or schedule impact
Library or IP support assumed before it is available
Vt strategy chosen without considering leakage and timing together
Foundry configuration changed after design enablement has started
TECH-02.fn: Two of the five weeks sit in step 7, which is signature time rather than engineering time. The sheet is a contractual artifact: once agreed it governs what the PDK contains and what the wafer costs, and changing it later reopens both.

TECH-03.t: Process PPA Benchmarking and DTCO Assessment
s: Define representative blocks and benchmark conditions
Collect process, library, and interconnect characterization inputs
Estimate or implement baseline PPA for each candidate configuration
Compare density, frequency, leakage, and power against product targets
Run DTCO studies on the largest PPA gaps
Evaluate sensitivity to key design and process assumptions
Summarize expected PPA capability and remaining risks
r: Technology selection report and decision record. The evidence half of the report—TECH-01 records the decision, this activity is why the decision is defensible.
Node risk assessment. Where a target is only just met, this study is what says so, and that margin is a node risk.
Process option / flavor sheet. The Vt menu and metal stack on the sheet are chosen from these results.
pu: Measure the candidate nodes against this product's targets rather than against the foundry's brochure—density, achievable frequency, leakage, SRAM Vmin and routing resource, on circuits that resemble the design.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
ex: PPA results are compared under consistent implementation assumptions
Key gaps to product targets are quantified for each candidate configuration
DTCO opportunities and remaining limitations are documented for downstream planning
rk: Benchmark conditions that favor one node or process option
Foundry marketing metrics used in place of product-relevant implementation data
Representative blocks that do not reflect actual design complexity
DTCO gains assumed without verifying library, rule, or flow support
PPA gaps hidden by optimistic utilization or routing assumptions
TECH-03.fn: Three of the eight steps run in parallel because they use different data and different people—power characterization, SRAM and congestion are separable studies. What cannot be parallelized is step 7: comparison needs all three to have landed.

TECH-04.t: Wafer, Mask, and NRE Cost Assessment
s: Define the pricing scope and required quotation items
Collect wafer, mask, NRE, MPW, and volume pricing
Normalize quotations to common volume and schedule assumptions
Identify one-time and recurring cost drivers
Review commercial assumptions and sensitivity with product finance
Release cost inputs to the product cost model
p: Approved wafer, mask, and NRE cost sheet
r: Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet. The deliverable its value is that the numbers are quoted rather than estimated.
Technology selection report. Cost is a selection criterion; a node that wins on PPA and loses on price is a decision, not a formality.
pu: Put a price on the technology—wafers at the forecast volume, the mask set, the NRE, the MPW shuttle, and every adder the flavor sheet carries—and hand it to the cost model as quotations rather than estimates.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Short-list closed and flavor options known
Volume forecast agreed with sales and finance
Die size estimate available from DEF-04
ex: Wafer, mask, and NRE costs are defined for the selected technology
Pricing assumptions are tied to stated volume and schedule conditions
Cost inputs are ready for use in DEF-04 and business-case updates
rk: Wafer pricing compared without matching volume assumptions
Mask and NRE costs omitted from early business-case analysis
Engineering-lot or MPW costs treated as production pricing
Quotation validity dates ignored as the program schedule changes
Commercial assumptions not updated after process-option changes
TECH-04.fn: The tier structure in step 6 is worth more than the headline price. A wafer price that only applies above a volume the product will not reach in its first year is a price the cost model should not be using.

TECH-05.t: Fab Capacity and Tapeout Slot Planning
s: Translate the program schedule into required tapeout and wafer-start windows
Review foundry slot availability and capacity outlook
Identify conflicts between program demand and available capacity
Evaluate priority, hot-lot, or alternate scheduling options where needed
Secure the required tapeout slot and capacity commitment
Integrate confirmed foundry dates into the program schedule
r: Capacity and tapeout slot commitment. The deliverable it is worth only as much as the escalation path written into it.
Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet. Committed volume is what the price tier is granted against, so the two documents have to agree.
pu: Convert the program's schedule into reserved fab capacity—a wafer-start profile, a tapeout slot, hot-lot terms and an engineering-lot allocation—and get it committed in writing.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Design agreement executed or in final redline
ex: Required tapeout windows are aligned with the program schedule
Engineering and production capacity assumptions are confirmed with the foundry
Capacity or slot risks have owners and mitigation plans
rk: Tapeout slots treated as available until late in the program
Capacity commitments based only on verbal alignment
Engineering-lot needs omitted from capacity planning
Hot-lot assumptions used without confirmed foundry support
Foundry schedule changes not reflected in the program critical path
TECH-05.fn: Steps 4 and 5 look like details and behave like insurance. Hot-lot priority is what turns an 18-week fab cycle into an 11-week one at FAB-04, and it is only available to programs that negotiated it before they needed it.

s: Identify required legal and commercial agreements
Execute the NDA required for technical data exchange
Review foundry design-agreement terms and design-data rights
Align IP licensing and third-party usage terms
Resolve commercial and legal exceptions
Execute the required foundry agreements
p: Design agreement issues and required changes
Closed legal and commercial issue list
Executed design agreement and legal package
r: Executed foundry design agreement (DA) and NDA. The deliverable until it executes the enablement band cannot legally start.
Capacity and tapeout slot commitment. Capacity is committed under the design agreement; the commitment has no standing without it.
pu: Put the legal frame in place that everything technical depends on—NDA, design agreement, PDK and library licensing, the foundry IP frame, and liability terms—and execute it.

This is the longest activity in the stage at eight weeks and one of the smallest at 2 M/M, which is exactly the shape it should have: the elapsed time belongs to two legal departments and almost none of the work belongs to the program. It is on the critical path anyway, because production PDK access, memory compilers and foundry IP all sit behind the design agreement.
en: Short-list narrow enough to engage legally
Corporate legal position and templates available
Compliance guidance for the candidate foundries
ex: Required legal agreements are executed before protected design data is needed
Design-data access and usage rights are clearly defined
IP licensing and commercial responsibilities are aligned with the program plan
rk: Technical data access blocked by an incomplete NDA
Design work started before usage rights are clear
IP licensing terms assumed to be covered by the foundry agreement
Legal review started only after the technology decision is final
Commercial exceptions left unresolved until procurement or tapeout
TECH-06.fn: Step 1 is deliberately first and deliberately short. Nothing technical can be discussed before the NDA executes, so every week it takes is a week subtracted from TECH-03—which is why the NDA is chased separately from the agreement it precedes.

TECH-07.t: Foundry Roadmap and Production Readiness Alignment
s: Map program milestones to foundry roadmap milestones
Review process maturity, model readiness, and risk-production timing
Assess yield-learning and manufacturing-readiness risk
Identify schedule dependencies on future foundry releases
Define mitigation for readiness gaps
Align the program schedule with confirmed foundry milestones
r: Node risk assessment—maturity, defect density, yield learning curve. The deliverable it is what the yield assumption in the cost model should be built on.
Technology selection report. Maturity is a selection criterion in its own right, separate from the PPA the node can deliver.
pu: Establish where each candidate node is on its maturity curve—risk production timing, defect density trend, yield learning rate, capacity ramp—and turn that into a risk assessment the program plans against.

A node chosen at the right time is a node in volume production when the program taped out. A node chosen too early gives the program the foundry's learning curve as a yield problem, and the schedule to absorb it was never in the plan.
en: NDA executed far enough to receive roadmap data
Program tapeout date estimated by DEF-08
ex: Program milestones are aligned with foundry technology-readiness milestones
Key maturity and production-readiness gaps are identified with mitigation plans
Schedule assumptions are updated to reflect realistic foundry readiness
rk: Program schedule based on foundry roadmap dates without maturity margin
Risk production treated as equivalent to stable high-volume manufacturing
PDK and model readiness assumed to track process readiness automatically
Yield-learning risk excluded from launch planning
Foundry milestone changes not propagated into the program schedule
TECH-07.fn: Step 2 asks for data the foundry treats as sensitive, and how much of it arrives is itself a signal. A foundry that will not share a defect density trend under NDA is telling the program something about the trend.

s: Define the business and supply reasons for a second source or migration path
Identify technically credible alternative nodes or foundries
Compare IP, library, design-rule, and architecture compatibility
Estimate redesign, validation, qualification, cost, and schedule impact
Evaluate whether the contingency provides sufficient business value
Define the selected contingency strategy and trigger conditions
r: Technology selection report and decision record. Single-source acceptance belongs in the selection record, priced, rather than being implied by its absence.
Node risk assessment. Supply concentration is a node risk, and its mitigation is either a second source or an accepted exposure.
pu: Decide, deliberately, whether the program accepts single-source risk—and if it does not, what dual-sourcing or migration readiness would cost in area, schedule and IP.
Most leading-edge programs end up single-source, and that is a defensible answer. What is not defensible is arriving there by default.
en: IP bill of materials direction available from IPR-01
Design rule sets accessible for at least one alternative
ex: Second-source or migration need is explicitly decided rather than assumed
Major technical, cost, and schedule impacts are quantified
Contingency path and trigger conditions are documented where required
rk: Second source assumed to be a simple database port
IP portability accepted without checking vendor and node support
Qualification and package changes excluded from migration planning
Contingency cost ignored in the business case
Backup strategy defined without clear trigger conditions
TECH-08.fn: Migration readiness is a design-time choice, not a later option: it constrains which IP can be used and how aggressively design rules can be pushed. Deciding after RTL starts means the decision has already been made by everyone who chose an IP.

TECH-09.t: OSAT and Backend Supply Chain Alignment
s: Define backend manufacturing and package capability requirements
Identify candidate OSAT and backend suppliers
Assess assembly, substrate, interposer, and test capability
Review capacity, lead times, and supply-chain constraints
Identify capability and schedule gaps
Align supplier assumptions with package and program schedules
Define follow-up actions and supplier engagement plan
r: Capacity and tapeout slot commitment. Front-end capacity without matching backend capacity delivers wafers that cannot be assembled.
Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet. Interposer and assembly pricing is the backend half of the technology cost, and the cost model needs both.
Technology selection report. On a 2.5D part the choice of foundry constrains the interposer options, so backend capability belongs in the selection record.
pu: Open the backend supply chain early—OSAT capability and capacity, substrate and interposer suppliers, the foundry-to-OSAT logistics model, and who owns known-good die—so package design starts against real constraints.

On a 2.5D part the backend is not a downstream detail; it is a second supply chain with its own lead times, its own capacity constraints and its own qualification. Advanced packaging capacity in particular is allocated far ahead, and a program that starts asking at PKGD-10 is asking late.
en: Package architecture assumption stated in the product requirements
Foundry selected, so interposer options are known
ex: Candidate OSAT and backend suppliers can support the required package technology
Major capacity, lead-time, and supply risks are identified with owners
Backend assumptions are aligned with the package-design and program schedules
rk: OSAT engagement started after package architecture is fixed
Substrate or interposer lead times omitted from early schedule planning
Supplier capability assumed from generic technology claims
Backend capacity risk evaluated only after wafer capacity is secured
Package and test dependencies not reflected in the program schedule
TECH-09.fn: Step 5 decides an argument before it happens. When a packaged unit fails, whether the die or the assembly is responsible is a contractual question, and settling it while nobody has lost money is far easier than settling it afterwards.

PDK-01.t: PDK Version Readiness and Change Management
s: Build the PDK release roadmap for the program
Track changes in design rules, models, extraction, and signoff content
Assess the impact of each major PDK update on active design work
Identify gaps that block library, IP, implementation, or signoff work
Align PDK adoption points with program milestones
Review readiness and open issues with the foundry and design teams
Maintain version history and release decisions through tapeout
p: PDK release timeline and maturity map
PDK readiness status and action list
r: PDK readiness dashboard. The deliverable it is a living document rather than a report—its value is entirely in being current.
Qualified library list. Every version transition potentially invalidates a qualification, and this activity is what says which ones.
Golden environment release notes. The environment cannot be released against a version that has not been assessed and frozen.
pu: Track what the foundry ships, version by version, and turn each release into a delta the program can act on—what changed, what it costs, and whether anything already done has to be redone.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Design agreement executed so PDK access is legal
Release calendar obtained from the foundry
ex: Current and planned PDK versions are mapped to the program schedule
Major release changes have documented design and signoff impact
Open PDK gaps have owners, mitigation plans, and target closure dates
rk: PDK updates adopted without impact analysis
Different teams using different PDK versions
Early PDK limitations treated as production-ready behavior
Signoff assumptions changed without updating downstream flows
Open PDK gaps not tied to program milestones
PDK-01.fn: Step 8 runs for twenty of the thirty-four weeks and is the activity most likely to be dropped when the team is busy. It is also the only artifact that tells the program which of its assumptions have quietly expired.

s: Review the design rule manual and foundry guidance
Identify restricted, recommended, and high-risk rules
Assess product impact for routing, density, macros, and reliability
Define required design practices and exceptions
Review critical rules with physical design, IP, and foundry teams
r: PDK readiness dashboard. An outstanding exception request is a readiness gap, and it belongs on the dashboard with a date.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. Rule dispositions become flow settings—what the tools are told to enforce and what they are told to allow.
pu: Read the design rule manual as a constraint on this design rather than as a document—identify which restricted rules bite, dispose of every recommended rule, and get the exceptions requested early.
Restricted and recommended rules are where a node's real density lives. A design that adopts every recommended rule is safe and large; one that ignores them is dense and fails DFM.
en: DRM released for the selected node and flavor
Exception request process agreed with the foundry
ex: Restricted and recommended rules are identified and categorized
Product-specific rule exceptions and risks are documented
Implementation teams have a clear rule disposition for early design work
rk: Recommended rules treated as optional without yield assessment
Restricted rules discovered only during late DRC closure
Rule interpretation differing across design teams
Product-specific exceptions not aligned with the foundry
Rule changes not propagated after PDK updates
PDK-02.fn: Exception requests in step 5 run in parallel because the foundry's response time is measured in weeks. Submitting them at the end of the review rather than as each one is identified adds a month to the answer.

PDK-03.t: Standard Cell Library Selection and Qualification
s: Inventory available standard cell libraries and variants
Compare track height, Vt, density, timing, and leakage tradeoffs
Check support for multi-bit, isolation, level-shifter, retention, and power cells
Verify required .lib, LEF, GDS, and related views
Run representative implementation checks where needed
Select and release the qualified library set
r: Qualified library list with .lib / LEF / GDS views. The standard cell half of the deliverable; PDK-04 adds memory and PDK-07 adds IO.
PDK readiness dashboard. An unqualified library is a readiness gap that blocks synthesis, and it shows on the dashboard as one.
Signoff corner definition. The corners a library is characterized at bound the corners signoff can be run at.
pu: Choose the standard cell libraries the design will be built from and qualify them rather than assume them—track height, Vt menu, multi-bit flops, and the timing models every downstream tool will trust.
Library selection is a PPA decision disguised as a procurement one. Track height sets density and drive strength; the Vt menu sets leakage; multi-bit flops set clock power.
en: Library release available under the design agreement
PPA and clock power budget available from ARCH-06
ex: Required standard cell variants are selected and qualified
Timing, power, physical, and low-power views are complete for the intended flow
Library limitations and usage guidance are documented for synthesis and physical design
rk: Library selected on timing alone without power and density tradeoffs
Low-power or specialty cells missing from the qualified set
Physical and timing views not aligned to the same release
Library limitations discovered after synthesis or floorplanning begins
Different blocks using inconsistent library variants
PDK-03.fn: Step 4 is the step that earns the activity. Foundry timing models are qualified by the foundry against the foundry's test cases; checking them at this design's corners and slew ranges is what catches the model error before it becomes a silicon failure.

PDK-04.t: Memory Compiler Evaluation and Instance Planning
s: Collect memory requirements from architecture and block planning
Inventory available memory compilers and supported configurations
Map required depth, width, ports, voltage, and aspect ratio to compiler options
Generate representative memory instances and views
Review PPA, physical constraints, and operating limits
Identify unsupported instances and escalation needs
Release the planned memory instance set to downstream teams
r: Qualified library list. The memory half of the deliverable—instances with every view a downstream tool consumes.
Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The capability screen is where the gap first appears; PDK-05 quantifies it.
PDK readiness dashboard. Compiler access and instance availability are tracked readiness items in their own right.
pu: Get the memory compiler licensed, evaluate what it can produce, and generate the instances the design asked for—with every view a downstream tool needs.

On an inference accelerator the memory array is a large fraction of the die, and the compiler decides most of it. What the compiler can generate is a hard boundary on the architecture: a configuration outside its range is not a compiler setting, it is a custom design program in AMS-05 costing four months.
en: PDK version stable enough to generate against
ex: Required SRAM and register-file configurations are mapped to available compilers
Critical memory instances can be generated with complete implementation views
Compiler gaps that may require custom memory development are identified
rk: Architecture assumes memory configurations the compiler cannot generate
Aspect ratio and floorplan constraints ignored during instance selection
Compiler views incomplete for synthesis, STA, or physical design
Operating voltage or Vmin capability assumed without characterization
Unsupported instances discovered after block design begins
PDK-04.fn: Step 3 is the one with a schedule consequence. A capability gap found here opens the PDK-06 decision with fifteen weeks of runway; found at instance generation, it opens the same decision with three.

s: Select representative and critical compiled memory instances
Collect timing, power, leakage, area, and Vmin data
Compare each instance against block-level budgets
Evaluate sensitivity to size, aspect ratio, Vt, and operating conditions
Identify instances that cannot meet the required budget
Review results with architecture, PDK, and AMS teams
r: Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The gap analysis half—PDK-06 adds the decision that follows from it.
Qualified library list. An instance that fails characterization does not belong on the qualified list, whatever the compiler says.
pu: Measure what the generated instances deliver—density, Vmin, access time, leakage—and set it against the budget each block was allocated.

This is the activity that decides whether the custom memory path opens. The compiler produces an instance that meets the specification; the question here is whether it meets the budget, and the answer is frequently no by a margin large enough to matter but small enough to be argued about.
en: Instances generated and released by PDK-04
ex: Critical memory instances are characterized against block PPA targets
Timing, density, Vmin, and leakage gaps are quantified
Instances requiring custom optimization are clearly identified
rk: Memory PPA assessed only at nominal conditions
Compiler marketing data used without instance-level characterization
Vmin gaps ignored until low-power validation
Area and aspect-ratio impact separated from timing analysis
Custom-memory need identified too late for the program schedule
PDK-05.fn: The gap analysis is quantified rather than described on purpose. "The compiler misses the budget" starts an argument; "the L2 array misses its density budget by 14%, which is 3.1 mm² of die" starts a decision.

s: Review memory gaps that cannot be closed with standard compiler options
Estimate achievable PPA benefit from custom or pushed-rule development
Assess design, verification, foundry, and schedule effort
Confirm pushed-rule feasibility and approval path with the foundry
Select standard, custom, or pushed-rule disposition for each instance
Integrate approved custom-memory work into AMS and program schedules
r: Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The decision half of the deliverable, and the record downstream stages will point at.
PDK readiness dashboard. An undecided memory gap is the most consequential open item the dashboard can carry—it holds both library closure and the AMS plan.
pu: Decide what to do about the memory shortfall—push rules, build a custom array, or change the architecture—and hand the chosen scope to AMS with a schedule attached.
This is a gate, not a study. The compiler instance missed the budget; the options each cost something different and one of them has to be taken.
en: AMS window and capacity known from the program plan
ex: Each unsupported or underperforming memory instance has a clear disposition
Custom-memory benefit and schedule impact are quantified
Required foundry approvals and development ownership are defined
rk: Custom memory selected without a quantified product benefit
Foundry pushed-rule approval assumed rather than confirmed
Verification and characterization effort omitted from the estimate
Custom-memory schedule not integrated with RTL and physical design needs
Standard compiler limitations accepted without exploring lower-risk alternatives
PDK-06.fn: Step 4 runs in parallel and can veto an option outright. A pushed-rule array the foundry will not approve is not an option, and finding that after the decision is taken costs the whole custom window.

PDK-07.t: I/O, ESD, and Latch-Up Library Qualification
s: Map interface and voltage requirements to available I/O cells
Review ESD and latch-up protection options and limits
Check package, bump, placement, and power-domain compatibility
Verify required logical, timing, LEF, GDS, CDL, and reliability views
Resolve unsupported interfaces or protection gaps
Release the qualified I/O, ESD, and latch-up library set
p: Qualified I/O and protection library list
r: Qualified library list. The IO and ESD half of the deliverable—the cells at the die edge, qualified rather than assumed.
Signoff corner definition. ESD and latch-up verification conditions are part of what signoff has to run, and they are defined here.
pu: Qualify the IO, ESD and latch-up collateral—the library that sits at the die edge and decides whether the part survives handling, and whether its interfaces meet their electrical specifications.

IO qualification is unglamorous and it is where parts die. An ESD strategy chosen late constrains the pad ring after the bump map is fixed; a latch-up rule missed produces a part that fails qualification for reasons no functional test would ever find.
en: Pad ring and bump plan drafted in ARCH-08
Foundry IO library and ESD rules released
ex: Required I/O voltage and interface combinations are supported
ESD and latch-up structures are qualified for the intended product use
Implementation views and placement constraints are ready for physical design
rk: I/O voltage support assumed from nominal library descriptions
ESD requirements checked independently of package and bump architecture
Latch-up constraints discovered during late physical verification
Required implementation or reliability views missing at integration
I/O placement constraints not reflected in early floorplanning
PDK-07.fn: The ESD strategy in step 3 has to precede pad ring layout, which in turn precedes the bump map freeze in ARCH-08. Late ESD is a pad ring change, and a pad ring change is a bump map change.

s: Define the required EDA tool chain and use cases
Review foundry-supported versions and required patches
Install and configure candidate tool versions with the target PDK
Run representative synthesis, P&R, STA, PV, extraction, and EM/IR tests
Resolve compatibility, runtime, and result-correlation issues
Freeze and release the approved tool-version matrix
p: Qualified EDA tool and version baseline
r: EDA tool and version matrix (qualified and frozen). The deliverable the freeze is the part that matters.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. The flow is written against specific tool versions; the guide and the matrix are read together.
Compute and license capacity plan. Which tools and how many concurrent seats is what the license plan is built from.
pu: Decide which tool at which version each flow step runs on, qualify that combination on the node, and freeze it—so that a result from one team means the same thing as a result from another.

Tool versions are a correctness question, not an IT one. A node this advanced needs certified versions for extraction, timing and physical verification, and mixing versions across teams produces disagreements that consume weeks before anyone suspects the tools rather than the design.
ex: Required EDA tools and versions are qualified for the selected PDK
Critical cross-tool handoffs and signoff interfaces are validated
Approved tool versions and known limitations are documented for the program
rk: Foundry-supported versions assumed to work in the internal flow without testing
Different implementation stages using incompatible tool versions
Required patches or hotfixes not captured in the release baseline
Cross-tool database and constraint handoffs not validated
Tool upgrades introduced during closure without regression
PDK-08.fn: Step 6 catches what per-tool qualification cannot. Each tool can be certified on the node and still disagree with the next one about a database format or a parasitic convention, and only a cross-tool check finds it.

PDK-09.t: Reference Flow Bring-Up and Methodology Development
s: Bring up the foundry reference flow in the internal environment
Validate major tool stages, inputs, outputs, and handoffs
Adapt scripts and settings to program-specific methodology
Add checks, automation, reporting, and reproducibility requirements
Run end-to-end regression on a representative design
Document methodology, known limitations, and usage guidance
Release the internal reference flow to design teams
r: Internal reference flow and methodology guide. The deliverable the pilot is what makes it credible.
Golden environment release notes. The environment in PDK-13 packages this flow; the two are released together.
PDK readiness dashboard. Flow readiness is tracked alongside library and deck readiness—a design cannot start on any one of them alone.
pu: Take the foundry's reference flow, adapt it into a methodology this design can run, and prove it on a representative block before the whole team depends on it.
A reference flow is a starting point written for a generic design. This one has hierarchical partitions, hard macros, multiple power domains and a memory subsystem the reference never contemplated.
en: Decks under version control from PDK-10
ex: The reference design runs through the required implementation and signoff stages
Program-specific flow changes are documented and regression-tested
Internal teams have a repeatable methodology and baseline scripts
rk: Foundry reference scripts used without understanding their assumptions
Flow customized without retaining regression coverage
Different teams creating separate local versions of the methodology
Signoff requirements added only after implementation begins
Known tool or PDK limitations omitted from the methodology guide
PDK-09.fn: Three of the ten weeks are the pilot, and it is the step under most pressure to be skipped. A flow that has never been run end to end on a real block is a flow whose first user is doing the debugging on the critical path.

PDK-10.t: Signoff Deck and QRC Version Control
s: Inventory required signoff decks and technology files
Map each deck to its PDK and tool compatibility requirements
Baseline the approved DRC, LVS, extraction, and QRC versions
Regression-test major deck updates on representative designs
Assess the impact of rule or extraction changes on active designs
Release approved updates with version history and usage notes
r: Internal reference flow and methodology guide. A flow is only reproducible if the decks it calls are versioned; the guide names the versions.
Golden environment release notes. The environment pins deck versions, and this activity is what makes pinning possible.
PDK readiness dashboard. Deck currency and validation status are readiness items on the dashboard.
pu: Put every rule deck, extraction file and verification runset under version control, validate them on known-good structures, and make deck changes a notified event rather than a surprise.
