Decks are the quiet dependency. A DRC runset revision that arrives without notice changes what passes verification, and if two teams are running different revisions the disagreement looks like a layout problem.
en: Foundry decks released under the design agreement
PDK version tracking established by PDK-01
ex: All signoff decks are tied to approved versions and PDK releases
Deck updates are regression-tested before program adoption
Design and signoff teams use the same controlled deck baseline
rk: Different teams using different signoff deck versions
Deck updates adopted without regression
QRC or extraction changes not propagated into timing and EM/IR flows
Foundry release notes not reviewed for design impact
Signoff results reported without recording the deck version
PDK-10.fn: Validation on known-good structures in step 4 is what makes a deck trustworthy. A runset that has never been tested against a layout with a known answer will report both false positives and, far worse, false negatives.

s: Collect product operating conditions and foundry signoff guidance
Define candidate PVT and RC corner combinations
Select OCV, AOCV, or POCV methodology and required derates
Evaluate coverage, pessimism, and runtime tradeoffs
Align the signoff methodology with the foundry and STA teams
Release the approved corner and derate definition
r: Signoff corner definition agreed with foundry. The deliverable "agreed" is the operative word—an internal corner set has no standing.
Compute and license capacity plan. Corner count multiplied by modes is the single largest driver of signoff compute demand.
pu: Agree with the foundry exactly which corners and derates signoff will be run at—PVT combinations, modes, and the OCV, AOCV or POCV methodology—and write it down before anyone closes timing against it.

A corner set is a contract. Sign off at corners the foundry does not recognize and the foundry will not accept the result; sign off at more corners than necessary and every closure iteration costs runtime and license capacity the program has not budgeted for.
en: Operating conditions and DVFS points defined by ARCH-05
Library characterization corners known from PDK-03
ex: Required functional and signoff PVT corners are defined
OCV and derate methodology is agreed with implementation and foundry teams
The corner set is usable consistently across synthesis, STA, and signoff
rk: Signoff corners defined after timing closure has started
Too few corners missing product operating conditions
Too many corners added without considering closure and runtime impact
Derates inconsistent between synthesis, implementation, and signoff
Foundry variation guidance interpreted differently across teams
PDK-11.fn: Step 6 exists because corner count multiplies. Nine corners across three modes is twenty-seven signoff runs per iteration, and the compute plan in PDK-12 is sized against whatever number this activity settles on.

PDK-12.t: Compute, License, and Storage Capacity Planning
s: Estimate compute demand by tool, stage, and program phase
Estimate EDA license demand during peak concurrent usage
Estimate working, checkpoint, regression, and archive storage needs
Compare demand against available infrastructure
Define procurement, reservation, or scheduling actions for gaps
Align infrastructure readiness with the program schedule
p: Compute, license, and storage capacity plan
r: Compute and license capacity plan. The deliverable its value is that it is dated against lead times.
EDA tool and version matrix. Which tools are pooled and at what seat count is decided against the matrix.
pu: Model what the program will need in compute, EDA licences and storage across its peak, and procure it against a lead time rather than discovering it during timing closure.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Flow steps and runtimes known from PDK-09
Corner and mode count settled by PDK-11
ex: Peak compute, license, and storage demand is estimated by program phase
Capacity gaps are identified with procurement or allocation actions
Infrastructure is available before the corresponding design workload begins
rk: Capacity estimated from average rather than peak concurrent usage
License demand planned independently from compute capacity
Storage growth underestimated for iterative physical design databases
Infrastructure procurement started after closure workloads begin
Shared farm commitments from other programs ignored
PDK-12.fn: The demand model is built per flow step rather than per team because that is how contention actually happens: three teams running the same tool at the same point in the schedule contend for one license pool, whatever the org chart says.

PDK-13.t: Golden Design Environment Release and Regression
s: Assemble the approved PDK, libraries, tools, decks, and flow configuration
Define release manifests, paths, environment variables, and access controls
Run end-to-end regression on representative designs
Resolve version, compatibility, and reproducibility issues
Document release notes, known limitations, and change history
Release the qualified environment to program teams
Maintain regression and controlled updates through tapeout
r: Golden environment release notes. This activity is the deliverable—the environment itself, with what is in it and what is known to be wrong with it.
PDK readiness dashboard. The dashboard closes when the environment releases; until then every readiness item is still individually tracked.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. The guide describes the flow; this environment is the flow, packaged and versioned.
pu: Package everything this stage produced into one environment every team runs from—tools, decks, libraries, scripts—prove it with a regression, and release it with known issues stated.

Enablement only becomes real when it is a single thing an engineer can load. Until then the program has a qualified library here, a validated deck there and a flow in someone's home directory, and every new engineer assembles a slightly different version of the design environment.
en: Decks validated and under version control
ex: PDK, libraries, tools, decks, and methodology are released as one controlled environment
End-to-end regression passes on representative designs
Version changes require documented impact assessment and release control
rk: Tools, libraries, and decks released independently without a common baseline
Environment updates made without regression
Local user overrides creating non-reproducible results
Known limitations not included in release notes
Golden environment changed during closure without impact review
PDK-13.fn: Step 5 is what makes the release trustworthy. If the golden environment produces different results from the PDK-09 pilot on the same block, something in the packaging changed the answer, and finding that after release means everyone's results are suspect.

s: Identify all IP blocks required by the architecture
Define functional and performance requirements for each IP
Define interface, clock, reset, power, and configuration requirements
Define process-node, PVT, reliability, and qualification requirements
Define required views, models, documentation, and delivery dates
Review and baseline the IP requirement set
r: IP bill of materials with make / buy / reuse decision per block. The bill half of the deliverable; IPR-03 adds the decision against each line.
IP readiness report. Readiness is assessed per line of this bill, so the bill's completeness bounds the report's.
pu: Decompose the product into the IP it needs—every block, with its specification, its interfaces and the requirement it traces back to—and publish it as a bill of materials the program can be held to.

An IP-BOM derived from the last program's list is the most common way to arrive at the wrong one. What this product needs follows from its requirements and its architecture, and the blocks that differ from last time are exactly the ones with the longest lead times.
en: Product requirements available at v0.9 from DEF-01
Architecture direction known well enough to name blocks
ex: Every required IP block has a defined requirement set
Requirements include technical, process-node, deliverable, and schedule needs
IP requirements are ready for internal reuse and vendor evaluation
rk: IP requirements written only as block names or protocol names
Architecture assumptions not translated into measurable IP requirements
Required implementation or verification views omitted
Process-node and qualification requirements added after vendor selection
Delivery dates not tied to RTL and physical-design integration needs
IPR-01.fn: Step 6's traceability check is what separates a list from a bill of materials. An IP that traces to no requirement is an IP nobody needs; a requirement that traces to no IP is a gap nobody has staffed.

s: Search the internal inventory against the required IP list
Confirm functional and interface fit for each candidate
Check node, process-option, library, and tool compatibility
Review available views, documentation, silicon history, and known issues
Classify each candidate as reusable, reusable with work, or not reusable
r: IP bill of materials. Reuse classification is one of the three answers the make / buy / reuse column can take, and it is decided here.
IP readiness report. An internal block on the wrong node is exactly as unready as an external one, and belongs in the same report.
pu: Audit what the organization already owns and can reuse on this node—not what it owns in general, which is a different and much longer list.

Reuse is where the schedule is won, and it is also where optimism concentrates. A block proven on the previous node is not available on this one until it has been ported, re-characterized and re-verified, and that work is a project with a duration.
en: Bill of materials available from IPR-01
Node selected so availability can be assessed
ex: Every required IP has been checked against the internal inventory
Reuse candidates are assessed for node, view, quality, and support readiness
Reuse gaps are identified before make / buy decisions
rk: IP counted as reusable because its name and function match
Prior-node IP assumed portable without checking technology dependencies
Known issues and silicon history excluded from the assessment
Missing views discovered only during integration
Internal ownership or support capacity not confirmed
IPR-02.fn: Step 4 asks who still maintains each block, and the answer is often nobody. An unmaintained block is technically reusable and practically a rebuild, because the first bug found has no owner.

s: Define common make / buy / reuse evaluation criteria
Assess internal reuse options and required modification effort
Estimate in-house development effort, schedule, and risk
Assess external sourcing availability, cost, maturity, and schedule
Compare options against program priorities and dependencies
Select and record the sourcing path for each IP
r: IP bill of materials with make / buy / reuse decision per block. The decision half of the deliverable, with the rejected options priced rather than forgotten.
IP risk register. Every buy decision creates a vendor dependency and every make decision creates a capacity dependency; both belong on the register.
pu: Take each line of the bill and decide, with a reason, whether it is made, bought or reused—and record what the rejected options would have cost.
Make/buy is a schedule decision more than a cost one. Building a PHY internally is cheaper on paper and costs nine months in AMS-03; buying it costs a license and a vendor dependency.
en: Bill of materials complete from IPR-01
AMS capacity known from the program plan
ex: Every required IP has a make, buy, or reuse disposition
Technical, schedule, cost, and maturity tradeoffs are compared consistently
Decisions and exceptions are recorded with owners
rk: Decision based on license price alone
Internal development effort treated as zero-cost capacity
Vendor maturity assumed from roadmap status
Integration and verification effort omitted from the comparison
Decision made without a fallback for schedule-critical IP
IPR-03.fn: Step 3 is the check that changes answers. A make decision assumes engineers who are also assigned to the custom SRAM and the PLL; capacity, not capability, is what usually decides.

s: Prepare the RFI / RFQ package from the approved IP requirements
Identify qualified candidate vendors
Review technical compliance against the requirement set
Evaluate node readiness, deliverables, support, and delivery schedule
Compare commercial terms and total integration impact
Resolve critical gaps through vendor clarification or technical review
Select the preferred vendor and record the rationale
r: Vendor evaluation matrix and selection record. The deliverable the matrix is what a later dispute is settled against.
Executed licences and POs. Selection precedes negotiation; IPR-07 contracts with whoever this activity chose.
IP readiness report. Vendor track record is part of an IP's maturity rating, not separate from it.
pu: Run a real evaluation of the vendors behind every buy decision—technical capability, deliverable quality, support model and track record—rather than choosing from a datasheet.

A PHY vendor is a nine-month dependency. What matters is less the block's peak specification than whether the deliverables arrive complete, whether the support engineer answers, and whether the last three customers taped out on schedule.
en: Specification stubs detailed enough to evaluate against
NDAs in place with candidate vendors
ex: Candidate vendors are evaluated against the same requirement set
Technical, delivery, support, and commercial gaps are explicitly identified
Preferred vendor is selected with documented rationale and backup options where needed
rk: Vendors compared using different requirement baselines
Roadmap claims treated as committed deliverables
Technical evaluation separated from delivery and support capability
Missing views or models discovered after purchase
Selection completed without a credible alternative for critical IP
IPR-04.fn: Step 4 is the step most often skipped and the one that predicts the outcome best. A vendor's last three customers know whether the deliverables arrived complete and on time, and they will usually say.

IPR-05.t: IP Silicon-Proven and Node Readiness Assessment
s: Define the evidence required to claim silicon-proven status
Collect silicon, test-chip, production, and qualification evidence
Compare proven configuration against the program's node and process options
Review known silicon issues, errata, and field history
Assess remaining technical and schedule risk
Define validation actions for IP not proven on the exact configuration
Record the readiness status for each selected IP
r: IP readiness report—silicon-proven status and maturity level per IP. The deliverable it is the one that replaces a claim with a fact.
IP risk register. Every block below the maturity bar is a risk with a name, an owner and a mitigation.
IP delivery schedule. An unproven block needs a hardening window, and the window has to be in the schedule.
pu: Establish, for each bought and reused block, whether it has run in silicon on this node and this process option—and if not, what it would take to get it there.

"Silicon-proven" is the most abused phrase in IP procurement. It can mean proven on a different node, on a different process option, at a different speed grade, or in a test chip that was never characterized.
en: Node and process option fixed by TECH-02
Vendor NDAs allow access to characterization data
ex: Silicon-proven status is defined against the exact node and process configuration
Evidence and remaining gaps are recorded for every critical IP
Unproven IP has a named validation or contingency plan
rk: Silicon proven accepted without defining what was actually proven
Evidence from a different node or process option treated as equivalent
Errata and production history excluded from the assessment
Unproven IP allowed onto the critical path without mitigation
Vendor claims accepted without supporting evidence
IPR-05.fn: Step 1 is not bureaucracy. Without an agreed evidence standard, every vendor's claim is accepted at its own definition, and the readiness report becomes a collection of adjectives.

IPR-06.t: IP Deliverable and Integration Readiness Review
s: Define the required deliverables by IP type and integration flow
Map each deliverable to its downstream consumer and required date
Review vendor or internal delivery manifests against the checklist
Validate format, version, and tool compatibility for critical views
Identify missing collateral and required corrective actions
Agree delivery content and dates with the IP owner or vendor
Track integration readiness through delivery
r: IP deliverable acceptance checklist. The deliverable its value is entirely in being agreed before the PO rather than after the delivery.
Executed licences and POs. The checklist becomes a contractual schedule, which is the only form in which it is enforceable.
pu: Define exactly what a complete IP delivery contains—every view, model, testbench and document—and get that list agreed before it becomes a contractual obligation.

Most IP delivery disputes are not about whether the block works; they are about whether a delivery counted as a delivery. A block that arrives without multi-corner timing views or without its verification collateral has arrived in a form the program cannot integrate, and the argument that follows is unwinnable if the checklist was never agreed.
en: Signoff corner intent known from PDK-11
ex: Every IP has an agreed deliverable checklist
Required views and models are mapped to the teams and milestones that consume them
Missing or late collateral has an owner and recovery date
rk: RTL or GDS delivery treated as complete IP delivery
Physical, timing, power, or verification views omitted from the checklist
Deliverable formats not checked against the program tool versions
Documentation and integration support treated as optional
Missing collateral discovered only when the consuming team starts work
IPR-06.fn: Step 5 turns the checklist into something enforceable. A list of expected files is a wish; an acceptance procedure that says what is checked, by whom, and what happens when it fails is a term.

s: Define required license scope, usage rights, and support terms
Review vendor quotation and commercial structure
Negotiate license, support, liability, and delivery terms
Resolve legal, procurement, finance, and security requirements
Confirm final deliverable scope and committed dates
Issue the purchase order or equivalent authorization
Complete license execution and access setup
Record commercial obligations and renewal or support milestones
r: Executed licences and POs with committed delivery dates. The deliverable the committed date is the part the schedule depends on.
IP delivery schedule. Committed dates are what IPR-09 aligns against the integration windows.
IP deliverable acceptance checklist. The checklist only has force once it is attached to an executed agreement.
pu: Turn selections into executed licences and purchase orders with committed delivery dates, including the deliverable checklist as a contractual schedule.

Twelve weeks for 5 M/M—this is the stage's longest activity and among its smallest in effort, because the elapsed time belongs to two legal departments and a procurement process. It is on the critical path regardless: nothing arrives until it executes, and RTL-03 has integration windows that assume it did.
ex: Required IP usage rights and license scope are executed
Purchase order or equivalent commercial commitment is in place
Delivery and support dates are contractually aligned with program needs
rk: Technical selection completed without budget or procurement alignment
License scope too narrow for intended product or derivative use
Delivery dates stated as targets rather than contractual commitments
Support and maintenance terms omitted from negotiation
PO or access setup started after the integration window opens
IPR-07.fn: Step 3 is the one the program cares about and the one commercial negotiation treats as secondary. A license with excellent terms and no committed delivery date has bought a block that arrives when the vendor is ready.

s: Identify IP requiring porting, re-characterization, or hardening
Define technology and implementation deltas from the source IP
Define design, characterization, verification, and signoff work
Assign ownership and estimate engineering effort
Build the development and validation schedule
Review readiness against the required integration date
r: IP readiness report. A block's maturity level is only actionable alongside the plan that raises it, and this activity supplies the plan.
IP delivery schedule. A hardening window is part of the delivery date, and omitting it produces a schedule that cannot hold.
pu: For every block that is not proven on this node, scope the work that gets it there—porting, hardening, re-characterization, re-verification—and put it in the schedule as a project with an owner.

Unproven IP does not become proven by being licensed. Someone ports it, re-characterizes it at the program's corners and re-verifies it, and that someone is either the vendor on a schedule the program does not control, or the program's own engineers who are already committed elsewhere.
en: AMS capacity known from the program plan
Integration windows known from RTL and PD planning
ex: Porting or hardening scope is defined for every affected IP
Required design, characterization, verification, and signoff work is scheduled
Delivery dates are aligned with downstream integration windows
rk: Porting treated as a simple process-node conversion
Characterization and signoff effort omitted from the plan
Source-IP assumptions incompatible with the target design environment
Foundry or vendor dependencies not included in the schedule
Ported IP delivered after the block integration window
IPR-08.fn: Step 3 decides who absorbs the risk. Vendor-executed hardening is on a schedule the program cannot influence; internally executed hardening competes with AMS-03 for the same analog engineers. Both are real answers and neither is free.

IPR-09.t: IP Delivery and Integration Schedule Alignment
s: Collect need-by dates from all downstream integration teams
Map required IP views and maturity levels to each need-by date
Overlay vendor, internal, and porting delivery commitments
Identify gaps between committed delivery and integration need
Define recovery, early-access, or staged-delivery actions
Baseline and track the IP schedule against program milestones
r: IP delivery schedule folded into the program plan. The deliverable "folded in" is the operative part—a separate IP schedule is one nobody tracks.
IP risk register. Every mismatch that cannot be closed becomes a tracked risk with a mitigation.
pu: Line up every IP delivery date against the window that needs it—RTL integration, synthesis, floorplan—and surface the mismatches while they can still be fixed.

An IP schedule is only meaningful against the design schedule. A PHY delivered in week 40 is early for RTL and late for the floorplan, because PD-02 needs the abstract long before RTL-03 needs the model.
en: Integration windows known from the program schedule
ex: Every required IP view has a need-by date and committed delivery date
Delivery dependencies are reflected in downstream team schedules
Schedule gaps have owners, recovery actions, and escalation dates
rk: Only the final IP delivery date tracked
Early RTL, model, LEF, or timing-view needs omitted
Vendor schedule not connected to the program critical path
Staged or preliminary releases used without maturity labels
Delivery slips not propagated to consuming teams
IPR-09.fn: Step 3 is where the useful detail lives. Vendors quote one date for a block; the design needs the LEF abstract for floorplan months before it needs the multi-corner .lib for signoff, and asking for the abstract early is often free.

IPR-10.t: IP Maturity Risk and Contingency Planning
s: Define common IP maturity and risk-rating criteria
Rate each critical IP for technical, maturity, delivery, and supplier risk
Identify IP whose failure can affect tapeout or launch
Evaluate second-source, internal, or architecture fallback options
Define mitigation actions, triggers, owners, and decision dates
r: IP risk register and contingency plan. The deliverable the triggers are what make it a plan rather than a list.
IP readiness report. Maturity and risk are read together—a mature block from a fragile vendor is not a low-risk line.
pu: Rate every IP line for maturity and supply risk, and decide where a contingency is worth having—a second source, an internal fallback, or an accepted exposure with a trigger.

Some risk here is unavoidable and pretending otherwise is what makes it dangerous. The point is not to eliminate single-vendor dependencies but to know which ones would stop the program, and to have decided in advance what would be done about each.
ex: Critical IP is rated using consistent maturity and schedule criteria
High-risk IP has a defined mitigation or contingency path
Fallback trigger conditions and latest decision dates are recorded
rk: Risk rating based only on vendor confidence
Schedule risk separated from technical maturity
Second source named without verifying node and deliverable readiness
Fallback decision delayed until the primary IP has already missed the integration window
High-risk IP not visible in the program-level risk register
IPR-10.fn: Step 5 defines triggers, not intentions. "We would build it internally if the vendor slipped" is worthless without the date at which that decision has to be taken to still be executable.

AMS-01.t: AMS IP Specification and Budget Definition
s: Identify all custom analog, mixed-signal, and memory blocks
Extract functional and electrical requirements for each block
Allocate power, area, performance, and noise budgets
Define interfaces, supplies, clocks, resets, and control requirements
Define PVT, reliability, and verification coverage
Review and baseline the AMS specifications and budgets
p: Approved AMS specification and budget baseline
r: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. This activity is the deliverable—the specifications every other AMS activity is executed and reviewed against.
Integration guide. The specification is what the integration guide's limitations are stated relative to.
pu: Turn each custom block from a name on the make list into a specification with budgets—jitter, BER, PSRR, area, power—that a circuit designer can start against and a reviewer can hold them to.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Custom memory scope handed over by PDK-06
Interface and clock architecture defined by ARCH-04 and ARCH-05
ex: Every AMS block has measurable electrical and PPA targets
Operating conditions, interfaces, and verification requirements are defined
Budgets are reviewed and accepted by architecture and integration teams
rk: AMS design started before measurable specifications are agreed
Power or area budgets allocated independently of system constraints
Interface and supply assumptions differ between AMS and digital teams
PVT and reliability requirements added after circuit design
Budget changes not propagated to architecture and integration teams
AMS-01.fn: Step 2 is the one that prevents the integration argument. A jitter budget divided explicitly between PLL, distribution and PHY gives each owner a number; an unallocated total gives each owner a reason to believe the problem is somewhere else.

s: Define the PLL / clock-generator architecture from the frequency plan
Select oscillator, divider, phase detector, charge-pump, and loop-filter implementation
Design and simulate the core loop at nominal conditions
Close frequency range, jitter, phase noise, and lock behavior across PVT
Analyze supply noise, reference noise, and spur sensitivity
Run Monte Carlo and mismatch verification
Define calibration, trim, test, and debug features
Complete layout-aware and extracted verification
Generate behavioral and integration models
Release the closed PLL / clock-generator macro
r: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The PLL review package is the largest single item in the set.
Characterization reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. Jitter across PVT is the headline number in the report.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The PLL is one of the macros AMS-15 abstracts and hands to physical design.
pu: Design the clock generation the whole chip runs on—PLLs, their loop dynamics, their supply immunity and their jitter—and close them across process, voltage and temperature.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: Jitter and PSRR budgets accepted in AMS-01
Clock architecture and DVFS points fixed by ARCH-05
Device models available from the tracked PDK
ex: Frequency, jitter, lock time, and operating-range targets are met across required corners
Variation and supply-noise sensitivity are verified
Required integration models and physical views are released
rk: PLL architecture selected without a complete frequency and jitter budget
Jitter verified only at nominal supply conditions
Supply coupling and reference spurs assessed too late
Calibration range insufficient for PVT and mismatch
Behavioral model not correlated to transistor-level behavior
AMS-02.fn: Step 8 is where the schedule risk lives. Post-layout jitter is routinely worse than pre-layout by more than the margin, and the fix is a layout change that takes the six weeks of step 7 again.

s: Define the target channel, data rate, BER, jitter, and compliance requirements
Select the PHY architecture or establish the vendor-hardening baseline
Develop or adapt TX, RX, clocking, equalization, and calibration circuits
Integrate package and channel models into link analysis
Verify eye, jitter, BER, and equalization margin across PVT
Run variation and calibration-range analysis
Close power, area, bump, and floorplan constraints
Verify test, loopback, training, and debug features
Complete extracted or vendor-hardening signoff
Release integration models, views, and constraints
r: Characterization reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. The PHY's eye and BER characterization is the report's most consequential section.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The PHY macros are the largest and most constrained of the set.
Integration guide with known limitations and errata. PHY limitations—training corner cases, unsupported modes—are what integration most needs stated.
pu: Deliver the high-speed interfaces—PCIe or CXL, die-to-die, HBM PHY—either designed from scratch or hardened from a vendor's deliverable onto this node and this flavor sheet.

At thirty-four weeks and sixty M/M this is the largest single activity in the entire template, and it is the one most likely to decide the tapeout date. Even a bought PHY is not free: hardening, integration, and closing its analog margins on this process option is a project, and the vendor's schedule for it is not the program's.
en: Vendor licences executed where PHYs are bought
Bump pitch and PHY placement known from ARCH-08
ex: PHY performance is verified against the target channel and package
PVT, jitter, equalization, and calibration margins are demonstrated
Required controller, physical, and verification interfaces are ready for integration
rk: PHY evaluated without the actual package and channel assumptions
Vendor hardening treated as integration-only work
Equalization and calibration range verified only at nominal conditions
Bump and floorplan constraints discovered after macro placement
Compliance and test features added after circuit closure
AMS-03.fn: Step 7 is eight weeks of layout because lane pitch is a floorplan constraint as much as a circuit one—the PHY has to fit the bump pitch ARCH-08 defined, and a pitch mismatch found here forces a change at the die edge.

s: Define rail, load, accuracy, noise, transient, and startup requirements
Select LDO, reference, monitor, and regulator architectures
Design the core regulation and reference circuits
Verify DC accuracy, PSRR, noise, stability, and transient response
Verify startup, shutdown, sequencing, and fault behavior
Run PVT and Monte Carlo verification
Define trim, test, monitor, and debug features
Release qualified macros and integration views
r: Characterization reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. Bandgap drift and LDO PSRR across corners belong in the same report as the PLL and PHY results.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. Power management cells are delivered as macros like any other analog block.
Reliability report. LDO pass devices and bandgaps carry EM and aging exposure that belongs in the reliability assessment.
pu: Build the power management cells everything else depends on—LDOs, bandgap references, bias generation—quietly and correctly, because every other block's specification assumes them.

These blocks are small, unglamorous and load-bearing. A bandgap that drifts moves every analog threshold on the die; an LDO with insufficient PSRR at the switching frequency turns the PLL's careful jitter budget into noise.
en: PSRR and load requirements available from AMS-01
ex: Regulation, reference accuracy, stability, startup, and transient targets are met across PVT
Load and package interactions are included in verification
Control, trim, test, and integration requirements are released
rk: LDO stability checked without realistic load and package parasitics
Reference accuracy verified without mismatch and temperature spread
Startup and sequencing behavior left to top-level integration
Noise coupling to sensitive blocks not budgeted
Trim range defined without production-test capability
AMS-04.fn: Step 8 is easy to leave until later and expensive to. A trim procedure that test engineering only sees at TEST-05 becomes a test-time cost, and a bandgap with no defined trim is a part with a distribution nobody can tighten.

s: Define capacity, width, ports, bandwidth, Vmin, and PPA targets
Evaluate available bitcell and pushed-rule options
Define row, column, banking, and mux organization
Define wordline, bitline, precharge, sensing, and write architecture
Define replica, tracking, and internal timing strategy
Estimate area, delay, power, and margin for candidate organizations
Select the preferred custom SRAM architecture
Hand off architecture constraints to circuit and layout design
r: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The specification half of the deliverable; AMS-08 supplies the yield half.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The array's architecture review is one of the stage's formal gates.
pu: Architect the custom SRAM instance the compiler could not deliver—bitcell choice, array organization, sense amplifier topology and replica timing—against the density and Vmin the block budget demands.

This activity exists only because PDK-06 opened it. That decision came with a quantified gap and a fixed window, and the architecture chosen here determines whether the rest of the custom memory chain can close inside it.
en: Custom instance decision taken by PDK-06 with a quantified gap
ex: Bitcell and array organization are selected against measurable PPA and Vmin targets
Banking, ports, sensing, and timing architecture are defined
Architecture is ready for circuit, assist, layout, and statistical-margin development
rk: Bitcell selected before array-level PPA is evaluated
Array organization optimized for area without bandwidth and timing impact
Replica timing copied from a prior node without revalidation
Pushed-rule benefit assumed before foundry approval
Floorplan aspect ratio considered after architecture freeze
AMS-05.fn: Step 7 closes the loop with PDK-05. If the projected density still misses the budget, the answer is to reopen the architecture now rather than to discover it after sixteen weeks of layout in AMS-07.

s: Identify the dominant read and write Vmin limitations
Evaluate candidate assist techniques for the selected bitcell and array
Design wordline, bitline, supply, or timing assist circuits as required
Optimize assist strength and timing across PVT
Run statistical read, write, and hold margin analysis
Verify reliability, disturb, and recovery behavior
Release the selected assist scheme and control requirements
r: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The Vmin the instance is specified at is the Vmin with assist enabled, and this activity produces it.
Characterization reports. Assist-enabled Vmin across corners is one of the report's core tables.
pu: Design the assist circuits that buy Vmin—wordline boost, negative bitline, VDD collapse—and decide how much of each the array needs.

Assist is what makes an aggressive array workable, and it is not free: each technique costs area, power and complexity, and some of them interact badly. The design question is not which assist is best but which combination reaches the Vmin target at the least cost, verified statistically rather than at nominal.
en: Vmin target set from the operating points in ARCH-05
ex: Assist benefit is quantified for read and write Vmin
Assist range is robust across PVT and statistical variation
Reliability, disturb, timing, and recovery constraints are satisfied
rk: Assist strength optimized at nominal conditions only
Read improvement traded for unrecognized hold or disturb risk
Boosted or negative voltages exceed device reliability limits
Assist supply-generation cost excluded from the PPA tradeoff
Statistical benefit claimed without array-level yield analysis
AMS-06.fn: Steps 3 and 4 run in parallel and step 2 decides whether both are needed. Write assist and read assist pull in opposite directions on the cell, and enabling both without studying the interaction can leave Vmin worse than either alone.

AMS-07.t: Custom SRAM Layout and Foundry Rule Closure
s: Define array floorplan, tiling, power, and pin architecture
Implement bitcell tiling and array routing
Implement periphery with matching and critical-parasitic constraints
Integrate assist, replica, and timing circuits
Run DRC, LVS, antenna, density, and manufacturability checks
Review pushed-rule violations and exceptions with the foundry
Close parasitic-driven layout issues against circuit targets
Release the physically verified macro layout
r: Per-macro DRC / LVS clean signoff, pushed rules approved by foundry. The deliverable the approval is the half that cannot be produced internally.
Custom SRAM instance specification. The achieved density is a layout result, and it is what the specification finally states.
pu: Lay out the custom array at pushed rules, and get the foundry to approve it—because a layout the foundry will not sign is a layout that cannot tape out.
Sixteen weeks of layout is what the density recovery costs. Pushed rules are the mechanism, and they carry an approval process with its own duration and its own possibility of refusal.
en: Foundry pushed-rule approval path agreed in PDK-06
ex: Array and periphery layout meet area and electrical constraints
DRC, LVS, antenna, density, and required reliability checks are clean
All pushed-rule usage has documented foundry approval
rk: Pushed-rule usage assumed acceptable without written foundry approval
Array compaction creates unmodeled parasitic or matching loss
Periphery layout optimized separately from replica timing
Density and fill impact evaluated after electrical closure
Foundry rule changes not propagated into the custom layout
AMS-07.fn: Step 5 runs in parallel out of necessity rather than choice. Waiting for approval before laying out would not fit the window, so the array is laid out against rules that may still be refused—which is why step 1's pre-alignment matters more than its two weeks suggest.

AMS-08.t: SRAM Statistical Margin and Yield Analysis
s: Define target failure probability and array-level yield requirement
Identify dominant read, write, and hold failure mechanisms
Build the required Monte Carlo or importance-sampling methodology
Characterize bitcell and critical periphery variation
Project read, write, and hold Vmin distributions to target array size
Evaluate assist and design sensitivity on yield
Set the signoff margin and report confidence
p: SRAM statistical margin and yield report
r: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The yield half of the deliverable, and the half the cost model depends on.
Characterization reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. The statistical results sit alongside the corner results, and the two say different things.
pu: Prove the array works at the tail of the distribution rather than at nominal—sigma-Vmin, bitcell variation, sense amplifier offset—using importance sampling because brute-force Monte Carlo cannot reach six sigma.

A memory array of this size fails at the tail by definition: with hundreds of millions of cells, the six-sigma cell is not a hypothetical, it is present in every part. Nominal simulation says nothing about it, and the yield the cost model assumed depends entirely on where that tail sits.
en: Array architecture and assist circuits complete
Foundry variation models and silicon data accessible
ex: Read, write, and hold failure distributions are quantified
Array-size impact is included in the yield projection
Vmin and margin targets are supported by statistically credible analysis
rk: Typical Monte Carlo used to estimate rare array failures
Cell-level sigma quoted without scaling to array size
Peripheral variation excluded from Vmin analysis
Importance-sampling model not validated against direct simulation
Yield margin reported without a confidence statement
AMS-08.fn: Step 2 is the step that makes the rest meaningful. A variation model that has not been validated against silicon produces a six-sigma number with an unknown error, and the number is then used to justify a yield assumption in the cost model.

s: Define repair coverage and spare-resource targets
Select row, column, or hybrid redundancy architecture
Define repair address encoding and storage format
Integrate memory repair controls with MBIST / BISR
Verify repair loading, application, and boot sequencing
Run fault-injection scenarios through detection and repair
r: Custom SRAM instance specification. Repairable and unrepairable yield are different numbers, and the specification has to state which it quotes.
Integration guide. The repair interface is one of the integration points most likely to be misunderstood, and it belongs in the guide.
pu: Build redundancy and repair into the array and make it match the BISR architecture DFT is designing—spare rows and columns, fuse allocation, repair algorithm, and the interface between them.
Redundancy is worth several points of yield and only if the two halves agree. The array provides spares and a repair interface; DFT-03 provides the BIST engine and the repair analysis.
en: BISR architecture intent available from DFT-03
ex: Spare row and column resources are defined from yield assumptions
Repair encoding and BISR interfaces are fully specified
Fault injection demonstrates detection, repair, and restored memory operation
rk: Spare resources selected without a yield model
Memory repair encoding differs from BISR assumptions
Fuse capacity checked after redundancy architecture is fixed
Repair sequence not verified across reset and power states
Fault injection proves detection but not restored operation
AMS-09.fn: Steps 3 and 5 are joint work with DFT-03 rather than handoffs. Both sides can specify a repair scheme that is internally consistent and mutually incompatible, and only writing them together prevents it.

AMS-10.t: Custom Memory Characterization and View Generation
s: Define the required characterization corners, arcs, and view set
Run extracted timing and power characterization
Generate Liberty and functional simulation models
Generate LEF, GDS, CDL / SPICE, and required physical views
Generate test, DFT, and integration collateral
Run cross-view consistency and downstream tool checks
Release the compiler-equivalent memory package
r: Custom memory views characterized to compiler equivalence. The deliverable equivalence is the standard it is measured against.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The custom array is delivered into the macro set on the same terms as the analog blocks.
pu: Generate the views the custom array needs to behave like a compiler instance—timing, power, physical, functional—characterized across the same corners, so nothing downstream has to treat it as a special case.

A custom array that cannot be dropped into the flow like a compiler macro has not finished. Synthesis, place-and-route, timing signoff and verification all expect a standard view set; anything missing becomes a manual exception that has to be remembered at every iteration by everyone.
en: Layout frozen and extractable from AMS-07
Tool view requirements known from PDK-08
ex: Required timing and power arcs are characterized across approved corners
All implementation views are generated from the same qualified macro release
Views pass consistency and integration checks in downstream tools
rk: Only nominal memory views generated
Timing, physical, and circuit views produced from different macro revisions
Characterization corners do not match program signoff corners
Internal timing arcs omitted from the Liberty model
Views released without downstream integration checks
AMS-10.fn: Step 6 is the test that matters. Dropping the custom instance into the flow in place of a compiler instance and confirming the tools behave identically is what proves the view set is complete—reading the file list does not.

AMS-11.t: AMS Schematic Design and Pre-Layout Verification
s: Select the circuit topology and device operating points
Implement the transistor-level schematic
Verify nominal DC, AC, transient, noise, and functional behavior
Run required PVT corner simulations
Run Monte Carlo and mismatch analysis on critical metrics
Verify startup, calibration, trim, and fault behavior where applicable
Release layout constraints and the pre-layout design baseline
r: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The pre-layout review package is the formal record that a block was fit to enter layout.
Characterization reports. Pre-layout corner results are the baseline post-layout results are compared against.
pu: Run the schematic-level design and pre-layout simulation that every analog block passes through—the common engineering discipline underneath the PLL, the PHY, the regulators and the array periphery.

This is the shared substrate rather than a block: topology exploration, device sizing, pre-layout corner simulation and the design reviews that gate a block into layout. Separating it makes the schedule honest—a block that has not passed pre-layout review is not ready for the sixteen weeks of layout that follow.
en: Device models available from a tracked PDK version
ex: Schematic meets required functional and electrical specifications across PVT
Critical variation and mismatch sensitivities are understood
Design is stable enough to proceed to layout with documented constraints
rk: Schematic optimized only at typical conditions
Monte Carlo deferred until after layout
Device operating points violate reliability limits at corners
Layout-critical matching and parasitic constraints not documented
Trim or calibration used to hide insufficient intrinsic margin
AMS-11.fn: Step 7 is a gate rather than a meeting. Layout is the longest and least reversible part of an analog block, and letting a schematic that has not closed at the corners enter layout guarantees that the corner failure is found after the layout is built.

AMS-12.t: AMS Custom Layout and Physical Verification
s: Define device placement, matching, shielding, and routing constraints
Place matched and sensitive devices
Route signal, bias, clock, and supply networks
Complete guard rings, shielding, taps, and reliability structures
Run DRC, LVS, and antenna checks
Insert required density fill and recheck sensitive parasitics
Review layout against electrical and integration constraints
Release the extracted-verification layout baseline
r: Per-macro DRC / LVS clean signoff. Every analog macro's physical signoff, alongside the pushed-rule approvals from AMS-07.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The layout is the GDS half of every macro delivery.
pu: Lay out every analog and custom block to DRC, LVS and antenna clean, with the matching, shielding and fill discipline analog requires—and get the layouts extractable.

Eighteen weeks is the largest single block of time in the stage after the PHY, and it is largely irreducible. Analog layout is where matching, isolation and parasitic control are implemented, and none of it can be automated or parallelized the way digital place-and-route can.
en: Schematics passed the AMS-11 layout entry gate
Design rules and exceptions available from PDK-02
Macro placement intent known from ARCH-08
ex: Layout matches the approved schematic and electrical constraints
DRC, LVS, antenna, density, and fill checks are clean
Critical layout assumptions are ready for extracted verification
rk: Matching-critical devices placed without common-centroid or gradient consideration where required
Sensitive nodes routed without coupling and shielding analysis
Fill inserted after electrical signoff without re-extraction
DRC-clean layout assumed to preserve schematic performance
Pin and supply geometry finalized without top-level integration review
AMS-12.fn: Step 5 is where careful layout is most often undone. Fill applied without regard to matching structures changes the parasitics the whole design was tuned against, and the effect is only seen in post-layout simulation.

s: Extract the layout with the qualified parasitic setup
Correlate extracted nominal results against the pre-layout baseline
Run required PVT simulations on the extracted design
Run Monte Carlo or mismatch analysis on critical metrics
Analyze coupling, RC, and layout-dependent performance loss
Iterate circuit or layout where margins are insufficient
Release the final extracted verification report
r: Characterization reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. This activity is the deliverable—the numbers every downstream consumer of these macros relies on.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. Post-layout results are what each block's final review is held against.
pu: Simulate every block with its layout parasitics extracted, across process, voltage and temperature and across the Monte Carlo distribution—and close whatever the layout took away.
Post-layout is where analog designs are judged. Parasitics reduce bandwidth, add mismatch, degrade PSRR and move every margin in the wrong direction.
en: Layouts frozen and extractable from AMS-12
ex: Extracted simulations meet the required electrical specification across PVT
Monte Carlo or statistical checks cover critical post-layout metrics
Any pre-to-post-layout degradation is understood and dispositioned
rk: Post-layout verification limited to nominal conditions
Extraction setup differs from the qualified signoff environment
Large pre-to-post-layout delta accepted without root cause
Monte Carlo run on schematic instead of the extracted critical paths
Layout changes made after extracted signoff without rerun
AMS-13.fn: Step 6 is planned iteration rather than contingency. Analog blocks essentially always need at least one layout turn after post-layout simulation, and a schedule with no allowance for it is a schedule that will slip on the first block.

s: Define the applicable reliability checks and mission profile
Check device voltage, current, and operating-area limits
Run EM / IR analysis on critical supply and high-current paths
Evaluate aging and lifetime degradation on sensitive circuits
Verify ESD protection paths and clamp assumptions
Review latch-up spacing, taps, guard rings, and injection risks
Close reliability violations and release the assessment
r: Reliability report—EM/IR, ESD, latch-up, aging. The deliverable it is what qualification will be checked against.
Integration guide. Reliability limits—maximum current, boost duty cycle, operating conditions—are integration constraints and belong in the guide.
pu: Check every analog macro for the failure modes that appear over time rather than at test—electromigration, IR, aging, ESD and latch-up—because none of them show up in a functional simulation.

Analog blocks carry high current densities in small geometries and run continuously for the product's life. A design that passes every corner and fails EM has passed everything the design flow checks and none of what qualification will.
en: Mission profile and lifetime requirements defined
ex: Applicable device, interconnect, aging, ESD, and latch-up checks pass
Worst-case operating and lifetime conditions are represented
Reliability violations are closed or formally dispositioned before release
rk: Reliability checked using typical rather than lifetime worst-case activity
EM evaluated without extracted current distribution
Aging analysis omitted for timing- or bias-sensitive circuits
ESD reviewed independently of package and I/O current paths
Reliability rerun omitted after late layout changes
AMS-14.fn: Step 4 is the one that needs the product's actual mission profile. Aging simulated at nominal conditions for a nominal lifetime says nothing about a part that runs at the top of its DVFS range continuously, which is exactly how an accelerator is used.

AMS-15.t: Hard Macro Abstraction and View Generation
s: Define the required hard-macro view set and release manifest
Generate LEF and physical abstracts
Generate timing and power models
Generate GDS, CDL / SPICE, and LVS collateral
Generate behavioral or functional models where required
Document placement, supply, clock, pin, and usage constraints
Run cross-view and downstream tool consistency checks
Release the version-controlled hard-macro package
r: Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The deliverable it is the stage's milestone—AMS Macro Handoff.
Custom memory views characterized to compiler equivalence. The custom array joins the macro set here on the same terms as the analog blocks.
Characterization reports. The views are generated from the characterization data and have to stay consistent with it.
pu: Wrap every finished block into a hard macro physical design can place and verification can simulate—GDS, abstract, timing views, netlist, power intent and a behavioural model.

This is the handoff the whole stage exists to make. The macro set has to arrive before PD-02 places it, and the abstracts specifically have to arrive well before the models do, because floorplan needs the shape long before signoff needs the timing.
en: View requirements confirmed with PD and DV
ex: Required hard-macro views are generated from the same qualified design revision
Views are mutually consistent and load successfully in downstream tools
Macro constraints and known limitations are documented for integration
rk: Views generated from different schematic or layout revisions
Timing model omits important mode or constraint behavior
Physical abstract does not match actual macro boundaries or pins
Integration constraints exist only in designer knowledge
Macro released without testing in downstream tools
AMS-15.fn: Step 7 is worth the two weeks. Placing every macro in a trial floorplan and running the flow over it finds abstract errors, pin conflicts and missing views before the whole physical design team is depending on them.

s: Define AMS–digital integration scenarios and abstraction levels
Integrate behavioral or real-number AMS models with the RTL environment
Verify clocks, resets, controls, status, and data interfaces
Verify startup, calibration, trim, and mode transitions
Verify relevant power-state and supply sequencing behavior
Correlate behavioral models against transistor-level or extracted results
Close integration issues and release models for regression
r: Integration guide with known limitations and errata. The deliverable it is what stops the same integration question being asked four times.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. Where co-simulation contradicts a specification, the specification is what gets corrected.
pu: Keep the analog and digital halves talking—co-simulation, integration support and the errata that come out of it—through the whole period when the macros are being integrated.
Completing this work early provides a clear basis for downstream design decisions and reduces late rework, schedule risk, and integration issues.
en: RTL integration environment available from RTL-03
ex: AMS–digital interfaces are verified in normal, reset, calibration, and power-state scenarios
Behavioral models are correlated to the qualified AMS implementation
Integration issues are closed and models are released for SoC regression
rk: AMS verification limited to standalone macro simulations
Behavioral model not correlated with the final circuit implementation
Reset and calibration sequences verified separately from system control
Power-state behavior omitted from mixed-signal integration
Late macro changes not propagated to SoC verification models
AMS-16.fn: Step 5 runs across the whole window and is the reason this activity is marked continuous. Integration questions do not arrive in a block; they arrive one at a time for four months, and the engineer who can answer them has to still be assigned.

TC-01.t: Test Chip Objectives and Risk Coverage
s: Define the production decisions the test chip must support
Select and prioritize the risks that require silicon evidence
Confirm that silicon results will arrive before the corresponding decisions
Select the test structures and measurements for each risk
Close the shuttle die-area and cost budget
Baseline the test-chip specification and risk coverage matrix
p: Production decision and test-chip objective statement
Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix
r: Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix. This activity defines the objective, selected risks, measurements, and decision criteria that later test-chip work is executed and reported against.
Design guidance and margin decisions. TC-01 determines which production risks can ultimately be informed by test-chip silicon.
pu: Define which product risks the test chip must retire, what must be measured, and which production decision each result will support.

The test chip should carry only experiments that can change or confirm a production decision while there is still time to act. Risk selection, measurement scope, schedule, die area, and cost therefore need to be resolved together before the vehicle is defined.
en: Node and technology risks from TECH-07
IP and memory readiness gaps from IPR-05 and PDK-06
Production schedule and decision dates from DEF-08
ex: Every selected structure traces to a named risk and production decision
Required measurements and decision criteria are defined before design starts
Schedule, area, and cost feasibility are confirmed before the specification is frozen
rk: Test-chip scope grows beyond the shuttle area or schedule
Silicon results arrive after the production decision they were intended to support
Structures are selected because they are easy to measure rather than because they address the highest product risk
Measurements are defined without a clear decision criterion
Area and cost are budgeted only after structures have been selected
TC-01.fn: Schedule feasibility is a real decision gate. If the selected shuttle returns silicon after the production design must commit, the test chip cannot retire that risk in time and the scope should be reconsidered before design begins.

s: Define the IP / circuits to be included and their target configurations
Design DUT wrappers, controls, and access paths
Define ring-oscillator and process-monitor arrays
Design measurement and PCM structures
Assemble the reusable test-structure library
Integrate the top level and close pad assignment
Define the pad ring, ESD, and external measurement interfaces
Verify all access paths and measurement modes
p: Integrated top-level netlist and pad assignment
r: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. TC-02 defines the selected test-chip content and target configurations, then provides the integrated design and measurement infrastructure that TC-04 converts into a physically signed-off shuttle database.
Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix. The selected IP, circuits, monitors, and measurement structures are checked against the risks and measurements committed in TC-01.
pu: Define and integrate the IP, circuits, process monitors, and measurement structures that will be placed on the test chip, together with the access, control, pad, and measurement infrastructure required to characterize them.

TC-01 identifies the risks that need silicon evidence. This activity turns those risks into concrete test-chip content: what will be fabricated, in which configuration, how each structure will be controlled and observed, and how the complete vehicle will be integrated before physical implementation.
en: Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix from TC-01
Candidate IP, circuits, memory structures, and process monitors available for silicon evaluation
Shuttle die-area, pad-count, and process-option limits
ex: Every selected risk is mapped to a defined test-chip structure and target configuration
Every test structure is reachable through a verified access and measurement path
Pad, ESD, control, and measurement-mode requirements close within shuttle limits
rk: Test-chip content is selected without tracing each structure back to a TC-01 risk
Target configuration differs from the configuration intended for the production design
Access paths or measurement modes are not fully verified before submission
Pad count or measurement resources force late changes to the selected structures
Critical experiments rely on a single structure with no redundancy
TC-02.fn: Content definition comes before integration. First decide exactly which IP, circuits, memory structures, and monitors will be fabricated and in what configuration; then build the wrappers, access paths, measurement structures, top-level integration, and external interfaces around that selected content.

s: Review MPW calendars and identify viable shuttle windows
Confirm foundry or broker pricing and process-option eligibility
Book the shuttle against the production decision timeline
Collect data-format, layer, and submission requirements
Build the backward-planned submission schedule and checklist
p: Foundry / broker pricing and eligibility record
r: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. This activity provides the confirmed shuttle slot, submission requirements, and backward schedule used to control the physical implementation and submission.
pu: Secure an MPW shuttle slot and translate its fixed submission date into the internal schedule the test-chip team must meet.

MPW dates are externally fixed. Missing a cutoff can delay silicon by an entire shuttle cycle, so format requirements, approvals, physical-verification closure, and data submission must be planned backward from the confirmed slot.
en: Test-chip objective and schedule feasibility from TC-01
Foundry or broker MPW calendars and pricing
Budget authority for the required shuttle slot
ex: The MPW slot and submission date are confirmed in writing
Submission formats, layer rules, and administrative requirements are understood
A backward-planned schedule with physical-verification margin is agreed with TC-04
rk: A shuttle slot is booked without checking when the production decision needs the result
Submission requirements are collected too late
The backward schedule does not include enough physical-verification margin
No contingency shuttle is identified
Shuttle cost is committed before budget approval
TC-03.fn: The key output is the backward-planned schedule. The shuttle submission date is fixed, so TC-04 needs an internal physical-verification deadline with margin rather than simply inheriting the foundry cutoff.

TC-04.t: Test Chip Physical Implementation and Signoff
s: Define the floorplan and place the measurement structures
Place and route the integrated test-chip design
Implement the measurement-grade power delivery network
Close timing on access and control paths
Complete fill, seal-ring, and shuttle-frame requirements
Close DRC, antenna, density, and required physical checks
Close LVS and final netlist consistency
Assemble the final GDS / OASIS and submit to the shuttle
p: Timing closure on access and control paths
r: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. This activity produces the physically verified shuttle database and final submission package.
Test chip silicon and characterization report. Measurement quality is determined here—a noisy vehicle produces uncertain results.
pu: Implement the test chip physically and close the database to shuttle submission requirements while preserving the electrical conditions needed for accurate measurement.

The test chip may be small, but physical-verification standards are not reduced. DRC, LVS, antenna, density, frame compliance, timing, and measurement-quality power delivery must all close before the booked submission date.
en: Confirmed shuttle date and submission requirements from TC-03
ex: The test-chip database is clean to the required physical-verification standard
Measurement-sensitive placement, routing, and power constraints are preserved
Shuttle frame, format, and final submission requirements are closed on schedule
rk: Submission is rejected because of frame, format, or physical-verification non-compliance
The PDN supports function but corrupts sensitive measurements
Physical verification is compressed because the die is small
Structure placement does not support the intended measurement or variation analysis
No schedule margin remains before the MPW cutoff
TC-04.fn: Measurement quality is part of physical closure. Power delivery, sensitive routing, monitor placement, and shuttle-frame compliance must be resolved together with DRC / LVS rather than deferred to the lab.

s: Confirm shuttle data acceptance and fabrication start
Track shuttle mask fabrication
Track WIP and communicate schedule changes
Track wafer processing through completion
Review e-test and PCM data as soon as released
Coordinate dicing, packaging, sample quantity, and delivery
p: Accepted shuttle submission and wafer-start confirmation
r: Test chip silicon and characterization report. TC-05 supplies the fabricated silicon, e-test / PCM data, and delivery record required for characterization.
pu: Move the accepted shuttle design through mask fabrication, wafer processing, e-test / PCM review, dicing, packaging, and delivery while keeping the program aligned to the actual fabrication status.

Most elapsed time is controlled by the shuttle and foundry. The program value comes from visibility: WIP changes, early PCM data, packaging readiness, sample quantity, and delivery status must be communicated as soon as they are known.
en: Shuttle database submitted and accepted from TC-04
Packaging and socket requirements defined with TC-06
Delivery logistics and required sample quantity defined
ex: Required test-chip parts are delivered for the characterization plan
E-test and PCM data are reviewed as soon as they become available
Fabrication and delivery changes are communicated to downstream owners
rk: Fabrication slips are communicated too late to downstream teams
Packaging or socket preparation is not aligned with wafer delivery
Available PCM data is not reviewed until packaged parts arrive
Delivered sample quantity is insufficient for the characterization matrix
Shipping, customs, or engineering-sample logistics delay silicon access
TC-05.fn: E-test and PCM data can answer some process questions before packaged parts arrive. Reviewing those results immediately enables early correlation and issue triage while assembly and delivery continue.

TC-06.t: Test Chip Board and Lab Preparation
s: Translate the coverage matrix into measurement and lab requirements
Design the board for supplies, bias, clocks, and measurement paths
Select and order the socket or probe solution
Fabricate and assemble the test boards
Develop measurement automation and data-capture scripts
Bring up the board and qualify the instrument setup
p: Socket / probe solution and lead-time commitment
Board bring-up and qualified instrument setup
r: Test chip silicon and characterization report. This activity provides the measurement platform and lab readiness needed to generate the characterization data.
pu: Prepare the board, socket or probe solution, instruments, and measurement automation before silicon arrives so characterization can begin immediately.

Board or socket work started after wafer-out gives back the schedule advantage the test chip was intended to create. The measurement platform must also meet the noise, bandwidth, accuracy, and automation needs of the TC-01 coverage plan.
en: Pad assignment and external interfaces from TC-02
Expected package or probe format from the shuttle plan
ex: Board and measurement setup are ready before silicon characterization begins
Socket or probe hardware and required instruments are available
Automation can execute and capture the planned characterization matrix repeatably
rk: Board development starts only after parts ship
Socket or probe-card lead time is discovered too late
Measurement automation is deferred until silicon arrives
Board noise floor, bandwidth, or accuracy is insufficient for the target measurements
Required lab instruments are not available during the characterization window
TC-06.fn: Socket or probe-card lead time can exceed board-development time, so it runs in parallel. Board hardware, instruments, and automation should all be treated as first-silicon prerequisites.

s: Perform incoming inspection and basic functionality checks
Characterize the selected IP and circuits across the planned matrix
Measure ring-oscillator frequency, leakage, and monitor structures
Extract PCM and device parameters
Set up corner-by-corner correlation against simulation
Analyze across-wafer and lot-to-lot variation
Investigate outliers and unexpected behavior
Compile the silicon-to-model correlation results with uncertainty
r: Test chip silicon and characterization report. This activity produces the measured silicon characterization results.
Silicon-to-model correlation report. It also quantifies the difference between measured silicon and pre-silicon prediction under matched conditions.
pu: Measure the test-chip silicon and correlate the results against the pre-silicon models and predictions used by the production design.

The useful output is not a set of measurements alone, but the quantified difference between prediction and silicon, including measurement uncertainty and observed variation. That correlation is what enables production margin and model decisions.
en: Silicon and available e-test / PCM data from TC-05
Pre-silicon predictions and models for comparison
ex: Required silicon parameters are compared with corresponding pre-silicon predictions
Correlation results include measurement uncertainty and observed variation
Significant model-to-silicon gaps have a root-cause assessment or follow-up plan
rk: Characterization results are reported without correlation to pre-silicon predictions
Sample size is too small to support variation claims
Measurement uncertainty is comparable to or larger than the observed model delta
Outliers are removed without root-cause analysis
Correlation results arrive too late for production changes
TC-07.fn: Correlation starts with the earliest available silicon evidence and expands to full device characterization. The final result must state the model-to-silicon delta under matched conditions, not only report measured values.

TC-08.t: Production Design Feedback and Margin Update
s: Quantify where silicon and pre-silicon models disagree
Define model-correction and re-characterization actions
Propose design-rule and methodology updates
Make quantified production margin decisions
Raise required production design changes through change control
Publish the guidance and track adoption to closure
r: Design guidance and margin decisions for the production chip. This activity converts silicon findings into model updates, margin decisions, methodology changes, and tracked production actions.
Silicon-to-model correlation report. The gap analysis is published with the correlation, so the finding and its consequence stay together.
pu: Convert test-chip correlation results into specific updates to production models, margins, rules, methodology, and design assumptions, and track those changes to adoption.
A test chip retires risk only when its results change or confirm a production decision. Each meaningful finding therefore needs a quantified disposition, an owner, and a completion date.
en: Current production design status, margins, and open risks
ex: Every material finding has a production action or explicit no-change disposition
Model and margin updates are quantified and communicated to affected teams
Adoption is tracked to closure before the relevant production design gate
rk: Guidance is published but not adopted by production teams
Findings arrive after the relevant production design has committed
Model corrections are requested without an owner or schedule
Only negative silicon findings change margins while validated margin opportunity is ignored
Findings are stated as observations rather than quantified production actions
TC-08.fn: Publication is not completion. The activity closes only when the corrected model, revised margin, methodology update, or production design change has been adopted or explicitly dispositioned.

s: Plan specification completion and assign block owners
Write the pipeline and datapath detail for each block
Specify control logic and state machines
Detail block interfaces and protocols against the NoC
Define exception, error and corner-case behavior
Define verification hooks and observability requirements with DV
Review each specification and run the implementation entry gate
p: Specification completion plan and block-owner assignments
Interface and protocol detail per block
Reviewed specifications with implementation entry gate records
r: Block and top-level RTL release. The specification is what the release is checked against; without it, review has nothing to compare code to.
RTL Freeze package. A block whose specification was never completed cannot be declared frozen against anything.
pu: Complete the microarchitecture specification for every block—pipeline, interfaces, control, register map—to the level of detail an implementer can write code against without inventing anything.

ARCH-10 started these inside architecture; this finishes them. The distinction matters: a block whose specification is still being written while its RTL is being written produces code that documents itself, and the specification then follows the code instead of leading it.
ex: Every block passes an entry gate before implementation starts
Corner-case behavior defined, not left to the implementer
Shared interfaces agreed by both sides
rk: Specification written alongside the code. The document then records what was built rather than defining it, and verification loses its independent reference.
Corner cases left undefined. The implementer decides, verification cannot check, and the disagreement surfaces at chip-level integration.
Interfaces specified from one side. Two blocks each documenting their own view of a shared protocol produces two consistent documents that disagree.
Entry gate skipped for schedule. Coding against an incomplete specification is faster for two weeks and slower for two months.
Observability requirements added later. Debug and coverage hooks designed in cost little; retrofitted they cost timing and an RTL change under control.
RTL-01.fn: Step 5 is the section most often left thin and the one verification spends the most time on. Corner-case behavior that the specification does not define is behavior the implementer chooses and the verification engineer has no basis to check.

s: Set the coding standard, directory structure and naming conventions
Implement first-pass RTL for each block
Insert block-level self-checking and assertions
Review block RTL against its specification
Implement parameterization and configuration options
Fix and refine blocks against block-level verification results
Refine block PPA against trial synthesis feedback
Freeze blocks and tag the release
p: Block release tags with known issues
r: Block and top-level RTL release, tagged. The block half of the deliverable; RTL-04 assembles the top.
Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports. Clean reports are a property of the code, and the coding standard set here largely determines them.
pu: Write the synthesisable logic for every block, to a coding standard that survives lint, CDC, synthesis and gate-level simulation without rework.

At 180 man-months this is the largest single activity in the entire template—nearly 5% of the program's effort in one line. It is also the one most exposed to specification churn: every change upstream lands here, multiplied by the number of blocks that inherit it.
en: Block specifications passed the RTL-01 entry gate
Coding standard and build environment available
Block-level verification environment starting up in DV-02
ex: Every block reviewed against its specification, not only linted
Blocks frozen only after their verification loop has closed
Releases tagged with known issues listed
rk: Specification churn arriving mid-implementation. Every upstream change lands here multiplied by the blocks affected, which is why RTL-10 exists.
Coding standard imposed after code exists. Retrofitting a standard across 180 man-months of code is a project nobody schedules and everyone half-does.
Assertions treated as verification's job. Assertions written by the implementer capture intent; written by someone else they capture observed behavior.
Blocks declared complete without verification feedback. First-pass code is not correct code, and a block frozen before its verification loop closes freezes its bugs.
Configurability added everywhere. Parameterization nobody uses multiplies the verification space at no benefit, and the cost lands on DV-03.
RTL-02.fn: Step 6 is seven weeks of fixing rather than writing, and it is the honest half of RTL. First-pass code is written in step 2; what makes it correct is the loop against block-level verification, and shortening that loop is where schedule pressure does the most damage.

s: Receive each IP delivery and inspect it against the acceptance checklist
Build the integration environment and wrapper framework
Implement wrappers and glue logic per IP
Configure, tie off and set parameters for each IP
Verify boundary and reset sequencing per IP
Integrate AMS macros with their behavioural models
Build the IP version manifest and handle vendor updates
Compile the integration report and escalate issues to vendors
p: Boundary and reset sequencing verification results
Integrated AMS macros with behavioural models
Integration report and vendor issue log
