r: IP integration report and version manifest. The integration report and the version manifest are assembled here, and the manifest is what makes an IP-related bug traceable to a version.
Block and top-level RTL release. Integrated IP is part of the release, and its versions are part of the tag.
pu: Bring every third-party, foundry and internal IP into the design—wrappers, glue, configuration and version control—and prove each one behaves as its documentation claims.

IP integration fails at the boundary rather than in the block. A PHY that meets its specification and a controller that meets its specification can still disagree about reset ordering, and the disagreement is found here or it is found in the lab.
en: IP delivery schedule aligned by IPR-09
ex: Every delivery inspected against its checklist on receipt
Boundary and reset behavior verified, not assumed from documentation
Version manifest complete and maintained through updates
rk: Deliveries accepted without inspection. Missing views and collateral then become the integration team's problem rather than the vendor's.
Boundary behavior assumed from documentation. Reset ordering, enable timing and calibration sequences are where IP integration actually fails.
Version manifest not maintained. An IP bug that cannot be traced to a version cannot be reported usefully or fixed reproducibly.
IP updates absorbed silently. A vendor drop applied without impact assessment can change behavior verification has already signed off.
Late IP compressing integration. The integration window is fixed at its far end by RTL-04; a late delivery does not move it, it shortens it.
RTL-03.fn: Step 1 is the acceptance check IPR-06 defined, and it is the last point at which an incomplete delivery is the vendor's problem. Accepting a delivery without inspecting it transfers the missing views to the integration team.

s: Define the top-level hierarchy and connectivity
Integrate the NoC and interconnect
Implement clock and reset distribution
Assemble the address map and configuration space
Elaborate the top level and run automated connectivity checks
Integrate the boot and bring-up path
Run chip-level smoke tests and the first boot in simulation
Close integration issues and release the top level
p: Assembled address map and configuration space
Elaborated top level with connectivity check results
r: Block and top-level RTL release, tagged. The top half of the deliverable—the object every downstream stage actually consumes.
RTL Freeze package. Freeze is declared on the top-level release, so its state is what the package describes.
pu: Assemble the blocks and the IP into one top-level design that elaborates, connects and boots—the first point at which the chip exists as a single object.

Chip-level integration is where every optimistic assumption made in isolation meets every other one. Connectivity, clock and reset distribution, address maps and configuration all become concrete here, and the defects found are the ones no block-level test could have seen.
en: Blocks stable enough to integrate from RTL-02
IP integrated and boundary-verified in RTL-03
ex: Connectivity verified automatically, not by inspection
Chip boots in simulation before freeze is contemplated
Top-level release tagged with its full IP manifest
rk: Connectivity checked by inspection. A chip this size has too many connections to review; automated connectivity checking is the only reliable method.
Integration started before blocks are stable. Integrating moving blocks produces defects that are re-found every time a block updates.
Address map assembled from block documentation. Generated maps agree with the code; hand-assembled maps agree with the documentation, which is a different thing.
First boot deferred. The boot path exercises reset, clocking, configuration and the fabric together, and delaying it delays every defect that only appears in combination.
Clock and reset distribution treated as a wiring task. It carries the crossing inventory from ARCH-05 and the CDC obligations that follow from it.
RTL-04.fn: Step 7—the first chip-level boot in simulation—is the moment the design becomes real. It is also slow, because the first boot exercises paths that no block test touched, and each failure takes a full-chip simulation to reproduce.

RTL-05.t: Clock, Reset, and Power Intent (UPF) Implementation
s: Implement power domain boundaries against the ARCH-05 definition
Implement the isolation, level-shifter and retention strategy
Implement CDC synchronisers against the crossing inventory
Implement reset sequencing and synchronization
Author the UPF and check tool acceptance in synthesis
Implement the power management controller RTL
Review the intent with synthesis, verification and physical design
p: Implemented isolation, level shifters and retention
Synchroniser coverage against the crossing inventory
r: UPF power intent file. The UPF file is authored and tool-checked here, and "tool-accepted" is the standard rather than "reviewed".
Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports. The synchroniser implementation is what CDC closure in RTL-06 is checking.
pu: Implement the clock, reset and power intent the architecture defined—domain boundaries, isolation, retention, crossing synchronisers—and produce a UPF file the tools accept.

Power intent is where architecture becomes an obligation on every downstream tool. Synthesis inserts isolation cells from it, verification checks against it, and physical design implements it. An intent file that is wrong or incomplete propagates the same error into all three.
en: Power and clock architecture fixed by ARCH-05
ex: UPF elaborates in synthesis, not only reviews well
Every crossing on the inventory has an implemented synchroniser
Intent accepted by synthesis, verification and physical design
rk: UPF written as a document. Intent that has never been elaborated in synthesis is intent whose errors are found by the first person who runs the flow.
Crossings implemented without reference to the inventory. A synchroniser strategy chosen per crossing by each designer produces inconsistency CDC will flag hundreds of times.
Retention strategy decided late. Retention cells cost area and change the physical implementation; adding them after floorplan is expensive.
Reset sequencing implemented from the block view. Reset order is a chip-level property, and blocks each releasing in their own order produces a boot that works in simulation and not in silicon.
Intent reviewed only by its author. Synthesis, verification and physical design each consume it differently, and each has to confirm it works for them.
RTL-05.fn: Step 5 includes a tool acceptance check because UPF that reads correctly to a human and fails to elaborate in synthesis is common. The file has to be exercised in the actual flow, not reviewed as a document.

s: Define the lint, CDC and RDC methodology and rule sets
Close lint at block level
Close CDC at block level
Close CDC at chip level against the crossing inventory
Close RDC and analyze reset domains
Review and disposition every waiver
Report closure and set up the closure regression
p: Lint, CDC and RDC rule sets
RDC closure record and reset domain analysis
Waiver list with dispositions and signatures
Closure regression in the CI flow
r: Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports with waiver list. The clean reports and the waiver list are produced here, and the waiver list is the part that needs review rather than filing.
RTL Freeze package. Freeze with open CDC violations is freezing a class of defect that will not appear until silicon.
pu: Drive lint, clock domain crossing and reset domain crossing to closure—every violation either fixed or waived with a reason someone signed.

These checks find the class of defect that simulation cannot: a crossing without a synchroniser works in every simulation and fails intermittently in silicon. The discipline is in the waivers—an unexamined waiver list is where the surviving bugs live.
en: Blocks stable enough to lint meaningfully
Tools set up and qualified by PDK-08
ex: Every violation fixed or waived with a signed reason
Chip-level CDC clean, not only block-level
Closure regressed in CI so it stays clean
rk: Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A waiver list nobody re-reads is where the surviving crossings hide, and they are the hardest silicon bugs to diagnose.
CDC run only at block level. The crossings that matter are usually between blocks, and neither owner runs the check that would find them.
Closure not regressed. Clean at one release and dirty at the next, with nobody noticing until the freeze package is assembled.
Rule set weakened to reduce noise. Turning off the rule that produces the most violations is the fastest way to a clean report and the slowest way to a working chip.
Crossing inventory not reconciled. Crossings found by the tool but absent from ARCH-05's inventory mean the architecture and the implementation disagree.
RTL-06.fn: Step 4 is chip-level rather than block-level because most real crossings are between blocks. Block-level CDC finds the easy ones; the crossing that fails in silicon is usually one neither block owner considered theirs.

RTL-07.t: Register Map / RDL Definition and Header Generation
s: Select the register description language and generation tooling
Allocate the address map across blocks
Define registers per block
Specify access policies, reset values and side effects
Build the generation flow for RTL, headers, documentation and the UVM model
Run the software review of the map
Release the map under change control
p: Generated RTL, headers, documentation and UVM model
Released register map with change control
r: Register map / RDL and generated headers. The register map source and its generated views are produced here, generated from one source rather than maintained in several.
Block and top-level RTL release. Generated register RTL is part of every block, so the map's release cadence is tied to the RTL's.
pu: Define the register map—the software contract—and generate the RTL, headers and documentation from one source so they cannot disagree.

The register map is where hardware and firmware meet, and it is the interface most often maintained in three places. Generating the RTL, the C headers and the documentation from a single description is what makes them consistent; hand-maintaining them is what produces a driver that writes to the wrong offset.
en: Address map intent from the architecture specification
ex: RTL, headers and documentation generated from one source
Map reviewed by firmware before it is frozen
Side effects and reset values specified for every register
rk: Map maintained in more than one place. RTL, headers and documentation drift apart, and the driver eventually writes to an offset that moved.
Software reviews the map after freeze. An awkward interface then gets worked around in the driver, and the workaround becomes the contract nobody documented.
Side effects undocumented. A read that clears a status bit is a behavior firmware has to know about, and discovering it in the lab costs days per instance.
Security access rules omitted. Registers that should be locked in production lifecycle states are locked late or not at all.
Reset values unspecified. Registers whose reset value is whatever the implementer chose produce a boot sequence that depends on undocumented behavior.
RTL-07.fn: Step 6 is a review by the people who will use the map rather than the people who wrote it. A register set that is natural to the hardware and awkward to drive is a set the driver will work around, and the workaround becomes the real interface.

RTL-08.t: Trial Synthesis and RTL PPA Feedback Loop
s: Set up the trial synthesis flow and bootstrap constraints
Run per-block trial synthesis and establish QoR baselines
Deliver timing feedback to block owners
Track area against the ARCH-06 budgets
Feed back power and clock-gating effectiveness to block owners
Flag congestion and routability early indications
Operate the recurring trial synthesis cadence and reporting
p: Timing feedback reports to block owners
Area tracking against the ARCH-06 budgets
Trial synthesis cadence and reporting record
r: Block and top-level RTL release. A block released without a trial synthesis result has an unknown PPA, and the release quality reflects that.
RTL Freeze package. The package states where each block sits against its budget, and this activity is where that number comes from.
pu: Run trial synthesis continuously against the evolving RTL and feed timing, area and power back to block owners while the code can still change cheaply.

RTL that has never been synthesized is RTL whose PPA is unknown. A block that misses its area budget by 30% is a redesign if found at SYN-02 and an afternoon if found here, and the difference is only whether anyone was running synthesis during implementation.
en: Library and environment available from PDK-13
ex: Every block has a current QoR result against its budget
Feedback delivered on a cadence, not on request
Overruns escalated rather than noted
rk: Trial synthesis run once. A snapshot tells a block owner where they were; only a cadence tells them whether they are improving.
Feedback delivered without constraints. Timing results against bootstrap constraints that do not resemble the real ones send block owners chasing paths that do not matter.
Area overrun tolerated because it is early. Blocks rarely shrink after implementation, and an overrun accepted at trial synthesis is an overrun accepted permanently.
Congestion ignored. Routability problems are cheaper to fix in RTL structure than in placement, and the early indication is the only chance to do so.
Results not tied to the budget. QoR reported in absolute terms rather than against ARCH-06 tells nobody whether the block is acceptable.
RTL-08.fn: Step 7 is the activity's real shape—a weekly cadence rather than a one-off study. A single trial synthesis is a snapshot; a weekly one is a feedback loop, and only the loop changes how blocks are written.

RTL-09.t: CI Build, Nightly Regression, and Release Management
s: Set up the build system and dependency management
Stand up continuous integration with per-commit checks
Define and schedule the nightly regression
Establish release tagging and the version manifest process
Manage compute and license capacity for regressions
Build the failure triage and notification workflow
Operate and maintain the machinery across the stage
p: Compute and license capacity management record
r: Integration testbench and build system. The build, regression and release machinery is built and operated here, and its measure is that every release is reproducible from a tag.
Block and top-level RTL release. Releases are produced and tagged by this machinery; without it a release is a directory copy.
pu: Run the build, regression and release machinery the whole stage depends on—continuous integration, nightly regressions, tagged releases and a reproducible environment.

This is infrastructure, and its value shows only in its absence. Without a nightly build, a break introduced on Tuesday is found on Friday by whoever needed the design; without release tagging, a bug cannot be reproduced against the version that had it.
ex: Every release reproducible from a tag
Nightly regression completing within the night
Failures triaged within a working day, with an owner
rk: Red builds tolerated. Once a broken build is normal, the signal is gone and every subsequent break is invisible.
Regression runtime exceeding the night. A nightly that takes thirty hours is not nightly, and the feedback loop silently doubles.
Releases produced by hand. An untagged release cannot be reproduced, and an IP bug found against it cannot be reported precisely.
Capacity not managed. Regressions competing with verification for the same licences slow both, usually at the point in the schedule where both matter most.
Triage unowned. Failures nobody is assigned to investigate accumulate until the regression result is meaningless.
RTL-09.fn: Twenty-two of the thirty weeks are step 7, which is maintenance rather than construction. A CI system that is not maintained degrades into one everyone ignores, and an ignored red build is worse than no build at all.

RTL-10.t: Specification Change Control and ECO Board
s: Define the change control process and ECO board charter
Build the change request intake and impact assessment workflow
Operate the ECO board and record decisions
Track approved changes across blocks, verification and synthesis
Define freeze criteria and track readiness against them
Assemble the RTL Freeze package
Declare freeze and publish the post-freeze exception policy
p: Change control process and ECO board charter
Change request log with impact assessments
Change tracking record across blocks, verification and synthesis
Freeze declaration with its exception policy
r: RTL Freeze package. The freeze package is assembled and declared here—the freeze, its criteria, its exceptions and the change history behind it.
Block and top-level RTL release. After freeze, a release is only produced through an approved exception.
pu: Control what changes and when—specification change requests, ECO board decisions and the freeze itself—so the design converges rather than oscillates.

Every stage downstream assumes RTL stops moving at some point. Change control is how that point is created: not by refusing changes, but by making each one visible, costed and decided by people who can see what it affects. The freeze is this activity's output, and its credibility is the whole program's.
en: Process agreed and board membership named
Change intake path published to every team
Freeze criteria defined in the program plan
ex: Freeze declared against criteria, not against a date
Every change carries an impact assessment before approval
Post-freeze exception policy published and used
rk: Freeze declared by date rather than by criteria. A gate that passes because it was scheduled teaches everyone that gates mean nothing.
Impact assessment skipped for small changes. The cost of a change is rarely in the block that changes; it is in the verification that has to be re-run.
Post-freeze exceptions ungoverned. Changes will be needed after freeze; without a policy they happen informally and nobody knows what the design contains.
Board without downstream representation. Verification and synthesis are the ones who pay for most changes, and a board without them approves costs it cannot see.
Change log not reconciled with the release. A freeze package that does not match what was actually built is a package nobody can rely on.
RTL-10.fn: Step 3 runs for twenty weeks and is a standing meeting rather than a task. Its discipline is impact assessment: a change that looks like an afternoon in one block can invalidate a month of verification, and the board exists so that cost is visible before the change is approved.

DV-01.t: Verification Plan and Coverage Model Definition
s: Extract the feature list from the architecture and block specifications
Assign a verification strategy per feature — simulation, formal or emulation
Define the coverage model — functional, code and assertion
Define closure criteria and signoff per block and at chip level
Model the resource, compute and schedule demand
Review the verification plan with design and architecture
p: Feature list extracted from the specifications
Coverage model — functional, code and assertion
Closure criteria per block and at chip level
r: Verification plan (vPlan) and coverage model. The plan and its coverage model are written here, and the coverage model is what every later closure claim is measured against.
DV closure signoff package. Closure is defined here; a signoff against criteria written later is a signoff against a moving target.
pu: Write the plan that says what will be verified, how, and how anyone will know it is done—feature by feature, with a coverage model behind each claim.

Verification is the largest line of effort in the program, and without a plan it is 650 man-months of activity with no definition of completion. The coverage model is what turns "we tested it" into a measurable statement, and the features nobody writes into the plan are the features nobody verifies.
en: Compute capacity model available from PDK-12
ex: Every specified feature has a verification strategy and a coverage point
Closure criteria written and agreed before verification starts
Plan reviewed by architecture and design, not only by verification
rk: Plan written from the RTL rather than the specification. It then verifies what was built rather than what was specified, and the two differ exactly where the bugs are.
Coverage model that measures activity rather than intent. Code coverage says lines were executed; functional coverage says features were exercised, and only the second answers the question.
Closure criteria left vague. "High coverage" is not a criterion anyone can sign, and it becomes whatever the schedule allows.
Architecture not in the review. The features the plan missed are exactly the ones only the specification's author would notice.
Resource model omitted. A plan that needs more compute or more engineers than exist is a plan whose closure date is fiction.
DV-01.fn: Step 6 is a review by the people who wrote the specification, and its purpose is to find features the plan missed. Verification reviewing its own plan confirms it is coherent; architecture reviewing it confirms it is complete, and incompleteness is the failure mode that matters.

s: Define the environment architecture and reuse strategy
Develop UVM agents for each interface
Integrate and configure third-party VIP
Develop scoreboards and reference models
Build the sequence library and stimulus infrastructure
Integrate the register model generated from the RDL source
Bring the environment up on the first real block
Release the environment with its documentation
p: Integrated register model from the RDL source
Environment bring-up results on the first block
r: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. The environment and its integrated VIP are built here—the infrastructure every subsequent verification activity runs inside.
Verification plan and coverage model. Coverage is collected by the environment, so what it can measure bounds what the plan can claim.
pu: Build the verification environment—UVM agents, scoreboards, sequences, VIP integration—that every test in the program will run inside.

The environment is infrastructure with a long lead time and no visible output until it works. Sixty man-months buys agents for every interface, scoreboards that actually check, and reusable sequences. Testbench bring-up running late is the single most common reason verification starts late, and it starts late invisibly.
en: Interface specifications stable enough to build agents against
ex: Environment running on a real block, not on a stub
Scoreboards checking against reference models
Environment documented and reused rather than rebuilt per block
rk: Bring-up slower than planned and invisible. Environment work has no test-pass metric, so slippage is not visible until testing should have started.
Scoreboards that check protocol rather than function. A legal transaction carrying wrong data passes, and the bug survives to chip level.
No reuse strategy. Every block building its own environment multiplies effort and makes results incomparable across blocks.
Register model hand-written. A model that diverges from the RDL source produces tests that pass against the wrong offsets.
VIP licences short. Verification concurrency is capped by VIP seats, and the cap is discovered when regressions start queuing.
DV-02.fn: Step 4 is where verification quality is decided. A scoreboard that compares against a reference model finds bugs; one that only checks protocol legality confirms the design does something rather than the right thing.

s: Instantiate per-block testbenches from the shared environment
Develop directed tests for specified behavior
Develop constrained-random stimulus and tune the constraints
Write and bind assertions
Run corner-case and error-injection testing
Analyze coverage and close holes per block
Run the debug and bug reporting loop with block owners
Close each block against the DV-01 criteria and sign off
p: Directed test suite for specified behavior
Constrained-random test suite with tuned constraints
Coverage analysis and hole closure records
Bug reports and debug log with block owners
r: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. Per-block testbenches extend the shared environment and are delivered with it.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Block coverage is the largest contributor to the dashboards DV-10 maintains.
DV closure signoff package. Block signoff is the substance of chip-level closure; the package aggregates it.
pu: Verify every block against its specification with constrained-random and directed testing, and drive each one to its coverage closure criteria.

Two hundred man-months—the largest activity in the template—spread across thirty weeks and every block in the design. This is where most bugs are found and most verification time is spent, and its efficiency is set almost entirely by decisions taken in DV-01 and DV-02.
en: Coverage model and criteria set by DV-01
ex: Every block closed against the DV-01 criteria, not its own
Coverage holes closed by tests, not by model changes
Signoff records complete per block
rk: Coverage closed by adding coverage points rather than tests. Redefining the model to match what was tested produces a closure number that measures nothing.
Constrained-random left unconstrained. Random stimulus without well-designed constraints spends compute exploring illegal or uninteresting space.
Corner cases skipped because the specification is silent. The gap belongs back in RTL-01, not quietly into the untested set.
Debug loop bottlenecked on block owners. Verification finds faster than design fixes, and the queue is where the schedule quietly goes.
Blocks signed off against different standards. Without enforced criteria from DV-01, each block closes to whatever its owner considered enough.
DV-03.fn: Step 7 runs in parallel across the whole window because debugging is continuous rather than a phase. It is also where the largest single share of the effort goes—finding a bug is usually quicker than proving what caused it.

s: Assemble the chip-level verification environment
Develop boot and configuration scenarios
Test end-to-end data paths and data integrity
Stress the interconnect for arbitration and deadlock under contention
Test power state transitions and DVFS scenarios
Inject errors and verify recovery at system level
Run realistic workload scenarios from the DEF-02 suite
Close chip-level coverage and sign off
p: System-level error injection and recovery results
Realistic workload scenarios in the testbench
Chip-level coverage closure and signoff record
r: DV closure signoff package. Chip-level closure is the part of the package that speaks to whether the system works, rather than the parts.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Chip-level scenarios are the slowest and most informative regressions on the dashboard.
pu: Verify the chip as one system running realistic scenarios—boot, configuration, traffic, power transitions, error recovery—rather than as a collection of verified blocks.

Blocks that each pass in isolation routinely fail together. Chip-level verification is where arbitration, ordering, deadlock, reset sequencing and end-to-end data integrity are actually tested, and none of those are visible from inside a block.
ex: Realistic workload scenarios run, not only synthetic ones
Deadlock and arbitration tested under contention
Chip-level coverage closed against the DV-01 model
rk: Started too late because blocks are not ready. Chip-level defects take longest to find and fix, and compressing the window pushes them into silicon.
Scenarios written by verification alone. Realistic use comes from the workload suite and from software; invented scenarios test what verification imagined.
Deadlock and arbitration untested. These fail only under contention, which random block-level stimulus does not create.
Power transitions verified functionally only. Retention, isolation and sequencing across a real power state change are where low-power designs actually fail.
Simulation too slow to run meaningful scenarios. If a boot takes a day, the scenario set shrinks to what fits, and emulation in DV-08 is the answer.
DV-04.fn: Step 7 uses the same workloads DEF-02 assembled and ARCH-01 modelled. Running them in simulation is slow and worth it: it is the only place the design, the model and the product's actual intent are compared against each other before silicon.

DV-05.t: Formal Verification of Control, Connectivity, and Security Properties
s: Select formal targets where proof beats simulation
Write property specifications per target
Prove connectivity and structural properties at chip level
Prove control logic and arbiter properties
Prove security and isolation properties
Review assumptions and check for over-constraint
Close proofs, state bounded results and report
p: Assumption list and proof closure report
r: Formal proof reports with assumption list. The proof reports and their assumption lists are produced here, and the assumption list is what makes the proofs auditable.
DV closure signoff package. Formally proved properties are a different kind of evidence from coverage, and the package should distinguish them.
pu: Use formal proof where simulation is weak—connectivity, control logic, arbiters, security properties, register access—and prove exhaustively what testing can only sample.

Formal answers a different question. Simulation shows that the cases tried worked; a proof shows that no case exists that does not. For arbiters, protocol state machines and security isolation, the space is too large to sample and the failure modes are exactly the ones random stimulus misses.
en: Block RTL stable enough to prove against
ex: Every proof reported with its assumptions and its bound
Assumptions reviewed for over-constraint, not just listed
Security properties proved rather than sampled
rk: Over-constrained proofs. Assumptions that exclude the failing case produce a green result and no information, and only assumption review catches it.
Formal applied where simulation is better. Datapath and workload behavior are poor formal targets; applying it there consumes specialist time for little return.
Bounded results reported as proofs. A property proved to depth twenty is not proved; the bound has to be stated with the result.
Properties written from the RTL. A property derived from the implementation proves the implementation matches itself.
Security properties omitted. Isolation and access control are exactly the properties simulation samples poorly and formal proves well.
DV-05.fn: Step 6 is what separates a proof from a false claim. A property that passes because assumptions excluded the failing case has proved nothing, and reviewing assumptions is the only way to know which of the two happened.

s: Set up the UPF-aware simulation environment
Run static UPF structural checks
Verify isolation and level shifters
Verify retention and state restoration through real power-down cycles
Verify power sequencing and the power management controller
Integrate power-aware tests into the standing regression
Close low-power coverage and report
p: Isolation and level shifter verification results
Power-aware tests in the standing regression
r: Low-power verification report. The report is produced entirely here, and it is the only evidence that the power architecture works as intended.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Power-aware regressions belong in the same dashboard as functional ones, not in a side report.
pu: Verify the design against its power intent—isolation, retention, level shifting, power sequencing—because none of it is visible in a normal functional simulation.

A design that passes every functional test can still corrupt state on a power-down, drive an isolated domain, or fail to retain what it needed. Low-power verification simulates the domains actually powering down, and it is the only place these failures appear before silicon.
en: UPF available and tool-accepted from RTL-05
ex: Domains simulated powering down, not only statically checked
Retention verified for both what is kept and what is not
Power-aware tests running in the regular regression
rk: Only static checking performed. Structural UPF checks find missing cells; only simulation finds a design that corrupts state when the domain actually goes down.
Retention verified for the intended state only. What is not retained matters as much as what is, and a design that retains too little fails on resume.
Power sequences tested in isolation. The failure is usually a power transition during traffic, not a clean idle transition.
Power-aware simulation excluded from regression. It is slow, so it gets run once; a later RTL change then breaks it silently.
UPF used for verification differing from synthesis. Two versions of the intent means verifying one design and building another.
DV-06.fn: Step 4 is the one that finds real bugs. Retention verification requires actually powering a domain down in simulation and checking what survives; a design that has never been simulated through a power cycle has never been tested for the failure mode.

s: Build the co-simulation environment and integrate the models
Review model fidelity against the AMS characterization results
Verify the control and configuration interfaces
Verify calibration and training sequences from the digital side
Verify startup, lock and ready signaling
Verify analog fault and degraded-mode behavior
Close co-simulation and report the findings
r: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. The co-simulation environment extends the shared testbench rather than standing beside it.
DV closure signoff package. Mixed-signal boundary closure is a distinct claim in the package, because it rests on models rather than on RTL alone.
pu: Verify the boundary between the analog macros and the digital design—control interfaces, calibration sequences, startup ordering—with the analog represented by models correlated to its circuits.

Analog blocks fail where they meet digital. A PLL that locks perfectly and a controller that sequences perfectly can still disagree about when lock is valid. Co-simulation is where those disagreements appear, and the alternative is finding them at bring-up with an oscilloscope.
ex: Every model correlated against its circuit before being relied on
Calibration sequences exercised from the digital side
Degraded and fault behavior verified, not assumed
rk: Models never correlated. Digital passes against a fiction, and the mismatch reaches silicon as a bring-up failure nobody predicted.
Calibration sequences untested from the digital side. A calibration that works when the analog engineer drives it manually is first exercised by firmware at bring-up.
Ready and lock signaling assumed. When a lock signal becomes valid is a contract; each side assuming a different answer produces intermittent boot failures.
Degraded modes unverified. What the digital side does when a PLL fails to lock is behavior that only matters in the field, where it matters a great deal.
Co-simulation too slow to regress. Run once and never again, it cannot catch a later change on either side.
DV-07.fn: Step 2 decides whether any of this is meaningful. Verification against a behavioural model that does not match the circuit proves the digital side works with a fiction, and the correlation in AMS-16 is what makes the model a proxy rather than a guess.

s: Select the platform and size the capacity
Partition the design across the platform
Model memories and interfaces on the platform
Bring the platform up to first boot
Build the debug and visibility infrastructure
Tune performance and throughput
Execute long scenarios and workloads
Hand the platform over to firmware and validation
p: Platform handover package to firmware and validation
r: Emulation platform and system test suite. The platform and its test suite are stood up here, and they serve firmware and validation as much as verification.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Emulation regressions cover scenarios simulation cannot reach, and belong in the same view.
pu: Stand up emulation and FPGA prototyping—partitioning, capacity, speed, debug—so that scenarios too long for simulation can actually be run.

A boot that takes a day in simulation takes minutes in emulation, and workload scenarios that are impossible in one are routine in the other. Emulation is also the platform firmware development runs on, which makes its availability date a dependency for a team outside this stage entirely.
ex: Design boots on the platform at usable speed
Debug visibility sufficient to diagnose a failure
Platform handed over to firmware on a scheduled date
rk: Partitioning consuming more time than expected. Splitting a large design across emulator capacity is difficult and iterative, and it is routinely underestimated.
Capacity contended with another program. Emulator capacity is expensive and shared; a program without a booked allocation runs when the other one is not.
Debug visibility inadequate. A platform that runs fast and cannot be probed produces failures that cannot be diagnosed.
Handover date not in the program schedule. Firmware plans against it, and treating it as an internal verification milestone means nobody outside knows when it slips.
Models diverging from the design. Memory and interface models built for the platform can drift from the RTL, and results then reflect the model.
DV-08.fn: Step 8 makes this activity a dependency for people outside verification. Firmware cannot start on real workloads until the platform runs, and the handover date belongs in the program schedule rather than in the verification plan alone.

DV-09.t: Performance and Bandwidth Validation Against the Architecture Model
s: Build performance measurement infrastructure into the testbench
Execute the workloads on emulation and simulation
Measure bandwidth and utilization against the model predictions
Analyze latency and queueing behavior
Identify bottlenecks and establish root causes
Correlate results against the ARCH-01 performance model
Report findings, recommendations and model reconciliation
r: DV closure signoff package. Performance evidence is part of tapeout readiness—functional closure alone does not say the product meets its KPIs.
Emulation platform and system test suite. The performance workloads become part of the standing suite the platform runs.
pu: Check that the design actually delivers the performance the architecture promised—bandwidth, latency, utilization—against the same workloads ARCH-01 modelled.

Functional correctness and performance are separate questions, and passing every test says nothing about the second. A design that computes correctly at 60% of modelled throughput is a product that misses its headline KPI, and finding that in silicon leaves no options.
en: Performance model predictions available from ARCH-01
ex: Real workloads measured, not only synthetic traffic
Every model disagreement resolved as design or model error
Findings delivered with time to act on them
rk: Performance treated as a bring-up activity. Discovered in silicon, a throughput shortfall has no remaining fix except software and marketing.
Measured only on synthetic traffic. Synthetic patterns exercise the interconnect; real workloads exercise the design, and only the second predicts the product.
Model and RTL disagreement left unresolved. Whichever is wrong, not knowing which means every downstream projection is unreliable.
Bottlenecks found without root cause. Knowing throughput is low is not actionable; knowing which queue saturates is.
No time left to act. Findings that arrive after RTL freeze can only be documented, not fixed.
DV-09.fn: Step 6 closes a loop opened at architecture. Where the RTL and the model disagree, one of them is wrong—and finding out which is what tells the program whether it has a design problem or a modeling problem.

DV-10.t: Coverage Closure and Regression Stability Management
s: Define and tier the regression suites
Build the regression infrastructure and manage capacity
Establish the failure triage process with ownership
Collect, merge and report coverage
Analyze coverage holes and target tests at them
Stabilize the regression and eliminate flaky tests
Publish the dashboard and track closure
Drive coverage to closure and assemble the signoff
p: Hole analysis and targeted test list
Regression stability and flake elimination record
r: Regression and coverage dashboards. The dashboards are built and maintained here, and their value is that the numbers are current and trusted.
DV closure signoff package. Closure is assembled here from the evidence every other DV activity produced.
pu: Keep the regressions running and the coverage moving toward closure—triage failures, manage capacity, publish where every block stands, and close the holes that remain.

Coverage closure is not a phase at the end; it is a curve that either bends or does not. This activity owns the curve: which holes are real, which tests would close them, and whether the regression is stable enough for the numbers to mean anything.
en: Test suites producing coverage from DV-03
ex: Regression stable enough that a red result is believed
Every hole analyzed before it is closed or waived
Coverage curve flat at signoff, not still climbing
rk: Flaky regressions tolerated. Once red results are routinely ignored, the regression has stopped providing information and nobody notices when it matters.
Coverage merged without stability. Numbers from an unstable regression are noise presented as a trend.
Holes closed by waiving rather than testing. A hole waived without analysis is untested behavior recorded as covered.
Capacity insufficient at peak. Regression queues at the point of closure directly extend the closure date.
Closure signed with the curve still climbing. Coverage still rising at signoff means the plan's completion criteria were not what stopped the work.
DV-10.fn: Step 6 is unglamorous and load-bearing. A regression with intermittent failures trains everyone to ignore red results, and once that habit forms the regression has stopped being a signal.

s: Build the gate-level environment and bring the netlist up
Run zero-delay functional gate-level simulation
Analyze X-propagation and reset initialization
Run SDF back-annotated timing simulation
Simulate DFT and scan modes
Run power-aware gate-level simulation
Debug failures and close the findings
p: Gate-level environment with the netlist brought up
Scan and DFT mode simulation results
r: Gate-level simulation report. The gate-level results—functional, timing-annotated, scan and power-aware—are produced here, and the report is a tapeout checklist item rather than an optional confirmation.
DV closure signoff package. Gate-level results close the gap between what was verified and what will be manufactured.
pu: Simulate the gate-level netlist, first functionally and then with real timing, to catch what RTL simulation structurally cannot—X-propagation, reset behavior, timing-dependent failures and synthesis or DFT-induced differences.

RTL simulation is optimistic about X and blind to timing. Gate-level simulation is slow, painful and the last check before the design becomes masks—it is also where scan insertion, clock gating and synthesis transformations are proved not to have changed behavior.
en: SDF available from PD-09 for timing runs
ex: X-propagation issues fixed rather than suppressed
Scan and test modes simulated, not only functional
Timing simulation run at the corners that matter
rk: Skipped because it is slow. The failures it finds—X propagation, reset, timing-dependent behavior—have no other pre-silicon detector.
Run only in functional mode. Scan and test modes are how the part is tested at ATE, and a scan mode that does not work makes the part untestable.
Started after netlist churn has settled. Waiting for a stable netlist means starting too late; running early on an imperfect netlist finds environment problems while there is time.
X failures suppressed rather than fixed. Forcing initial values to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialized state the check exists to find.
Timing simulation on a subset of corners. Timing-dependent failures appear at specific corners, and the corner skipped is the one that fails.
DV-11.fn: Step 3 finds the class of bug RTL simulation is structurally incapable of seeing. RTL X-optimism hides uninitialized state; at gate level the X propagates, and a design that boots in RTL can fail to come out of reset in gates.

s: Define bug tracking, severity and the triage process
Charter the disposition board and set its membership
Run continuous triage and disposition
Analyze bug rate and closure trends
Assess the risk of every deferred bug
Run escape analysis on late-found defects
Compile the open bug list and risk statement for tapeout
Issue the DV closure recommendation
p: Bug rate and closure trend analysis
Open bug list and risk statement
r: DV closure signoff package. The open bug list and its risk statement are the part of the package the Go / No-Go decision actually reads.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Bug find and closure rates sit alongside coverage as the two curves that say whether verification is converging.
ef: Open bug list and risk statement
pu: Run the bug disposition board—triage every defect, decide what gets fixed, and make the risk of what does not explicit and owned.

Every program reaches tapeout with open bugs. The question is whether they were assessed and accepted or simply ran out of time, and the difference is entirely this activity. Its output at the end is the errata list bring-up will work against and the risk statement the Go / No-Go decision reads.
en: Bug tracking system and severity scheme agreed
Tapeout criteria defined in the program plan
ex: Every deferred bug carries an assessed, owned risk
Bug find rate turned over before closure is recommended
Errata list ready for bring-up on day one
rk: Bugs deferred without risk assessment. An unassessed open bug at tapeout is a risk nobody quantified being accepted by nobody in particular.
Severity assigned by the finder. Consistent severity requires a board; without one, the same defect is critical in one block and minor in another.
Bug rate still rising at closure. A find rate that has not turned over means the design has more defects than have been found, whatever the coverage says.
No escape analysis. The process that let a bug survive to week 34 will let the next one survive too.
Errata list assembled after tapeout. Bring-up needs the known-issue list on day one, and assembling it later means debugging problems that were already known.
DV-12.fn: Step 6 is the loop that improves the process rather than the design. Asking why a bug found in week 34 was not found in week 12 usually points at a missing coverage point or an untested mode, and fixing that finds the next one earlier.

DFT-01.t: DFT Architecture and Test Strategy Definition
s: Define the test strategy — what is tested where and how
Define the scan architecture and chain organization
Select the compression architecture and ratio against the cost model
Partition hierarchical DFT against the design hierarchy
Define the test modes and mode control
Write the architecture specification and run its review
r: DFT architecture specification and coverage plan. The architecture specification and coverage plan are written here, and everything else in the stage is executed against them.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. An architecture that was never fixed cannot be signed off against.
pu: Decide how the chip will be tested before it is built to be testable—scan style, compression ratio, hierarchical partitioning, and the test modes the design will support.

Every one of these choices constrains the design rather than following it. Compression ratio decides pattern volume and therefore test cost; hierarchical DFT decides whether a block can be tested independently; and both have to be settled before SYN-01 writes constraints against them.
en: Coverage and test-time targets agreed in DFT-02
Test platform direction available from TEST-02
ex: Architecture fixed before synthesis writes constraints against it
Compression ratio chosen against a test cost model
Specification reviewed by test and product engineering
rk: Architecture decided after synthesis starts. Scan insertion and constraints depend on it; deciding late means re-running both.
Compression ratio chosen without the test cost model. Ratio trades pattern volume against silicon area, and only TEST-09's cost model says which side to favor.
Hierarchical DFT ignored on a large die. Flat scan on a design this size produces pattern volumes and runtimes that become their own schedule problem.
Test modes defined without the security architecture. Every test mode is an access path, and ARCH-07 has to lock the ones that should not exist in production.
Architecture written and not reviewed by test engineering. A scheme that is elegant in design and unrunnable on the chosen ATE is discovered at TEST-08.
DFT-01.fn: Step 3 is a cost decision disguised as an architecture one. Compression ratio sets pattern volume, pattern volume sets tester memory and test time, and test time is a per-unit cost for the life of the product.

DFT-02.t: Test Coverage and Test-Time Target Negotiation
s: Translate the DPPM quality target into required coverage
Derive the test time budget from the product cost model
Select the fault models — stuck-at, transition, cell-aware
Set coverage targets per fault model and per block class
Negotiate the targets and record the agreement
p: Coverage target derived from the DPPM requirement
r: DFT architecture specification and coverage plan. The coverage plan half—the numbers DFT-01's architecture is chosen to reach.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. The report is measured against the targets set here, not against what the tool happened to reach.
pu: Agree the coverage and test-time targets with the people who pay for them—product engineering, who own quality, and test engineering, who own the tester seconds.

Coverage and test time pull against each other, and neither belongs to DFT alone. A defect-per-million target sets required coverage; a cost-per-unit target sets allowable test time; and the architecture in DFT-01 is chosen to sit between them. Negotiating this first is what makes the architecture decidable.
en: Test cost budget from the DEF-04 model
ex: Coverage target derived from DPPM, not inherited
Test time budget traced to a per-unit cost
Targets signed by product and test engineering
rk: Coverage target set by convention. "99% stuck-at" carried from the last program may be far from what this product's DPPM requirement needs.
Test time budget not derived from cost. A test time nobody costed becomes whatever the patterns need, and the per-unit cost is discovered at production.
Fault model chosen at pattern generation. Adding cell-aware late multiplies pattern volume against a tester memory budget already fixed.
Targets agreed without product engineering. The organization that owns field quality has to own the coverage number, or it will be renegotiated when patterns run long.
No per-block differentiation. Memory-dominated blocks and control logic need different approaches, and a single flat target over-tests one and under-tests the other.
DFT-02.fn: Step 3 has a large downstream cost. Cell-aware patterns catch defects the other models miss and multiply pattern count doing it, so the decision belongs here with the cost model in the room rather than at DFT-07 when the patterns are being generated.

DFT-03.t: MBIST / BIRA / BISR Architecture for Embedded Memories
s: Inventory the memories and set a test requirement per instance
Architect MBIST and allocate the engines
Select test algorithms per memory type
Architect the BIRA and repair analysis
Integrate BISR and the fuse path with ARCH-07
Agree the repair interface jointly with the memory designers
Insert and integrate the MBIST logic
Verify the architecture and release its specification
p: Repair interface agreement with the memory designers
r: MBIST / BISR insertion and test collateral. The MBIST / BISR architecture, its insertion and its collateral come from here, including the repair collateral test engineering will run.
DFT architecture specification. Memory test is a large part of the overall architecture, not a separate subject.
pu: Architect memory test and repair—MBIST engines, BIRA analysis, BISR repair and the fuse path—for a design where memory is most of the die.

On an accelerator the arrays dominate both area and defect exposure, and they cannot be tested by scan. MBIST is how they are tested and repair is how the yield is recovered; both have to be designed jointly with AMS-09, because the array provides the spares and this activity provides the engine that uses them.
en: Redundancy scheme from AMS-09 in progress
Fuse map and lifecycle model from ARCH-07
ex: Repair interface written jointly with the memory designers
Repair path verified end to end, not in pieces
MBIST runtime inside the test time budget
rk: Repair interface specified separately from the array. Two consistent specifications that disagree, found at pattern generation when both are frozen.
Algorithms chosen without the failure modes. March algorithms differ in what they catch; a default choice misses the defect modes this array actually exhibits.
Fuse capacity insufficient. Repair data has to be stored, and an allocation made without counting the worst-case repair set produces unrepairable parts.
MBIST runtime unbudgeted. Memory test on an array-dominated die can dominate test time, and it is often costed after the architecture is fixed.
Repair not verified end to end. A repair path proven in pieces and never exercised from failure through analysis to fuse blow fails at production test.
DFT-03.fn: Step 6 is the joint decision with AMS-09. Both sides can specify an internally consistent repair scheme that the other cannot implement, and writing the interface together is the only reliable way to avoid it.

DFT-04.t: TAP, Boundary Scan, and IJTAG Debug Access Architecture
s: Define the access architecture — TAP and IJTAG network topology
Implement boundary scan per IEEE 1149.1
Build the IJTAG instrument network and its description files
Define the debug and trace access paths
Integrate security lockdown per lifecycle state
Verify the access network and generate the description files
p: Instrument network with ICL and PDL descriptions
Access network verification results and description files
r: JTAG / IJTAG description files (BSDL, ICL, PDL). The BSDL, ICL and PDL description files are generated and validated here, and they are what board test and ATE consume.
DFT architecture specification. The access network is how every other DFT feature is reached.
pu: Design the access network—boundary scan, IJTAG, TAP controller and the debug paths—that every test, every repair and every silicon debug session runs through.

The TAP is the door into the chip. It is used at wafer sort, at package test, during bring-up and in the field, and it is also the door ARCH-07 needs to lock in production. Designing it is a negotiation between access and security rather than a purely technical exercise.
en: Security lockdown policy defined by ARCH-07
Pin and bump budget known from ARCH-08
ex: Lockdown transitions tested, not only implemented
Description files generated and validated before tapeout
Debug access preserved for the lifecycle states that need it
rk: Debug access designed out for security. A part that cannot be debugged in the field is a part whose first field failure has no diagnostic path.
Lockdown untested. The lifecycle transition that locks the TAP is the one nobody exercises, because exercising it makes the part undebuggable.
Description files generated late. BSDL and ICL are consumed by board test and ATE; generating them near tapeout leaves no time to validate them.
Access network verified only in functional mode. The network exists to work when the design does not, and that is the mode that needs proving.
Pin budget for debug not reserved. Trace ports need pins, and a bump map fixed without them means debug through a narrow channel.
DFT-04.fn: Step 5 is where the negotiation with ARCH-07 lands. Every path this activity opens for debug is a path security has to close in production lifecycle states, and the lock has to be testable without making the part permanently undebuggable.

DFT-05.t: On-Chip Clock Controller Design for At-Speed Test
s: Establish the at-speed test requirement per clock domain
Architect the OCC and its PLL interface
Design launch-capture sequencing and pulse control
Define the multi-domain and cross-domain at-speed strategy
Insert and integrate the OCC logic
Verify at-speed clocking across the domains
r: DFT architecture specification. At-speed clocking is what makes transition-fault coverage achievable, so it belongs in the architecture.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. Transition patterns cannot be generated for domains the OCC cannot clock at speed.
pu: Design the on-chip clock controllers that generate at-speed test clocks—because transition-fault testing needs clock pulses the tester cannot supply at frequency.

Stuck-at testing runs slowly and catches static defects. The defects that matter for a high-frequency part are timing-related, and catching them needs launch-capture pulses at functional speed. The tester cannot produce them, so the chip has to produce them for itself.
en: Clock architecture and domains fixed by ARCH-05
PLL test-mode behavior known from AMS-02
ex: At-speed clocking available on every domain that needs coverage
Cross-domain at-speed strategy defined and verified
OCC inserted before clock tree synthesis, not after
rk: At-speed test not supported on every domain. Coverage then has a hole exactly where the fastest logic is, which is where transition defects concentrate.
Cross-domain paths untested at speed. These are among the most timing-marginal paths in the design and the hardest to cover.
OCC interaction with the PLL unverified. A controller that cannot get a clean clock from the PLL in test mode produces patterns that fail on good silicon.
Power during at-speed test ignored. Scan shift followed by at-speed capture creates switching activity far above functional, and the IR drop can cause failures on good parts.
OCC inserted late. It sits in the clock path, so adding it after clock tree synthesis means redoing the tree.
DFT-05.fn: Step 4 is the difficult part. Single-domain at-speed test is well understood; testing paths that cross domains at speed requires the domains to have a defined phase relationship in test mode, which is a constraint on the clocking architecture rather than on DFT.

DFT-06.t: Scan Insertion and DFT DRC Closure
s: Set up and configure scan insertion
Insert and stitch the scan chains
Insert the compression logic
Insert test points for coverage improvement
Analyze DFT DRC and close the violations
Verify scan chain integrity in simulation
Sign off insertion and hand off the netlist
r: DFT DRC clean report. The clean report is produced here, and clean means every violation fixed or explicitly accepted with its coverage cost.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. Coverage achievable at DFT-07 is bounded by how clean this activity got.
pu: Insert the scan chains, compression and test logic into the design during synthesis, and drive DFT design-rule checking to clean.

This is where the architecture becomes logic. DFT DRC violations—uncontrollable clocks, unresettable flops, blocked scan paths—reduce coverage silently, and each one is a set of faults ATPG will never be able to target.
ex: Every DRC violation fixed or accepted with a measured coverage cost
Chains balanced against the shift time budget
Chain integrity verified in simulation before ATPG
rk: DRC violations accepted without measuring their coverage cost. Each one silently removes faults from the targetable set, and the total is invisible until ATPG reports a low number.
Test points inserted without area budget. They improve coverage and cost area and timing, and adding them late competes with closure.
Chain balance ignored. Unbalanced chains set shift time by the longest one, and shift time is most of the test time.
Insertion done once and not re-run. Netlist changes after insertion leave chains stale, and the mismatch appears at pattern validation.
Chain integrity unverified. A broken chain makes everything behind it untestable, and finding that at ATE rather than in simulation costs a silicon turn.
DFT-06.fn: Step 5 is the substance. Every DFT DRC violation is a region of logic ATPG cannot control or observe, and the coverage loss is silent—the tool simply reports a lower number without saying which violation caused it.

DFT-07.t: ATPG Pattern Generation and Coverage Closure
s: Set up ATPG, constraints and test mode configuration
Generate stuck-at patterns and analyze coverage
Generate transition and at-speed patterns
Generate cell-aware patterns
Analyze untestable faults and justify the coverage
Reduce and compact the pattern volume
Close coverage against the DFT-02 targets
Assemble and release the pattern sets
p: Stuck-at pattern set with coverage analysis
r: ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. The pattern sets and their coverage report are generated here, and the coverage report is what the quality target is measured against.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. Coverage against target is one of the checklist's quantitative entries.
pu: Generate the ATPG patterns—stuck-at, transition and cell-aware—and drive coverage to the targets DFT-02 agreed, inside the pattern volume the tester can hold.

Two constraints pull against each other here: coverage has to reach the quality target and pattern volume has to fit tester memory and test time. Every technique that raises one raises the other, and closing both is the work.
en: Scan-inserted netlist available and DRC clean from DFT-06
Tester memory and test time budget known from TEST-09
ex: Coverage meets the DFT-02 targets per fault model
Pattern volume inside tester memory without splitting
Untestable faults analyzed rather than accepted
rk: Coverage target missed and accepted late. The remedies—test points, DRC fixes, architecture changes—all need an RTL or netlist change, and none are available near tapeout.
Pattern volume exceeding tester memory. Patterns that do not fit have to be split across loads, which multiplies test time and cost.
Untestable faults accepted without analysis. A fixable DRC violation reported as an untestable fault is coverage given away.
Cell-aware added late. It multiplies pattern count against a budget already set, forcing a choice between coverage and test time with no room to negotiate.
Patterns generated on a netlist that then changes. Any netlist change after generation invalidates the set, and regeneration takes weeks.
DFT-07.fn: Step 5 is what makes a coverage number honest. Faults reported as untestable are either genuinely untestable—tied off, redundant—or untestable because of a DRC violation, and only analysis distinguishes a real limit from a fixable one.

DFT-08.t: Gate-Level Pattern Validation and ATE Format Conversion
s: Set up the pattern simulation environment
Validate patterns in zero-delay gate-level simulation
Simulate patterns with SDF timing annotation
Debug pattern failures and regenerate the affected sets
Convert patterns to STIL and WGL formats
Validate tester format and timing sets against the ATE
Release the patterns and sign the DFT tapeout entry
r: Pattern validation (GLS) report and ATE-ready pattern files. The validated, ATE-ready pattern files are produced here—patterns proved to run rather than assumed to.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. DFT signs the checklist on validated patterns, not on generated ones.
pu: Prove the patterns actually run—simulate them against the netlist with timing, convert them to tester format, and hand ATE a set that works.

A pattern set that passes in ATPG and fails in gate-level simulation is a pattern set that would have failed on silicon. This activity is the last place a pattern problem is cheap, and it is also where the format conversion for the tester is proved rather than assumed.
en: Netlist and SDF available from PD-09
ex: Patterns validated with timing, not only zero-delay
Format conversion validated against the actual tester capability
DFT tapeout checklist entry signed on validated patterns
rk: Validation skipped for schedule. A pattern failure then appears at ATE bring-up, where the diagnosis competes with everything else happening at first silicon.
Only zero-delay simulation run. Timing-related pattern failures are exactly what at-speed patterns are meant to detect, and they are invisible without SDF.
Format conversion assumed. STIL and WGL translation has tool-specific quirks, and a set that converts cleanly can still time incorrectly on the tester.
Regeneration cost underestimated. A pattern failure requiring regeneration puts the whole set back through DFT-07, which takes weeks not days.
Timing sets not validated against the actual tester. A pattern that assumes an edge placement the ATE cannot produce fails on hardware for a reason no simulation shows.
DFT-08.fn: Step 3 catches what zero-delay cannot: patterns that violate timing at the capture edge. On an at-speed pattern set this is not a formality—a launch-capture sequence that closes in ATPG and fails in timing simulation would have produced yield loss on good die.

DFT-09.t: Scan Compression and Chain Routing Feasibility with Physical Design
s: Analyze chain routing feasibility against the floorplan
Align the compression network topology to the physical partitions
Define the chain ordering and reordering strategy
Assess the congestion impact of the test network
Confirm test clock distribution feasibility
Agree the physical DFT plan with physical design
p: Compression topology aligned to physical partitions
r: DFT architecture specification. An architecture that cannot be routed is not an architecture, and this is where that is established.
DFT DRC clean report. Physical feasibility findings often send work back into insertion, so the two are closed together.
pu: Work with physical design on whether the scan chains and compression network can actually be routed—and fix the plan before routing rather than after.

Compression networks connect every chain to a shared decompressor and compactor, which produces long routes across the die competing with functional signals for the same resource. A compression ratio that is optimal on paper and unroutable in practice is discovered at PD-06, when the remedies are expensive.
en: DFT architecture and compression defined by DFT-01
Scan insertion in progress in DFT-06
ex: Compression network confirmed routable at the chosen ratio
Chain reordering strategy preserves diagnosis capability
Physical DFT plan agreed before detailed routing starts
rk: Compression ratio unroutable. A ratio chosen for pattern volume alone produces a network that consumes routing resource the functional design needs.
Chain reordering breaking diagnosis. Physical reordering improves routing and can destroy the chain-to-block mapping diagnosis depends on.
Test clock distribution treated as functional. Scan shift clocks reach every flop and have their own skew and power requirements.
Feasibility assessed after routing starts. The findings then arrive when the only remaining remedy is to reduce coverage.
Hierarchical partition boundaries ignored. Chains crossing physical partitions carry a routing and timing cost that a logical view does not show.
DFT-09.fn: Step 3 is where the two disciplines usually collide. DFT wants chains ordered for balance and diagnosis; physical design wants them ordered for routing. Reordering after placement is the standard compromise, and agreeing it here avoids arguing about it during closure.

DFT-10.t: eFuse, Chip ID, and Memory Repair Infrastructure
s: Inventory the fuse consumers — repair, trim, ID, lifecycle, security
Allocate capacity against the worst-case need
Integrate the eFuse array and its programming path
Design the fuse read, shadow register and distribution logic
Define the chip identity and traceability scheme
Agree the lifecycle state encoding with ARCH-07
Verify the fuse infrastructure end to end
p: eFuse array integration and programming path
Lifecycle state encoding agreed with the security architecture
r: MBIST / BISR insertion and test collateral. Repair is only useful if the repair data can be stored and read back, which this activity provides.
JTAG / IJTAG description files. Fuse programming and readback run through the access network, and the instrument descriptions cover them.
pu: Build the fuse and identity infrastructure—eFuse arrays, chip ID, repair storage, lifecycle state—that repair, traceability and security all depend on.

Fuses are written once and read forever. They store memory repair, trim values, chip identity and lifecycle state, and every one of those consumers has its own requirements. Getting the capacity or the read path wrong produces parts that cannot be repaired, identified or secured.
en: Repair storage requirements known from DFT-03
ex: Capacity sized against worst-case, not average, repair need
Programming and read paths verified before tapeout
Lifecycle transitions exercisable in test
rk: Capacity sized to the average repair need. Repair need is a distribution, and the parts needing most repair are exactly the ones the allocation fails.
Programming path untested. Fuses are one-time; a programming path that does not work correctly produces parts that are permanently wrong.
Fuse read timing in the boot path unconsidered. Repair and trim values have to be distributed before the logic that uses them is released from reset.
Traceability scheme designed late. Chip identity is needed for yield analysis and field returns, and retrofitting it means parts that cannot be traced.
Lifecycle encoding without a test path. A lifecycle transition that cannot be exercised in test is a transition whose correctness is unknown until the field.
DFT-10.fn: Step 2 is the step that fails silently. Every consumer asks for a modest allocation, the total is set once, and the worst-case repair set—which is a distribution rather than an average—exceeds it on the parts that most needed repairing.

s: Collect debug requirements from validation and design
Architect the observability — trace, triggers, snapshot
Budget the trace ports and bandwidth
Design the trigger and cross-trigger network
Implement internal state snapshot and scan dump capability
Verify the debug infrastructure and document it for the lab
r: JTAG / IJTAG description files. Debug instruments are part of the access network and are described alongside it.
DFT architecture specification. Design-for-debug is part of the DFT architecture rather than a separate concern.
pu: Design the observability the lab will need—trace, triggers, internal visibility, design-for-debug—because at bring-up the only view into the chip is the one designed in months earlier.

Silicon debug is constrained entirely by what was built. A failure that cannot be observed cannot be diagnosed, and the difference between a two-day debug and a two-month one is usually whether someone put a trigger and a trace port where it was needed.
ex: Debug paths verified before tapeout, not first used at bring-up
Trace bandwidth sufficient for the events validation named
Capabilities documented for the people who will use them
rk: Debug traded away for area. The saving is small and the cost is paid at bring-up, in weeks, by a different team.
Requirements collected from design rather than validation. The people who will debug the silicon know what they need to see; the people who built it usually assume it works.
Trace bandwidth inadequate. A trace port too narrow to capture the event of interest produces a debug capability that cannot answer the question.
Debug infrastructure unverified. It is used first when the chip is misbehaving, which is the worst moment to discover the debug path is broken.
No documentation. A capability the lab does not know exists is a capability that was not built.
DFT-11.fn: Step 5 is the cheapest debug capability available. Scan chains already reach every flop; adding the ability to halt and dump their contents turns the test infrastructure into a full internal state view for almost no extra area.

s: Enumerate the modes and corners against the operating conditions
Define clocks and generated clocks across the design
Specify exceptions, false paths and multicycle paths
Write the IO and interface timing constraints
Write the test mode and scan constraints
Validate the constraints with quality checking tools
r: Validated SDC constraint set per mode and corner. The constraint set is developed and validated here, and "validated" is what distinguishes it from a file of assertions.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. QoR is only meaningful against constraints; an unconstrained path reports as passing.
pu: Write the constraints the whole implementation is optimized and signed off against—clocks, generated clocks, IO timing, exceptions, test modes—and validate them rather than assume them.

Constraints are the specification synthesis and physical design actually read. A missing clock definition produces a design optimized for a path nobody cares about; a wrong false path produces one that closes in the tool and fails in silicon. Every hour spent validating them here saves days at PD-09.
en: Corner and mode definition available from PDK-11
RTL hierarchy stable enough to constrain
ex: No unconstrained paths in the design
Every exception justified by a design reason, not by a violation
One constraint set used by both synthesis and signoff
rk: Unconstrained paths reported as clean. A path with no constraint is a path the tool ignores, and it appears in the report as no violation at all.
Exceptions written to close timing. A false path added because the path would not close is a silicon failure being converted into a green report.
Constraints diverging between synthesis and signoff. Two constraint sets means optimizing against one and being judged against the other.
Test mode constraints written late. Scan shift and at-speed modes have their own timing, and a design closed only in functional mode fails at ATE.
IO constraints assumed from the interface specification. Actual budgets come from the package and channel analysis in SIPI-07, not from the protocol document.
SYN-01.fn: Step 6 is not review, it is tooling. Constraint quality checkers find unconstrained paths, conflicting exceptions and clocks that reach nothing, and they find them in minutes—which is why every drop should be re-checked rather than checked once.

s: Select the library and mapping strategy
Run baseline mapping and optimization
Optimize datapath and arithmetic structures
Configure multi-bit banking and useful skew
Recover area on non-critical paths
Analyze QoR and iterate the optimization
r: Synthesis QoR report per drop. The QoR the report describes is produced here, drop after drop.
N1 and N2 netlist drops. Each drop is this activity's output at a point in time, with whatever optimization was enabled.
pu: Map the RTL onto the qualified library and optimize it for the PPA budget—Vt mix, multi-bit banking, useful skew, datapath structure.

Technology mapping is where architecture becomes gates and where most of the achievable PPA is decided. The same RTL mapped two ways can differ by 20% in area and a hundred millivolts in achievable frequency, and the difference is entirely in how this activity is configured.
en: Libraries qualified and frozen by PDK-03
ex: Area recovered on non-critical paths, not only speed optimized
Vt menu used across its range, not defaulted
QoR reported normalized so drops are comparable
rk: Everything optimized for speed. Area and leakage on non-critical paths are given away for performance nobody asked for, and the die grows.
Multi-bit banking configured late. Clock power depends heavily on it, and adding it after closure means re-timing the design.
Useful skew used to hide a timing problem. It buys real margin and also makes the clock tree harder to build; using it to rescue a path that should be restructured moves the problem to PD-07.
Library subset used without knowing it. Synthesis using only part of the Vt menu produces avoidable leakage, and nobody notices because the design closes.
QoR compared drop to drop without normalizing. A netlist with more RTL in it is not directly comparable to the last one, and the trend becomes noise.
SYN-02.fn: Step 5 is where area is won without cost. Most of a design is not on the critical path, and recovering area and leakage there is free performance-wise—but it only happens if someone configures the flow to do it rather than optimizing everything for speed.

s: Define the N0 scope — what must be representative, what may be stubbed
Black-box and stub the incomplete blocks
Bootstrap the constraints for N0
Elaborate the netlist and run structural sanity checks
Release N0 and hand it over to physical design
p: N0 scope definition — representative versus stubbed
Released N0 netlist with a stated limitation list
r: N0 flow-flush netlist for PD flow setup. The N0 netlist is assembled and released here, and its value is entirely in arriving early rather than in being correct.
Physical design handoff package per drop. N0 is the first handoff, and it sets the format every later one follows.
pu: Release the N0 flow-flush netlist—functionally incomplete, structurally representative—so physical design can build and debug its flow against a real database months before the design is ready.

N0 exists to be wrong in the right way. It has the right hierarchy, the right macros and roughly the right size, and it does not need to work. Its entire purpose is to let PD-01 find its flow problems on a throwaway netlist rather than on the one the schedule depends on.
en: Enough RTL exists to elaborate a representative hierarchy
PD flow setup ready to receive a netlist
ex: Representative in hierarchy, instance count and macro content
Limitations stated explicitly with the release
Delivered on the date PD's flow setup needs it, not when it is good
rk: N0 delayed until it is good. The point is to be early; a correct N0 delivered late has become N1 and left PD's flow undebugged.
Not representative in the dimensions that matter. A netlist with a tenth of the instances exercises none of the runtime and capacity problems PD needs to find.
Limitations not stated. Physical design chasing timing on a stubbed netlist wastes a week before someone explains it was never going to close.
Stub strategy that changes the hierarchy. A hierarchy that differs from the real one means the flow is set up for a structure that will not arrive.
Treated as a milestone rather than a tool. N0 is scaffolding; celebrating it as progress distracts from the fact that no real design has been synthesized.
SYN-03.fn: Step 1 is the whole activity. N0 has to be representative in the dimensions PD's flow cares about—hierarchy, macro count, instance count, pin count—and can be arbitrarily wrong in everything else. Getting that distinction right is what makes it cheap.
