s: Set up the physical-aware flow with the floorplan
Run floorplan-aware mapping and optimization
Model macros and blockages in placement
Run the congestion feedback loop with physical design
Restructure logic in the congested regions
Compare QoR against the non-physical synthesis result
r: Synthesis QoR report per drop. Physical-aware results are the ones that predict what physical design will actually achieve.
Physical design handoff package per drop. A netlist synthesized against the floorplan is a materially better handoff than one synthesized against a wire model.
pu: Synthesize with the floorplan in the loop—physical-aware mapping, congestion feedback, placement-driven restructuring—so the netlist that reaches physical design is already routable.

Logic synthesis without physical information optimizes for a wire model that does not exist. On a large die the difference between estimated and actual wire delay is large enough to invalidate the optimization, and the correction happens either here or as weeks of congestion work at PD-06.
en: Floorplan available and stable from PD-02
ex: Netlist synthesized against a floorplan PD is actually using
Congestion feedback flowing in both directions
Runtime cost justified by a measured QoR improvement
rk: Floorplan too immature to synthesize against. Physical-aware synthesis against a floorplan that then changes produces optimization for a layout that never exists.
Congestion feedback one-directional. Synthesis restructures and physical design re-places; without both, each optimizes against the other's stale result.
Runtime cost not justified. Physical-aware flows are slow, and without the QoR comparison nobody knows whether the extra hours bought anything.
Restructuring breaking hierarchy. Aggressive cross-boundary optimization improves QoR and makes the netlist harder to close hierarchically and harder to equivalence-check.
Blockages not modelled. Macros and their keep-out regions dominate placement on this die, and synthesis blind to them produces logic that cannot be placed where it assumed.
SYN-04.fn: Step 6 answers whether the added runtime is worth it. Physical-aware synthesis is slower; comparing its QoR against the wire-load-model result is what justifies the cost, and occasionally shows the floorplan is the problem rather than the logic.

SYN-05.t: N1 Netlist Drop and QoR Baseline
s: Take in the RTL drop and review the delta against N0
Run synthesis and close at block level
Incorporate the physical design feedback
Analyze the QoR delta against the N0 baseline
Compile the issue list for the next drop
Release N1 and hand it off to physical design
p: RTL drop intake and delta review
r: N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The first of the two quality drops, with the baseline it establishes.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. N1 sets the baseline the QoR trend is measured from; every later drop's delta is read against this number.
pu: Release the N1 drop—the first netlist meant to be closed—against PD's feedback from its flow setup, and establish the QoR baseline every later drop is measured against.

N0 proved the flow ran. N1 is where the design's actual QoR first becomes visible: real timing, real area, real congestion. The number it establishes is the one PD-05 will work from and the one everyone will argue about for the next three months.
en: RTL stable enough that a drop is meaningful
PD flow setup complete and feedback available from PD-01
ex: QoR baseline established against a substantially complete design
Delta against N0 explained, not only reported
Issue list handed forward to N2
rk: N1 released before RTL is worth synthesizing. A drop taken from unstable RTL produces a baseline that means nothing and a PD turn that chases moving targets.
QoR delta not analyzed. Knowing the numbers without knowing what changed them leaves the next drop guessing about what to fix.
Issue list not carried forward. N2 then rediscovers the same problems, and the drop cadence loses its cumulative benefit.
PD feedback arriving after the drop. Feedback from flow setup has to reach synthesis before N1 is run, not after it is released.
Baseline set on a partial design. A QoR baseline missing significant blocks flatters the trend and hides the growth that follows.
SYN-05.fn: Step 5 is what makes the drop cadence a process rather than a sequence of releases. Each drop should hand forward a named list of what it could not fix and why, so the next one starts from a position rather than from scratch.

s: Establish the power analysis baseline and identify hot spots
Insert clock gating and analyze its efficiency
Optimize the Vt mix for leakage
Implement operand isolation and datapath gating
Re-optimize with real switching activity data
Report power QoR against the budget
p: Power analysis baseline and hot spots
Clock gating insertion and efficiency report
r: Synthesis QoR report per drop. Power is one of the three QoR axes, and the only one that needs external activity data to measure honestly.
Power intent implementation report. Dynamic power optimization sits alongside the UPF implementation from SYN-07 in the same report.
pu: Reduce power where it is actually spent—clock gating, operand isolation, Vt mix—driven by real switching activity rather than by defaults.

Power optimization without activity data is guesswork. Clock gating inserted everywhere costs area and saves little; inserted where the data says the logic is idle it saves a meaningful fraction of dynamic power. The activity data comes from verification, which makes this a cross-stage dependency more than a synthesis setting.
ex: Optimization driven by real activity data, not defaults
Clock gating efficiency measured, not assumed
Power reported at the operating point the product uses
rk: Optimization driven by default activity. Uniform switching assumptions produce gating where it saves nothing and none where it would.
Clock gating efficiency unmeasured. Gates inserted without measuring how often they actually gate cost area and leakage for no benefit.
Vt mix skewed to low-Vt for timing. Leakage grows non-linearly, and a design closed on low-Vt everywhere blows its static power budget.
Power measured at the wrong operating point. The number that matters is at the DVFS point the product runs at, not at nominal.
Optimization deferred to the final turn. Power changes timing; a design closed on timing and then power-optimized has to be re-closed.
SYN-06.fn: Step 5 is what separates power optimization from power decoration. Switching activity from the DV-04 workload simulations tells the tool which logic is actually idle; without it, gating is inserted by structural heuristic and saves a fraction of what it could.

SYN-07.t: Low-Power Synthesis and UPF Consistency Checking
s: Ingest and elaborate the UPF in the synthesis flow
Infer and insert isolation cells and level shifters
Handle always-on and feed-through paths
Insert retention cells and their control
Check UPF-to-netlist consistency
Write the power intent implementation report
p: Elaborated UPF in the synthesis flow
Inserted isolation and level shifter cells
Retention cell insertion and control logic
r: Power intent implementation report. The implementation report is produced here—what was inferred, what was inserted, and where intent and netlist agree.
Formal equivalence clean report per drop. Low-power cells complicate equivalence checking, and the two activities have to agree on how they are handled.
pu: Implement the power intent in the netlist—isolation cells, level shifters, retention flops, always-on paths—from the UPF, and prove the netlist and the intent still agree.

UPF describes what should happen; synthesis is where it becomes cells. An isolation cell missing at a domain boundary is a design that corrupts data on power-down, and it is invisible in any functional check that does not model power. The consistency check between netlist and intent is the only reliable detector.
en: UPF available and tool-accepted from RTL-05
ex: Every domain boundary has verified isolation
UPF and netlist consistent, checked rather than assumed
Retention and always-on requirements handed to physical design
rk: Isolation inferred but not verified. A missing cell at one boundary corrupts state on power-down and appears in no functional test.
Retention cells inserted without physical planning. They have a different footprint and power connectivity, and adding them late disturbs the floorplan.
Always-on paths not identified. Logic that must survive a domain shutting down and is not marked always-on is powered down with it.
UPF and netlist diverging. Two descriptions of the same intent, and downstream tools reading different ones.
Level shifters omitted between voltage domains. The design functions in simulation and fails at the voltage extremes in silicon.
SYN-07.fn: Step 5 runs in parallel and is the one that must not be skipped. The netlist and the UPF are two descriptions of the same intent, and any divergence between them propagates into physical design and verification as a defect nobody can attribute.

SYN-08.t: N2 Netlist Drop and Closure Risk Statement
s: Take in the RTL and ECO changes since N1
Run full synthesis with all optimizations enabled
Assess the impact of late RTL changes
Check congestion and timing convergence
Incorporate the turn-1 feedback from physical design
Release N2 with a closure risk statement
p: RTL and ECO intake record since N1
r: N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The second quality drop, and the last structurally changeable one.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. The N2 QoR is the best available prediction of what the final turn will reach.
pu: Release the N2 drop with everything enabled—full optimization, power, low-power intent, physical awareness—and state honestly how much closure risk remains.

N2 is the last drop before the FFN and the last chance to change anything structurally. Its QoR is the best prediction available of what the final turn will achieve, and the closure risk statement it carries is what tells the program whether the tapeout date is credible.
en: Turn 1 complete with feedback from PD-05
Power and low-power optimization available from SYN-06 and SYN-07
RTL changes since N1 controlled through RTL-10
ex: Closure risk stated specifically, with paths, blocks and options
Turn-1 feedback incorporated rather than deferred
Late changes assessed before inclusion
rk: Closure risk understated. An optimistic risk statement at N2 removes the program's last opportunity to take a frequency or feature concession while it is still cheap.
Late RTL changes absorbed without assessment. A functional change arriving between N1 and N2 can invalidate the turn-1 closure work entirely.
All optimizations enabled for the first time at N2. Enabling power, low-power and physical awareness together for the first time produces a QoR nobody can attribute.
Turn-1 feedback not incorporated. N2 then repeats N1's physical problems, and turn 2 spends its time on the same issues.
Treated as the final netlist. N2 is not the FFN, and freezing behavior around it removes the RTL freeze discipline that SYN-09 depends on.
SYN-08.fn: Step 6 is the honest part. A drop released with "timing is converging" tells nobody anything; one released with "forty paths in two blocks remain, all in the compute cluster, requiring a restructure or a frequency concession" gives the program a decision.

SYN-09.t: FFN (Final Full Netlist) Release and Functional Freeze
s: Confirm RTL freeze and take the final intake
Run the final synthesis
Freeze the constraint set
Verify final equivalence and UPF consistency
Assemble the handoff package for the final turn
Release the FFN and declare functional freeze
p: Final equivalence and UPF consistency results
Handoff package for the final turn
FFN release with functional freeze declaration
r: FFN—final full netlist, release-tagged. The final netlist is released and tagged here, and it is the milestone the stage ends on.
Validated SDC constraint set. Constraints freeze with the FFN—closing against moving constraints is closing against nothing.
Physical design handoff package per drop. The final handoff, and the one PD-13 closes against.
pu: Release the FFN—the final full netlist—against frozen RTL, with constraints frozen and equivalence proved, and declare that nothing functional changes after it.

The FFN is a commitment more than a deliverable. Everything after it is physical: PD-13 closes on this netlist and SO-02 signs off on what PD produces. A functional change after the FFN restarts both, which is why the freeze around it has to be real.
en: N2 closure risk understood from SYN-08
Equivalence methodology proven across earlier drops
ex: Equivalence proved on the actual FFN, not on a proxy
Constraints frozen with the netlist
Functional freeze declared and its exception process published
rk: FFN released against RTL that is not actually frozen. The final turn then closes against a moving netlist, and every change restarts it.
Constraints still changing after the FFN. A design closed against one constraint set and signed off against another has not been signed off.
Equivalence not proved on the final netlist. The last synthesis run is the one most likely to contain a transformation error, and the least likely to be checked under schedule pressure.
Functional freeze declared and not enforced. Post-FFN functional ECOs are sometimes unavoidable and must be exceptional, visible and costed.
Handoff package incomplete. The final turn needs constraints, UPF, DFT collateral and abstracts together; a missing item stops closure at its start.
SYN-09.fn: Step 1 is a confirmation rather than a formality. If RTL-10 has not actually declared freeze, the FFN is a snapshot of a moving design, and the final turn in PD-13 will be closing against something that changes underneath it.

SYN-10.t: RTL-to-Netlist Formal Equivalence Checking per Drop
s: Set up the equivalence methodology and tools
Check block-level equivalence per drop
Handle black-boxes and constraints for incomplete drops
Check chip-level equivalence per drop
Configure DFT and clock gating transformation handling
Debug and resolve the non-equivalences
Report equivalence results per drop
Run continuous checking across the drop sequence
p: DFT and clock gating handling configuration
Equivalence checking log across the drop sequence
r: Formal equivalence clean report per drop. The per-drop equivalence reports are produced here, and "per drop" is what makes them a control rather than a final check.
FFN—final full netlist. An FFN that has not been proved equivalent is a netlist nobody can claim was verified.
pu: Prove that every netlist still means what the RTL meant—formal equivalence per drop, including through DFT insertion, clock gating and low-power transformations.

Synthesis rewrites the design, and the tools that do it are not infallible. Equivalence checking is the only evidence that the netlist implements the RTL that verification actually verified; without it, a transformation error is discovered in silicon as behavior nobody can trace to a bug.
en: DFT insertion methodology known from DFT-06
ex: Every drop checked, not only the final one
Non-equivalences resolved rather than waived
Chip-level equivalence clean on the FFN
rk: Equivalence run only on the final netlist. A transformation error introduced at N1 is then found at the FFN, when the debug competes with tapeout.
Non-equivalences waived to make progress. Each waiver is a place where the netlist may not implement the verified RTL, and they accumulate quietly.
DFT transformations not modelled. The checker reports thousands of differences and everyone stops reading the report.
Black-box handling too permissive. Boxing out a block to get a clean result excludes exactly the logic that was not checked.
Debug capacity underestimated. A single real non-equivalence on a design this size can take a week to localize, and there is rarely a week available.
SYN-10.fn: Step 5 is where most of the difficulty lives. Scan insertion and clock gating change the netlist in ways that are correct and not structurally equivalent, and setting up the checker to accept those and reject everything else is the skilled part of the activity.

SYN-11.t: Per-Drop QoR Reporting Against PPA Budgets
s: Build the reporting framework and ingest the budgets
Report and analyze timing per drop
Compare against budget and apply the escalation rules
Report area and power per drop
Analyze trends across the drop sequence
Run continuous reporting across the stage
r: Synthesis QoR report per drop against PPA targets. The per-drop QoR reports are produced here, and "against targets" is what makes them usable.
N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The delta report accompanying each drop comes from here—the normalized comparison that says what changed between drops and why.
pu: Report timing, area and power against the budget after every drop, and escalate when a block is diverging rather than when it has already blown its allocation.

QoR reported in absolute terms tells nobody anything. Reported against the ARCH-06 allocation and trended across drops, it says which blocks are converging, which are not, and how much of the gap is still recoverable—which is the only version a program manager can act on.
en: Reporting framework agreed with the PPA lead
ex: Every report references the budget, not only the absolute number
Divergence escalated on a rule, not on judgment
Trends normalized so drops are comparable
rk: QoR reported in absolute terms. Numbers with no budget reference cannot be acted on, and everyone forms their own opinion of whether they are acceptable.
No escalation rule. Divergence noticed and not escalated becomes a surprise at the final turn, when there is nothing left to do about it.
Reports not normalized across drops. More RTL in a later drop makes the trend meaningless unless the comparison accounts for it.
Power reported at nominal only. The number that matters is at the product's operating point, and reporting at nominal understates it consistently.
Reporting stopping between drops. The interesting question is whether a block is improving, and that needs data between releases as well as at them.
SYN-11.fn: Step 5 is the part that predicts. A block 10% over budget and improving is a different problem from one 5% over and flat, and only a trend across drops distinguishes them.

SYN-12.t: Per-Drop Netlist Handoff and QoR Delta Review
s: Define the handoff package contents and format
Assemble the package for each drop
Agree acceptance criteria with physical design
Review the QoR delta with physical design per drop
Track issues between drops
Run the continuous handoff across the drop sequence
p: Handoff log across the drop sequence
r: Physical design handoff package per drop. The handoff packages are assembled and accepted here, and acceptance rather than delivery is the standard.
N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The delta review is where the drop is actually transferred: the joint reading of the QoR delta is what turns a delivered package into an accepted one.
pu: Hand each netlist to physical design as a complete, accepted package—netlist, constraints, UPF, DFT collateral, abstracts—and review the QoR delta together rather than throwing results over a wall.

The handoff is where two teams either share a picture of the design or maintain two. Six man-months across the stage buys a structured package and a joint review per drop, and it prevents the pattern where physical design spends a week discovering what synthesis already knew.
en: First netlist drop ready in SYN-03
Acceptance criteria negotiable with physical design
ex: Every package accepted rather than merely delivered
QoR delta read jointly at every drop, not asynchronously
Issues tracked across drops rather than re-raised
rk: Packages delivered without acceptance. Physical design discovers the gap mid-turn, and the turn absorbs the delay.
QoR reviewed asynchronously. A report read separately produces two interpretations, and the disagreement surfaces at the next escalation.
Issues not tracked between drops. Each handoff then starts fresh, and the same problems are raised at every drop.
Package contents changing between drops. Physical design automates against the format, and an inconsistent package breaks their flow.
Handoff treated as a synthesis milestone. It is a shared event; a handoff that PD has not accepted has not happened.
SYN-12.fn: Step 3 is what makes a handoff a transaction rather than a delivery. Acceptance criteria mean physical design can reject a package that is incomplete, and rejection at handoff is far cheaper than discovering the gap three days into a turn.

PD-01.t: Flow Setup and MMMC Environment Build on N0
s: Define the flow scope and build the script framework
Build the MMMC environment across corners and modes
Integrate the scripts, decks and libraries
Run N0 through the flow end to end
Define the hierarchical and block-level flows
Measure the runtime baseline and assess capacity
p: MMMC environment across corners and modes
r: Flow setup release—MMMC environment, scripts and runtime baseline. The flow, the MMMC environment and the runtime baseline are built here, and the runtime baseline is the part the schedule depends on.
MCMM timing closure reports. The scenario set built here is what every later closure report is generated from.
pu: Build the flow—scripts, MMMC environment, decks, runtimes, capacity—and debug it on the N0 flow-flush netlist rather than on the netlist the schedule depends on.

This is why SYN-03 releases a netlist nobody expects to close. Every flow problem—a deck that does not load, a scenario that does not converge, a runtime that exceeds the night—is found here on a throwaway database, weeks before the same problem would have cost a turn.
en: Corner and mode definition final from PDK-11
ex: Flow runs end to end on N0, not on a fragment
Runtime baseline measured and fed to capacity planning
Hierarchical and block-level flows both defined
rk: Flow setup on the first real netlist. Every flow problem then costs a turn, and the turns are the schedule.
MMMC scenarios incomplete. A corner or mode missing from the setup is one the design is never closed at, and it is found at SO-02.
Runtime not measured. A flow that works and takes two days per iteration produces a closure schedule nobody planned, discovered when closure starts.
Hierarchical flow deferred. A design this size cannot be closed flat; deferring the block-level flow means building it under pressure.
Capacity assumed rather than booked. The flow's peak concurrency is known here, and licences take weeks to procure.
PD-01.fn: Step 6 is what makes the schedule credible. A flow that runs correctly and takes forty hours per iteration sets a closure cadence nobody planned for, and knowing that number now is what lets PDK-12 buy capacity before it is needed.

PD-02.t: Floorplan, Macro Placement, and Partition Definition
s: Define the partitions against the design hierarchy
Place the macros — memories, PHYs, analog
Plan standard cell area and set utilization targets
Plan the block boundaries and pin placement
Define the keep-outs, blockages and halos
Review the floorplan and freeze it
r: Floorplan and PDN specification. The floorplan half; PD-03 supplies the power grid it is built against.
Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases. Every turn is placed and routed inside this floorplan; changing it invalidates the turns.
pu: Decide where everything physically goes—partitions, macros, block boundaries, pins, utilization—and freeze it, because everything downstream is built on it.

The floorplan is the most consequential and least reversible decision in the stage. Macro placement sets routing congestion, block boundaries set what can be closed independently, and pin placement sets the top-level routing burden. A floorplan changed at turn 2 invalidates the clock trees, the power grid and the routing built on it.
en: Floorplan intent and bump map from ARCH-08
ex: Floorplan frozen before turn 1 starts
Macro placement validated against congestion, not only access
Pin placement reviewed for top-level routing cost
rk: Macro placement not congestion-aware. Macros placed for access and not for the logic between them produce routing congestion that cannot be fixed at PD-08.
Floorplan changed after turn 1. Clock trees, power grid and routing are all built on it, and all of them are invalidated.
Utilization set too high. A dense floorplan closes area and cannot be routed or timing-closed, and the discovery comes after weeks of work.
Pin placement ignoring top-level routing. Block pins facing the wrong way make top-level routing expensive for the whole rest of the program.
Partitions that do not match the design hierarchy. Closing blocks that cut across logical boundaries makes timing budgets and equivalence checking harder for no gain.
PD-02.fn: Step 2 is where a memory-dominated die is won or lost. Hundreds of macro instances have to be placed so their access paths are short, their power can be delivered and the logic between them can be routed—and moving one late moves everything around it.

PD-03.t: Power Delivery Network Design and Early IR Analysis
s: Define the PDN topology and grid per domain
Implement the grid and insert the straps
Plan the power switches and always-on regions
Run early static IR analysis on the placed design
Plan and place the decap
Refine the PDN and freeze it
r: Floorplan and PDN specification. The power grid half of the deliverable, frozen alongside the floorplan it sits in.
MCMM timing closure reports. IR drop consumes timing margin, so the PDN's quality shows up in closure.
pu: Build the power delivery network—grid topology, straps, switches, decap—and prove by early IR analysis that it can actually feed the die at its power envelope.

The PDN is built early because everything routes around it. Grid density trades directly against routing resource: too sparse and IR drop eats timing margin, too dense and there is nothing left to route with. Getting it wrong is discovered at SO-04, when the fix is a metal change across the whole die.
en: Power budgets per domain from ARCH-06
Bump and rail assignment progressing in PD-04
ex: Static IR analyzed on a placed design with real power numbers
Grid density justified against routing resource
PDN frozen with the floorplan, not after it
rk: Grid density traded against routing without analysis. Both constraints are real, and choosing by feel produces either IR problems or congestion.
IR analyzed only statically. Dynamic IR under real switching is worse, and SIPI-04 with the package model is worse again.
Decap placed where there is room. Decoupling works where the current is drawn, not where the floorplan left space.
Power switches planned late. They need area, always-on routing and their own control, and retrofitting them disturbs the floorplan.
PDN frozen before power numbers are real. A grid designed against estimates and fed a design that draws more is a grid that fails at signoff.
PD-03.fn: Step 4 has to happen while the grid can still change. Static IR on a placed design with real power numbers tells you whether the grid works; running it after routing means any fix competes with a routed design for the same metal.

PD-04.t: Bump and RDL Planning with Chip-Package Co-Design
s: Ingest the bump map from the architecture budget
Plan the RDL and redistribution
Assign the power bumps and rails
Iterate the co-design with package design
Plan the signal escape with the substrate
Freeze the bump map and release the interface files
p: Bump map with signal and power assignment
Signal escape plan with the substrate
Frozen bump map and package interface files
r: Bump map, RDL and package interface files. The bump map, RDL and interface files are produced here and consumed directly by package design.
Floorplan and PDN specification. Bump position constrains where power can be delivered, so the two documents have to agree.
pu: Turn the architecture's bump budget into an actual bump map and RDL, iterating with package design until both sides can build what the other needs.

The bump map is the contract between the die and the package, and it is negotiated rather than declared. Signal escape on the package constrains bump position; power delivery constrains bump count; and the die's floorplan constrains where either can go. All three have to close at once.
en: Floorplan and IO ring available from PD-02
ex: Bump map frozen on the date package design needs it
Escape routing confirmed feasible on the substrate
Power bump count sufficient for the delivery requirement
rk: Bump map frozen late. Package design and the substrate order both wait on it, and the substrate lead time makes the delay a wafer-out delay.
Escape routing not checked on the package side. A map that is optimal on the die and unroutable on the substrate has to be redone.
Power bump count reduced to fit signals. The signals that fit are then fed by a PDN that cannot deliver, and SIPI-04 finds it.
RDL treated as free. Redistribution has its own rules and resistance, and a plan that ignores them produces IR and EM problems in the RDL itself.
Co-design conducted by file exchange. Two teams iterating asynchronously on the same interface converge slowly or not at all.
PD-04.fn: Step 6 is a hard date rather than a milestone. PKGD-11 freezes package design against this map, and the substrate order that follows has a twenty-week lead time—a late bump map moves wafer-out by moving the substrate.

PD-05.t: Turn 1 on the N1 Netlist and QoR Baseline
s: Take in N1 and set up the turn
Place and optimize the design
Analyze congestion and apply mitigation
Synthesize the first-pass clock trees
Analyze timing and run the first ECO round
Run the first full route
Analyze power on the placed and routed design
Establish the QoR baseline and feed findings back to synthesis
p: Feedback list to synthesis and RTL
r: Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases with QoR delta reports. The first turn, and the baseline the second is measured against.
MCMM timing closure reports. The violation burn-down starts here, with turn 1's numbers as its origin.
pu: Run the first real turn on the N1 netlist—place, build clocks, route—and establish the QoR baseline that says how far the design is from closing.

Turn 1 is the first honest measurement of the design's physical difficulty. Everything before it was estimate; this produces real congestion, real timing and real power on a real floorplan, and the gap it reveals is what the next two turns exist to close.
ex: QoR baseline measured on a substantially complete netlist
Feedback to synthesis specific enough to act on
Congestion characterized as structural or local
rk: Turn 1 expected to close. It will not, and treating the gap as a crisis rather than as data produces panic instead of a plan.
Feedback not specific. "Congestion is high" changes nothing; "the compute cluster is over 90% utilization in three regions and needs restructuring" changes the next drop.
Turn run on an incomplete netlist. A baseline missing blocks understates the difficulty and misleads the closure plan.
Congestion mitigated locally. Fixing congestion by rip-up and reroute hides a structural problem that only synthesis or floorplan can solve.
Clock tree built before the floorplan is stable. A CTS on a floorplan that then changes is work thrown away.
PD-05.fn: Step 8 is what makes turn 1 worth its cost. The turn's purpose is not to close—it will not—but to produce a measured baseline and a specific list of what synthesis and RTL must change before turn 2.

PD-06.t: Turn 2 on the N2 Netlist and Closure Risk Quantification
s: Take in N2 and assess the delta against turn 1
Place with congestion mitigation
Restructure congestion hot spots with synthesis
Refine the clock trees
Converge timing through ECO rounds
Converge the route
Converge power and IR
Quantify the closure risk for the final turn
r: Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases with QoR delta reports. The second turn, and the last one before the netlist is frozen.
MCMM timing closure reports. The burn-down trend across turns is what predicts whether the final turn closes.
pu: Run the second turn on N2 and converge—congestion, timing and power—then quantify honestly how much closure risk remains for the final turn.

Turn 2 is where the design either starts converging or reveals that it will not. Its output is a number: how many violations remain, in which blocks, and whether the trend from turn 1 projects to closure. That number is what the program uses to decide whether the tapeout date holds.
en: Turn 1 QoR baseline available from PD-05
Congestion feedback loop running with SYN-04
ex: Convergence trend measured against turn 1, not only reported
Structural congestion addressed structurally
Closure risk stated with paths, blocks and options
rk: Closure risk understated at turn 2. This is the last point at which a frequency or feature concession is cheap, and an optimistic number removes the option.
Congestion fixed locally rather than structurally. Rip-up and reroute buys a turn and leaves the problem for the final one, when there is no time.
Turn 2 not compared against turn 1. The absolute number matters less than the trend, and only the delta says whether the design is converging.
Power convergence deferred. Power fixes change timing; leaving them to the final turn means re-closing timing after every one.
Late RTL changes absorbed into turn 2. A functional change mid-turn invalidates the comparison the turn exists to produce.
PD-06.fn: Step 3 is joint work with SYN-04 rather than a physical design task. Congestion that survives placement optimization is structural, and the only remedies are logic restructuring or a floorplan change—both of which belong to someone else.

PD-07.t: Clock Tree Synthesis with Skew and Jitter Budgeting
s: Plan the clock architecture implementation
Synthesize the clock trees per domain
Optimize clock power
Balance skew and insertion delay
Manage the jitter and OCV budgets
Handle cross-domain relationships and useful skew
Run clock DRC and quality checks
Refine the trees continuously across turns
p: Clock tree refinement record across turns
r: MCMM timing closure reports. Clock skew and insertion delay are inputs to every timing number in the report.
Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases. Each turn contains its own clock tree, rebuilt and improved.
pu: Build and refine the clock trees across turns—skew, insertion delay, jitter budget, power—for a design with dozens of domains and crossings between them.

Clock tree synthesis is rebuilt every turn and improved each time. Skew directly buys or costs timing margin; insertion delay costs power and OCV; and cross-domain paths need a defined phase relationship that only a deliberately built tree provides. It is one of the few areas where a good result is worth several percent of frequency.
en: Placement available from the current turn
ex: Clock power inside the ARCH-06 budget
Cross-domain relationships defined and closed
Clock DRC clean, not only timing-clean
rk: Clock power ignored. The clock network is a large fraction of dynamic power on a design this size, and a tree optimized only for skew is expensive to run.
Useful skew applied without a plan. It buys margin and complicates every subsequent ECO, because moving one path's timing moves its neighbors'.
Cross-domain phase relationship undefined. Paths between domains cannot be closed reliably, and the failure appears as intermittent silicon behavior.
Insertion delay allowed to grow. Deep trees increase OCV derate and jitter accumulation, consuming the margin the skew balancing bought.
Tree quality not checked. Clock DRC violations—transition, capacitance, pulse width—degrade the tree in ways timing analysis reports as margin loss without explaining.
PD-07.fn: Step 6 is the hardest part and the one that pays. Useful skew moves margin from paths that have it to paths that need it, and cross-domain handling decides whether those paths can be closed at all—but both make the tree harder to build and harder to verify.

s: Define the routing strategy and layer plan
Run global routing and assess congestion
Run congestion-driven rip-up and reroute
Run detailed routing
Optimize antennas and vias
Converge DRC to clean
Check routing quality and manufacturability
Route continuously across turns
r: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. The interim DRC / LVS clean is produced here at each turn, and clean here is what makes SO-03 tractable.
Final-turn routed database on the FFN. The final route is this activity's last execution—the same routing and DRC convergence run one final time on the FFN database.
pu: Route the design and drive it to DRC clean—global, detailed, antenna, via optimization—across every turn, on a die where routing resource is the scarcest commodity.

Routing is where the floorplan, the synthesis and the power grid are all judged. Sixteen weeks and forty man-months buys convergence on a design where congestion is structural rather than local, and where every metal layer is contested between signals, clocks and the power grid.
en: Placement and clock trees available for the turn
Metal stack and routing rules available from PDK-02
ex: DRC clean at each turn, not only at the final one
Congestion resolved structurally where it is structural
Manufacturability addressed during routing, not after
rk: Congestion treated as a routing problem. Structural congestion cannot be routed around, and rip-up cycles spent on it consume time without converging.
Antenna violations left late. Fixes need diodes or layer jumps, both of which need space that a fully routed design does not have.
DRC convergence assumed linear. The last violations are the hardest, and planning as if the rate is constant produces a schedule that misses.
Manufacturability ignored until signoff. DFM-clean routing is cheaper to produce than to retrofit, and SO-08 finds what was not.
Layer plan not respecting the PDN. Signals and the power grid contend for the same upper layers, and a plan that ignores the grid produces conflicts everywhere.
PD-08.fn: Step 6 takes four weeks because DRC convergence on an advanced node is iterative and asymptotic. The last few hundred violations take as long as the first hundred thousand, and they are the ones that need manual attention.

s: Set up timing and define the MMMC scenarios
Close setup timing
Track and report the violation burn-down
Close hold timing
Generate and apply timing ECOs
Converge across corners and modes
Correlate against the signoff timing flow
Run continuous closure across turns
r: MCMM timing closure reports with violation burn-down across turns. The closure reports and the violation burn-down are produced here, and the burn-down is the program's best schedule predictor.
Final-turn routed database. A database is only handed to signoff when this activity says it is closed.
pu: Close timing across every corner and every mode—setup, hold, cross-corner, cross-mode—and drive the violation burn-down that decides the tapeout date.

Twenty-two weeks and sixty man-months, the largest activity in the stage. Multi-corner multi-mode closure on a large die is a long grind of analysis, ECO and re-analysis, and its burn-down curve is the single best predictor the program has of whether it will tape out on time.
en: Routed database available from the current turn
Corner and derate definition final from PDK-11
Signoff flow available for correlation from SO-01
ex: Closed at every corner and mode, not a subset
Implementation and signoff timing correlated within a stated tolerance
Burn-down trend projecting closure before the tapeout date
rk: Closing at some corners and deferring others. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails when there is no time to fix it.
Implementation and signoff timing diverging. A design closed in one tool and judged in another can be weeks from closure without anyone knowing.
Hold fixed after setup. Hold fixes add buffers that change setup, and doing them sequentially means iterating both.
Burn-down not tracked. Without a trend nobody can distinguish a design that is converging slowly from one that is not converging at all.
ECO volume exceeding what the database can absorb. Thousands of ECOs degrade the physical result, and at some point a re-run is cheaper than another ECO round.
PD-09.fn: Step 7 prevents the worst surprise available. A design closed in the implementation tool and re-analyzed in the signoff tool will show differences; discovering their size early lets the team close with the right margin rather than re-closing after SO-02 reports.

s: Set up SI and run the crosstalk analysis
Fix crosstalk — spacing, shielding, buffer sizing
Analyze noise and glitches
Analyze and fix electromigration
Iterate dynamic IR with the PDN
Iterate SI and PI to closure
p: Dynamic IR results and PDN adjustments
r: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. SI and EM fixes are routing changes, so they close together with DRC.
MCMM timing closure reports. Crosstalk-induced delay is part of timing, and SI fixes change timing in both directions.
pu: Fix what the routing did to the electricals—crosstalk, noise, electromigration, dynamic IR—before signoff has to reject the design for them.

Signal and power integrity problems are created by routing and found by analysis. Crosstalk between adjacent nets, EM in high-current wires and dynamic IR under real switching are all consequences of physical decisions, and fixing them means changing routing that was closed for timing.
en: Signoff SI/PI methodology agreed with SO-05
ex: Crosstalk included in timing closure, not analyzed after it
EM checked on signal nets as well as power
Dynamic IR analyzed with realistic, localized activity
rk: SI analyzed after timing closes. Crosstalk delay is timing, and closing without it means closing against numbers that will move.
EM checked only on power. High-toggle signal nets on advanced nodes carry EM exposure too, and they are usually the ones nobody checks.
Dynamic IR analyzed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and localized, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case badly.
Fixes applied without re-timing. Shielding and spacing change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has moved the problem rather than solved it.
Package effects excluded. Die-only dynamic IR is optimistic; SIPI-04 with package inductance is the number signoff will use.
PD-10.fn: Step 6 is an iteration rather than a step, because every fix perturbs something else. Widening a wire for EM changes its coupling; adding shielding consumes routing resource; and both change timing, which sends the design back to PD-09.

PD-11.t: Chip Power Model (CPM/CPS) Extraction and Handoff
s: Define the power model requirements with SIPI
Extract the CPM per domain and operating mode
Select the switching scenarios for the extraction
Validate the model against internal IR analysis
Hand the model off under version control
p: Chip power model per domain and mode
r: Floorplan and PDN specification. The power model is the PDN's behavior expressed for external consumers.
Bump map, RDL and package interface files. The model is part of what the package side needs alongside the physical interface.
pu: Extract the chip power model the package co-verification needs—per domain, per mode, with realistic switching—and hand it over as a versioned artifact.

SIPI-03 cannot analyze the die, package and board as one power delivery network without a model of the die's current draw. Producing that model is a small activity with an outsized dependency: without it the co-verification cannot start, and the co-verification gates mask release.
ex: Model extracted under realistic worst-case switching
Validated against the die's own IR analysis
Delivered versioned, on the date SIPI needs it
rk: Model extracted under average activity. The package has to supply the transient, and an averaged model hides exactly the event that matters.
Delivered late. Co-verification is on the critical path to mask release, and it cannot start without this model.
Model not validated. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own IR analysis is wrong in one of the two places, and nobody knows which.
Single model for all modes. Different DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model cannot represent them.
No version control. The package team analyzing against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that no longer exists.
PD-11.fn: Step 3 determines whether the model is useful. A CPM extracted under average activity understates the transient the package has to supply; extracting under the worst realistic burst is what makes SIPI-04's answer meaningful.

PD-12.t: Scan Chain Reordering and DFT-Aware Routing
s: Analyze the physical scan chains and their routing cost
Reorder the chains for routing efficiency
Preserve the diagnosis mapping through the reorder
Route and shield the test paths DFT-aware
Route the test clocks and manage their skew
Verify the chains after the reorder
r: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. Scan routing is routing, and it closes with everything else.
Final-turn routed database. The chains in the final database are the ones ATPG patterns were generated against.
pu: Reorder and route the scan chains physically—shorter routes, less congestion—without destroying the chain-to-block mapping diagnosis depends on.

Scan chains as stitched by synthesis follow logical order and route terribly. Physical reordering fixes the routing and can scramble the relationship between chain position and physical location, which is exactly what failure diagnosis uses. Both constraints are real.
en: Physical DFT plan agreed in DFT-09
ex: Chains verified after every reorder
Diagnosis mapping preserved or explicitly traded
Chain order frozen before ATPG generates patterns
rk: Reordering breaking diagnosis. Failure analysis relies on mapping a failing bit to a physical location, and a scrambled chain removes that.
Chains not verified after reorder. A break makes everything behind it untestable, and ATE bring-up is a costly place to find that.
Patterns generated before the final reorder. Any chain change after DFT-07 invalidates the pattern set and costs weeks of regeneration.
Test clock skew ignored. Scan shift reaches every flop, and skew on the shift clock produces shift failures that look like design bugs.
Chain imbalance after reorder. Physical reordering can lengthen one chain and shorten another, and shift time follows the longest.
PD-12.fn: Step 6 is not optional. Reordering rewrites the netlist's scan connectivity, and a chain broken by the reorder makes everything behind it untestable—a failure that would otherwise be discovered at ATE bring-up.

PD-13.t: Final Turn on the FFN and Full Closure
s: Take in the FFN and assess the delta against N2
Place the final netlist
Enforce ECO-only change discipline and gatekeeping
Synthesize the final clock trees
Converge power and IR finally
Run the final routing
Converge DRC and LVS
Close final timing across all corners and modes
Report closure and disposition the remaining violations
Freeze the database and hand it to signoff
p: Final power and IR convergence results
Final placed, clocked and routed database
Final timing closure across corners and modes
r: Final-turn routed database on the FFN, per block and top. The final-turn routed database is closed and frozen here, and it is what signoff and tapeout consume.
MCMM timing closure reports. The final turn's closure report is the one Design Freeze is granted against.
pu: Run the final turn on the FFN and close it completely—timing, power, DRC, LVS—with no functional change admitted and no next turn to fall back on.

Everything the stage has done is preparation for this. Fifty-five man-months over eleven weeks, on a frozen netlist, closing every corner and every mode to signoff standard. The discipline that matters is refusing functional change: an ECO that alters behavior restarts verification, and there is no schedule for that.
en: FFN released by SYN-09 against frozen RTL
Turn 2 closure risk understood from PD-06
ex: Closed at every corner and mode to signoff standard
No functional change admitted, or each one escalated and recorded
Database frozen LVS-clean and accepted by signoff
rk: Functional change admitted during the final turn. It restarts verification and equivalence, and no schedule allows for that at this point.
Closure gap larger than turn 2 predicted. If the prediction was optimistic, the discovery comes with no remaining turns and only concessions available.
ECO volume degrading the database. Thousands of ECOs on a final database produce a physical result worse than a clean re-run, but a re-run costs weeks.
Remaining violations dispositioned informally. Every violation that survives to signoff must be a named, accepted waiver rather than an oversight.
Database frozen before LVS is clean. A handoff that fails LVS at SO-03 sends everything back with no time to spare.
PD-13.fn: Step 3 runs across the whole turn and is a gate rather than a task. Every change request during the final turn has to be classified—timing ECO, functional change, or bug fix—and only the first is admitted without escalation.

s: Set up the ECO flow and methodology
Build the functional ECO implementation capability
Assess and track the impact of each ECO
Implement the timing ECOs
Establish the spare cell and metal-only ECO strategy
Operate the ECO machinery continuously across turns
r: ECO log and change control record. The ECO log and change control record are maintained here, and the log is what makes a late database traceable to the design that was verified.
Final-turn routed database. The final database is the FFN plus its ECO history, and the two are inseparable.
pu: Run the ECO machinery—flow, spare cells, metal-only strategy, impact tracking—that every turn depends on and that the final turn depends on absolutely.

ECOs are how a closed design absorbs change without a full re-run. The infrastructure matters more than any individual ECO: a spare cell strategy decided at floorplan time determines whether a late fix is metal-only or needs a base layer change, and that distinction is worth several weeks and a mask set.
en: Spare cell placement decided in PD-02
Change control process running in RTL-10
ex: Metal-only fix path available at tapeout
Every ECO tracked and reconcilable against the netlist
Functional and timing ECOs distinguished in the log
rk: No spare cell strategy. A late functional fix then requires base layers and a full mask set rather than a metal-only change.
ECOs applied without impact tracking. A database with untracked changes cannot be reconciled against the netlist that was verified.
ECO volume unbounded. Beyond some number, the physical result degrades enough that a clean re-run would be better—and nobody notices the crossing point.
Functional and timing ECOs not distinguished. They have completely different verification consequences, and conflating them lets functional change in unnoticed.
Spare cells consumed early. Using them for convenience during turn 1 leaves none for the fix that actually needs them at tapeout.
PD-14.fn: Step 5 is decided early and matters late. Spare cells distributed through the floorplan cost area now and make a metal-only fix possible at tapeout; without them, a late functional fix needs base layers and a full mask set.

s: Implement the seal ring and die edge
Apply metal fill to density compliance
Analyze the fill impact on timing and extraction
Place alignment marks, logos and die identification
Apply dummy fill and meet CMP compliance
Verify the finishing against the closed database
p: Seal ring and die edge implementation
r: Final-turn routed database. The database handed to tapeout is the finished one, and the finishing is part of it.
Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. Density and fill rules are DRC rules, and finishing is where they are met.
pu: Finish the die as a manufacturable object—seal ring, metal fill, dummy, alignment marks, identification—and verify that none of it broke what was closed.

Chip finishing is mechanical and it is not free. Metal fill changes coupling capacitance and therefore timing; the seal ring consumes die edge; and dummy fill interacts with the analog matching that AMS-12 spent weeks building. Every one has to be applied and then re-verified.
en: Fill and seal ring rules available from PDK-02
Analog fill exclusions defined by AMS-12
ex: Timing verified after fill, not before it
Analog matching structures protected from fill
Die identification present and readable
rk: Timing signed off before fill. The taped-out database has fill and the signed-off one did not, which is a signoff against a different design.
Fill applied over analog matching structures. It disturbs the parasitics AMS-12 tuned, and the damage is invisible until silicon characterization.
Seal ring area not reserved. Discovered late, it forces the die edge inward and moves the bump map.
Die identification omitted. Traceability at yield analysis and field return depends on being able to identify the die, and it cannot be added later.
Finishing treated as a checkbox. Each step changes the physical database, and each needs verification against what was closed.
PD-15.fn: Step 3 is why finishing is not a formality. Fill adds capacitance to every net near it, and a design closed before fill and taped out after it has been signed off against a database that no longer exists.

PD-16.t: Hierarchical Block Closure and Top-Level Assembly
s: Define the block closure criteria and handoff
Close the blocks at block level
Set inter-block timing budgets and close the interfaces
Generate the block abstracts and timing models
Manage top-level routing and feedthroughs
Assemble the top level
Correlate hierarchical timing — block model against flat
Verify the top-level integration
r: Signoff-ready database handoff. The signoff-ready database is assembled here—the top level signoff and tapeout actually consume.

Final-turn routed database on the FFN, per block and top. The per-block half of the deliverable comes from here: each closed block database, correlated against flat analysis, is what the top level is assembled from.
pu: Close the blocks independently and assemble them into a top level that meets timing across their boundaries—the hierarchical discipline a die this size requires.

A design of this size cannot be closed flat: runtime and capacity make it impossible. Hierarchical closure lets blocks converge in parallel, at the cost of interface budgets that have to be right. A block that closes internally and misses its boundary budget has not helped.
ex: Block models correlated against flat analysis
Every block closed to one shared criterion
Top level assembled and verified before the final turn ends
rk: Block models disagreeing with flat analysis. The top level is then closed against an abstraction that does not represent the block.
Interface budgets set late. Blocks close internally and fail at their boundaries, and the fix requires reopening blocks that were declared done.
Feedthroughs not planned. Signals crossing a block have to be routed through it, and a block closed without feedthrough provision blocks the top level.
Blocks closed to different criteria. Without an enforced standard, each block closes to what its owner considered sufficient, and the top level inherits the weakest.
Top-level assembly left to the end. Assembly finds interface problems, and finding them after the final turn leaves no time to fix them.
PD-16.fn: Step 7 is the check that keeps hierarchy honest. A block's timing model is an abstraction, and if it disagrees with a flat analysis of the same block then the top level has been closed against a fiction.

SO-01.t: Signoff Flow Dry Run on the Turn 2 Database
s: Assemble the signoff flow and integrate the decks
Run the dry run on the turn 2 database
Measure runtime and capacity
Build the violation triage process and tooling
Resolve the flow issues and record the rehearsal findings
p: Assembled signoff flow with integrated decks
r: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. The rehearsal is what makes the real campaign's schedule credible.
STA signoff reports. The flow that produces them is built and debugged here, so the first full-chip signoff run happens on a rehearsed flow rather than on the critical path.
pu: Rehearse the entire signoff flow on the turn 2 database—decks, runtimes, capacity, violation triage—so the final turn is not the first time it runs at full chip.

Signoff is a large, slow, deck-heavy flow, and the first run always finds problems that have nothing to do with the design. Finding them on turn 2 costs a week of a database nobody is waiting for; finding them on the final turn costs a week of the tapeout schedule.
en: Decks validated and versioned by PDK-10
ex: Flow runs end to end at full chip before the final turn
Runtime measured and the campaign scheduled against it
Rehearsal findings fixed, not only listed
rk: Dry run skipped for schedule. The flow's first full-chip run then happens on the critical path, and every problem it finds costs tapeout days.
Runtime not measured. A signoff campaign planned without knowing its runtime is planned against a guess.
Dry run on an unrepresentative database. Turn 2 has to be close enough in size and structure that the runtimes and violation counts mean something.
Triage tooling built during the real campaign. Thousands of violations arrive at once, and sorting them by hand is how a week disappears.
Findings not fixed before the final turn. A rehearsal that identifies problems and does not resolve them has only produced a list.
SO-01.fn: Step 3 sizes the signoff campaign. Signoff runtime on a die this size is measured in days per corner, and knowing the number before the final turn is what lets the schedule be built rather than discovered.

SO-02.t: Multi-Corner Multi-Mode Signoff STA and Closure
s: Set up signoff STA on the final database
Analyze setup timing across all corners and modes
Analyze hold timing across all corners and modes
Triage violations and classify root causes
Iterate ECOs with physical design
Sign off cross-mode and test-mode timing
Close timing signoff and disposition the waivers
p: Setup timing analysis across corners and modes
Hold timing analysis across corners and modes
Timing signoff reports and waiver list
r: STA signoff reports across all corners and modes, with waiver list. The STA signoff reports and the waiver list are produced here, and the waiver list is the part that carries risk into silicon.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Timing signoff is the largest single input to the freeze decision.
pu: Prove the final database meets timing at every corner and every mode, in the signoff tool, and dispose of every remaining violation as a fix or a signed waiver.

This is the largest activity in the stage and the one Design Freeze most depends on. It differs from PD-09 in that it is judgment rather than optimization: the signoff tool, the foundry-agreed derates and the full corner set, with no ECO loop to fall back on.
en: Final database frozen and handed over by PD-13
Corner and derate set agreed in PDK-11
ex: Every corner and mode analyzed, none deferred
Every waiver carries a root cause and a signature
Test modes signed off alongside functional
rk: Corners deferred to fit the schedule. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails in silicon where there is no fix.
Waivers granted without root cause. A waived violation with no understood cause is a silicon risk being accepted blind.
Test modes not signed off. Scan shift and at-speed timing failures produce parts that work functionally and fail at ATE.
Signoff and implementation disagreeing late. If SO-12 has not correlated the two, the first signoff run can show a design weeks from closure.
ECO loop reopening after signoff starts. Each ECO invalidates the analysis it was based on, and uncontrolled iteration never converges.
SO-02.fn: Step 6 covers the modes that are easy to forget and expensive to miss. Scan shift, at-speed capture and any low-power mode each have their own timing, and a design signed off functionally and not in test mode produces parts that fail at ATE.

SO-03.t: Full-Chip DRC, LVS, Antenna, and Density Verification
s: Set up full-chip DRC and the hierarchical run strategy
Execute full-chip DRC and triage the violations
Verify and fix antennas
Execute LVS and debug the mismatches
Verify density and fill
Close physical verification and prepare the waivers
p: Full-chip DRC results with triaged violations
Physical verification clean reports and waiver candidates
r: Clean DRC / LVS / antenna / density reports. The clean reports are produced here, and they are a precondition for mask release rather than an opinion.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. A design with open physical violations cannot be frozen; the clean or formally waived reports produced here are a freeze precondition.
pu: Run full-chip physical verification—DRC, LVS, antenna, density—to clean, on the database that will become masks.

Physical verification is binary and unforgiving: the foundry will not accept a database with violations it has not waived. On a die this size the runs take days, the violation counts start in the tens of thousands, and the last hundred are the ones that need a human.
en: Decks validated and versioned in PDK-10
ex: DRC, LVS, antenna and density all clean or formally waived
LVS mismatches resolved, not waived
No database change after the last clean run
rk: LVS mismatch traced late. Full-chip mismatches take days to localize, and they are frequently caused by macro views rather than by the design.
Runs started too late. Each full-chip run takes days, and the iteration count is what sets the schedule rather than any single run.
Antenna fixes needing space that is gone. Diodes and layer jumps need room, and a fully routed design has none.
Waivers assumed acceptable. Foundry waivers are granted case by case, and a design that assumes one will be granted may not tape out.
Verification on a database that then changes. Any ECO after a clean run invalidates it, and re-running costs days.
SO-03.fn: Step 4 is where the hardest problems hide. An LVS mismatch on a full chip can take days to localize, and the causes are usually elsewhere—a macro abstract that disagrees with its layout, or an ECO applied to one view and not the other.

SO-04.t: Static and Dynamic EM / IR-Drop Signoff
s: Set up EM/IR and define the activity scenarios
Analyze and close static IR drop
Analyze dynamic IR under realistic switching
Analyze electromigration on power and signal nets
Assess the IR-aware timing impact
Close EM/IR and disposition the waivers
p: Dynamic IR results under real switching
EM analysis on power and signal nets
r: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The EM and IR half of the deliverable; SO-05 supplies the SI/PI half.
STA signoff reports. IR-aware timing is timing, and the two signoffs have to be reconciled rather than reported separately.
pu: Sign off electromigration and IR drop—static and dynamic, with real switching—because a design that meets timing and fails EM will not survive its warranty.

EM and IR are reliability and performance at once. IR drop consumes timing margin the STA assumed; EM limits how long the part will work. Both are analyzed on the final database with real activity, and both can send routing back for changes that reopen timing.
en: Realistic switching activity available from DV-04
Package co-analysis results available from SIPI-04
ex: IR back-annotated into timing signoff
Dynamic IR analyzed with realistic localized activity
EM checked on signal nets as well as power
rk: IR not back-annotated into timing. The design is then signed off at a supply voltage it never sees, and the margin was never real.
Dynamic IR analyzed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and local, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case.
Package effects excluded. Die-only IR is optimistic; the number that matters includes the package inductance SIPI-04 models.
Signal EM overlooked. High-toggle nets on advanced nodes carry real EM exposure, and checking only power misses them.
EM fixes reopening timing. Widening wires changes delay, and a fix applied after timing signoff invalidates it.
SO-04.fn: Step 5 closes a loop that is often left open. IR drop lowers the local supply and slows the logic, and unless that is back-annotated into timing the STA has been run at a voltage the die does not actually see.

s: Set up SI signoff and extract the coupling
Analyze crosstalk delay and its timing impact
Analyze noise and glitches
Run victim-aggressor analysis on the critical nets
Reconcile the power integrity signoff
Close SI signoff and report
p: SI signoff setup and coupling extraction
Crosstalk delay analysis and timing impact
r: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The signal integrity half of the deliverable—crosstalk delay, noise and glitch results reconciled into the timing signoff numbers.
STA signoff reports. Crosstalk delay is part of the timing number, not a separate finding.
pu: Sign off signal integrity—crosstalk delay, noise, glitch—on the final database, and confirm the numbers the timing signoff assumed.

Crosstalk is timing. Coupling between adjacent nets changes delay in both directions and can inject glitches that propagate as functional failures. The analysis is separate from STA and its results feed straight back into it, which makes the two inseparable at signoff.
en: Final database and extraction available from PD-13
ex: Crosstalk delay included in the timing signoff numbers
Glitch analysis run, not only delay analysis
Noise thresholds set from library data, not defaults
rk: Crosstalk reported and not reconciled with timing. Two separate reports means the design is signed off against timing that excludes coupling.
Glitch analysis omitted. Noise on a static net can propagate as a functional failure that no timing analysis would show.
Analysis on a subset of nets. Coupling is a property of adjacency, and the critical net set is not the same as the coupled net set.
Fixes applied after timing signoff. Spacing and shielding change delay, and a late fix invalidates the timing it was meant to protect.
Thresholds set by tool default. Noise thresholds are a library and technology property, and defaults are either optimistic or unnecessarily punitive.
SO-05.fn: Step 4 is where the analysis becomes actionable. A global crosstalk number tells nobody what to fix; a victim-aggressor list on the critical paths tells routing exactly which nets to space or shield.

s: Take in the SIPI results and confirm the scope
Reconcile die-only against system-level IR
Review channel compliance against the interface budgets
Review the power-aware timing correlation
Review the co-verification signoff and disposition the criteria
r: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The system-level results belong in the same report as the die-only ones, reconciled rather than filed separately.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Co-verification signoff is a freeze precondition, since mask release follows it.
pu: Review the chip-package-system co-verification result as a signoff item in its own right, rather than assuming the die-only analysis covers it.

SIPI analyzed the die, package and board as one electrical system. This activity brings that result into the signoff record and reconciles it against the die-only numbers—because where they disagree, the system-level answer is the one silicon will produce.
en: Die-only IR results available from SO-04
ex: Die-only and system-level results reconciled, not merely compared
Channel compliance reviewed against the specification mask
Review completed before Design Freeze, not after
rk: Co-verification treated as a package deliverable. It constrains the die's signoff, and excluding it from the signoff record means freezing without it.
Discrepancies explained rather than resolved. Where die-only and system-level disagree, one is wrong, and the difference is real margin.
Channel compliance reviewed against internal assumptions. The interface specification's mask is what compliance means, and internal budgets can be more generous.
Review scheduled after Design Freeze. The freeze is what gates mask release, and a co-verification finding afterwards has nowhere to go.
Power-aware timing not reviewed. STA at nominal voltage and IR analysis showing droop are two views of the same design, and only the reconciliation is the truth.
SO-06.fn: Step 2 is the reconciliation that matters. Die-only IR analysis excludes package inductance, and the difference between the two numbers is margin the design either has or does not—a discrepancy that has to be resolved before mask release rather than explained afterwards.

SO-07.t: ESD, Latch-Up, and Soft Error / FIT Verification
s: Collect the reliability requirements and set up the rules
Verify ESD paths through the full chip
Verify latch-up structures and guard rings
Estimate the soft error rate and FIT
Close reliability and disposition the waivers
p: Soft error rate and FIT estimate
r: Reliability reports—ESD, latch-up, FIT. The reliability reports are produced here, and they are what MP-03 will be measured against.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Reliability findings are part of the risk the freeze decision accepts.
pu: Verify the reliability requirements the product will be qualified against—ESD paths, latch-up structures, soft error rate—on the final database rather than in the qualification lab.

Qualification failures are the most expensive kind: they arrive after silicon, after packaging and after months of stress testing. Every one of these checks has a design-time equivalent, and running them here converts a possible respin into a layout fix.
ex: ESD paths traced through the full chip, not assumed from strategy
Latch-up checked internally as well as at the ring
FIT estimated against the product requirement
rk: ESD verified as a strategy rather than a path. A clamp with no complete discharge path to it protects nothing, and only a full-chip trace finds the gap.
Latch-up checked only at the IO ring. Internal structures near power domain boundaries can latch up too, and they are rarely checked.
Soft error rate not estimated. FIT is a product requirement in many markets, and estimating it after qualification leaves no mitigation options.
Reliability waivers granted without lifetime analysis. A waiver with no quantified impact cannot be defended when qualification fails.
Analysis on a database that then changes. Late ECOs can break an ESD path, and nobody re-runs the check.
SO-07.fn: Step 2 traces the discharge path through the actual layout rather than confirming the strategy. A clamp that exists and a path that reaches it are different claims, and only the full-chip trace establishes the second.

SO-08.t: DFM, Lithography Hotspot, and CMP Analysis
s: Set up the DFM decks and confirm the model versions
Detect and analyze lithography hotspots
Simulate CMP and density
Score recommended rule compliance
Fix the hotspots and close DFM
p: DFM deck setup and model versions
Hotspot fixes and DFM closure report
r: DFM and lithography hotspot report. The DFM and hotspot report is produced here, and its compliance score is a yield predictor.
Clean DRC / LVS / antenna / density reports. DFM fixes are layout changes and close alongside physical verification.
pu: Check the design against manufacturability—lithography hotspots, CMP density, DFM recommended rules—so the foundry can print it at yield.

A DRC-clean design can still be difficult to manufacture. Litho hotspots print differently from what was drawn, and CMP density variation produces thickness variation that moves timing. Both are checked with foundry-supplied models and both are cheaper to fix here than to yield-learn in production.
en: DFM decks and current litho models available
ex: Hotspots fixed or accepted with a yield impact estimate
Compliance scored rather than assumed
Fixes re-verified against DRC and timing
rk: DFM checked after routing is frozen. Hotspot fixes are layout changes, and a frozen database has no room for them.
Recommended rules ignored without scoring. The yield cost of ignoring them is real and unmeasured unless someone scores compliance.
Litho models outdated. Foundry models improve through the node's life, and an old model finds the wrong hotspots.
CMP variation not linked to timing. Thickness variation changes resistance and capacitance, and the timing impact is rarely fed back.
Fixes applied without re-verification. A DFM fix is a layout change, and it can create DRC or timing problems of its own.
SO-08.fn: Step 4 quantifies what PDK-02 decided. Recommended-rule compliance is a score rather than a pass, and it correlates with yield—a design that scored 60% on the rules it chose to ignore is a design whose yield learning curve starts lower.

SO-09.t: Final Formal Equivalence and LVS Netlist Consistency
s: Set up final equivalence against the FFN and the RTL
Prove RTL to final netlist equivalence
Reconcile every difference against the ECO log
Confirm netlist to layout consistency
Resolve the non-equivalences and issue the final report
p: RTL to final netlist equivalence results
r: Final formal equivalence report. The final equivalence report is produced here, and it is the last evidence that verification's conclusions still apply.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Freezing a database that has not been proved equivalent freezes an unverified design.
pu: Prove for the last time that the database being taped out is the design that was verified—final formal equivalence and netlist-to-layout consistency.

Between the FFN and the tapeout database sit hundreds of ECOs, a scan reorder, fill and finishing. Each was individually correct; the question is whether the composition still implements the RTL that DV signed off. This is the last check that answers it.
ex: Equivalence proved against the verified RTL, not only the FFN
Every netlist difference traced to an approved ECO
Run performed after the last database change
rk: Equivalence run against the FFN rather than the RTL. That proves the ECOs preserved the netlist and not that the netlist implements the verified design.
ECO log not reconciled. A difference that no ECO explains is an unapproved change, and it is exactly what this check exists to find.
Non-equivalences waived under tapeout pressure. Each waiver is a region where the silicon may not do what verification proved.
Run before the last ECO. Any change after the equivalence run invalidates it, and re-running takes days nobody has.
Layout consistency assumed from LVS. LVS compares layout to netlist; that the netlist is the right one is a separate claim.
SO-09.fn: Step 3 pairs the formal result with the ECO log from PD-14. Equivalence proves the netlists match; reconciliation proves that every difference between them was an ECO somebody approved rather than a change nobody noticed.

SO-10.t: Waiver Review Board and Foundry Waiver Alignment
s: Take in and classify waivers across all signoff domains
Establish root cause and quantify risk per waiver
Align and submit the foundry waivers
Run the board review and disposition each waiver
Write the residual risk statement
Assemble the signoff summary and Design Freeze package
p: Classified waiver intake across signoff domains
Root cause and risk quantification per waiver
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package
r: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. The signoff summary and Design Freeze package are assembled here, and they are what the tapeout decision is taken on.
STA signoff reports with waiver list. The timing waiver list is dispositioned here rather than inside the STA activity.
pu: Run the waiver review board—every violation that survives signoff, examined, owned and either fixed or accepted—and assemble the Design Freeze package.

Every large design tapes out with waivers. What distinguishes a controlled tapeout from a hopeful one is whether each waiver was understood, quantified and signed, or simply ran out of time. This board is where that distinction is made, and its package is what the Go / No-Go decision reads.
en: Foundry waiver process understood from TECH-06
Board membership named with authority to refuse
ex: Every waiver has a root cause, a quantified risk and a signature
Foundry waivers submitted and answered before freeze
Residual risk summarized in one statement for the gate
rk: Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A register nobody dispositioned is a set of accepted risks nobody accepted.
Foundry waivers submitted late. Their review is on the foundry's schedule, and an unapproved waiver blocks mask release.
Risk quantified qualitatively. "Low risk" is not a basis for a tapeout decision; a stated failure mode and probability is.
Board without authority. A review that cannot refuse a waiver is a review that approves everything.
Residual risk not summarized. The Go / No-Go decision needs one statement of what is being accepted, not a register of two hundred entries.
SO-10.fn: Step 3 has a duration outside the program's control. Foundry waivers are reviewed on the foundry's schedule, and a design that assumes approval and does not receive it cannot release masks—which makes early submission worth more than a complete submission.

s: Generate the final SDF and set up the simulation
Run timing-annotated functional simulation
Simulate the reset and initialization sequences
Simulate the test modes with final timing
Debug the failures and report the signoff
r: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Dynamic evidence on the final database belongs in the freeze package alongside the static analysis.
STA signoff reports. A gate-level failure with clean STA means the constraints described a different design, which is a timing finding.
pu: Run gate-level simulation with the final SDF—the last dynamic check that the design behaves correctly with real timing on the database being taped out.

Static timing analysis proves paths meet constraints; it does not prove the design works. Simulating with final timing catches what STA structurally cannot—race conditions, reset behavior under real delays, and any place where the constraints described a design different from the one built.
en: Final database and SDF available from PD-13 and PD-09
ex: Simulated against the final SDF, not an earlier one
Reset and initialization simulated with real delays
X failures fixed rather than forced
rk: Skipped because STA is clean. They answer different questions, and the failures gate-level simulation finds are invisible to static analysis.
Run on an earlier database. A simulation against pre-final timing says nothing about the database being taped out.
Reset simulation omitted. Reset ordering under real delays is a common silicon failure and one of the cheapest to catch here.
X failures forced away. Initializing signals to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialized state that will fail at power-on.
Runtime prohibiting meaningful scenarios. Full-timing simulation is slow, and a scenario set trimmed to fit may exclude the case that matters.
SO-11.fn: Step 3 is the check most likely to find something. Reset behavior depends on relative delays across the die, and a sequence that works with estimated timing can fail with the real numbers—a failure that would otherwise appear at first power-on.

SO-12.t: Signoff Corner Correlation Against Foundry Decks
s: Define the correlation methodology and select reference cases
Correlate the implementation tool against the signoff tool
