Correlate against the foundry decks and derates
Correlate extraction and parasitics
Publish the correlation findings and margin guidance
r: STA signoff reports. Correlation is what makes the signoff numbers comparable to the ones physical design closed against.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. A stated correlation is part of what makes the signoff result defensible to the foundry.
pu: Correlate the signoff flow against the foundry's own decks and the implementation tool, so that a number produced here means the same thing everywhere it is read.

Three parties analyze this design: the implementation tool, the signoff tool and the foundry. If they disagree, the design can be closed in one and rejected by another. Establishing the correlation early is what lets physical design close with the right margin instead of re-closing after signoff reports.
en: Foundry decks and derates available from PDK-11
ex: Correlation established on representative, difficult paths
Margin guidance published and adopted by physical design
Foundry deck differences understood, not assumed away
rk: Correlation established after signoff starts. The gap is then discovered on the final database, when closing it means re-opening closure.
Correlation on unrepresentative paths. Tool differences concentrate on long, heavily coupled paths, and correlating on short clean ones shows agreement that does not generalize.
Extraction differences overlooked. Parasitic differences between flows can exceed timing tool differences and are less often checked.
Margin guidance not adopted. Correlation that physical design does not close against has produced information nobody used.
Foundry decks assumed identical to internal ones. Derates and corner definitions can differ in detail, and the foundry's version is the one that decides acceptance.
SO-12.fn: Step 5 is the output physical design actually uses. Knowing that signoff reads 40 ps more pessimistic than implementation on long paths lets PD-09 close with that margin built in, rather than closing to zero and discovering the gap at SO-02.

TO-01.t: Final GDSII / OASIS Assembly and Layer Map Verification
s: Take in the closure database and check its provenance
Stream out the GDSII / OASIS from the closed database
Merge the macro and hard IP GDS
Verify the layer map against the foundry definition
p: Merged macro and hard IP GDS
r: Released GDSII / OASIS database with checksum record. The released database and its checksum record are produced here, and the checksum is what makes every later reference unambiguous.
Tapeout checklist with signoff matrix. Database assembly and layer verification are checklist entries in their own right.
pu: Assemble the final GDSII or OASIS database from the closed design—every block, every macro, every layer—and verify that the layer map the foundry will read matches the one the design was built with.

This is a mechanical activity with no tolerance for error. A layer misassigned in the stream-out produces masks that are wrong in a way no verification would have caught, because the design was correct and the translation was not.
en: Foundry layer map and format confirmed
ex: Layer map verified against the foundry's definition, not the internal one
Every macro GDS traced to its released version
Database checksummed and recorded
rk: Layer map mismatch. A misassigned layer produces masks that are wrong in a way no design verification would have found.
Macro GDS from the wrong version. An abstract that matched and a layout that did not is discovered at LVS, or worse, not at all.
Stream-out from an unfrozen database. The design has to stop moving before it is streamed, or the streamed version is not the signed-off one.
No checksum. Without one, the question "is this the database we signed off" has no answer.
Assembly compressed to hours. Stream-out on a die this size takes real time, and rushing it is how a merge error is missed.
TO-01.fn: Step 4 is checked against the foundry's layer map rather than the internal one. The two are usually identical and occasionally are not, and the difference is only visible at the mask shop—by which point the masks exist.

TO-02.t: Final Full-Chip Verification Re-Run on the Released Database
s: Set up verification on the released database
Re-run full-chip DRC
Re-check density and fill
Re-run LVS and antenna
Confirm the checksums against the released database
p: Verification setup on the released database
r: Released GDSII / OASIS database with checksum record. The release is only complete when the released bytes have been verified.
Tapeout checklist with signoff matrix. Verification on the released database is one of the checklist's non-waivable entries.
pu: Re-run full-chip physical verification on the released database—not on the one signoff checked, but on the exact bytes going to the mask shop.

Between the signoff run and the released database sit stream-out, macro merge and possibly a late fix. Each is a chance to introduce something. This re-run is short, expensive in compute and non-negotiable: it is the only check that the thing being released is the thing that was verified.
en: Decks versioned and matching the submission
ex: Verification run on the exact released database
Checksums confirmed identical between verified and released
No violations outstanding that were not already waived
rk: Skipped because signoff was clean. Signoff checked a different database, and the difference between them is exactly what this run exists to catch.
Run on the signoff database rather than the released one. That repeats the earlier check and proves nothing new.
Compute capacity unavailable. A full-chip run takes days and needs to be scheduled, not requested.
New violations discovered with no time to fix. Which is why SO-03 has to close cleanly rather than nearly.
Checksums not compared. Verifying one file and releasing another is a documented failure mode with a trivial defense.
TO-02.fn: Step 5 sounds pedantic and prevents the worst class of error. Verifying one database and releasing another has happened on real programs, and the only defense is confirming the checksum of what was verified against the checksum of what was sent.

TO-03.t: Tapeout Checklist Completion and Owner Signoff
s: Assemble the checklist per domain
Collect the evidence for each item
Chase the gaps and escalate them
Collect the owner signoffs
r: Tapeout checklist with signoff matrix. The completed checklist and its signoff matrix are assembled here, and the signoff matrix is what makes accountability explicit.
Go / No-Go decision minutes. The decision reads the checklist; entries without evidence are decisions being taken blind.
pu: Walk the tapeout checklist—every domain, every entry, evidence attached, owner signed—so the Go / No-Go decision is taken on facts rather than on confidence.

The checklist is the program's collected memory of what has to be true before masks are cut. Its value is entirely in the evidence: an entry ticked because the owner believes it is true is worth nothing, and the difference between a checklist and a ritual is whether anyone reads the attachments.
en: Checklist template maintained across the program
ex: Every entry carries evidence, not an assertion
Signatures from accountable owners, not proxies
Gaps escalated with time to close them
rk: Entries ticked without evidence. A checklist of assertions is a ritual, and it produces confidence rather than information.
Signoff by proxy. An entry signed by someone other than the accountable owner has moved the signature without moving the accountability.
Checklist assembled at tapeout. It should be maintained across the program; assembling it in the last week means discovering gaps with no time to close them.
Domains missing from the checklist. Test, package and reliability entries are easy to omit from a design-centred checklist and expensive to miss.
Gaps escalated too late. An unsigned entry three days before the Go / No-Go is a decision the meeting cannot take.
TO-03.fn: Step 3 runs in parallel because it is where the time goes. Chasing an owner who has not signed, or an entry whose evidence does not exist, is the real work—the checklist itself takes an afternoon.

TO-04.t: Open-Issue Risk Assessment and Waiver Acceptance
s: Consolidate open items across design, verification and test
Classify each risk and assess its consequence
Identify mitigation options per item
Accept each risk and assign its owner
p: Risk acceptance record with named owners
r: Open issue and risk acceptance record. The risk acceptance record is produced here, and named ownership is what distinguishes acceptance from omission.
Go / No-Go decision minutes. The decision is largely a decision about this list: what the meeting accepts is the classified risks and mitigations assembled here.
pu: Take every open issue the program is carrying—bugs, waivers, unclosed items—and turn it into an accepted risk with a name against it.

No large program tapes out with nothing open. The question is whether what remains was assessed and accepted, or simply ran out of time. This activity converts a list of loose ends into a set of decisions, each with an owner, a consequence and a mitigation.
en: Bug and waiver lists available from DV-12 and SO-10
Test and package open items collected
ex: Every open item classified with a stated consequence
Mitigation options identified where they exist
Each accepted risk has a named owner
rk: Items carried without assessment. An open issue nobody classified is a risk being accepted without anyone accepting it.
Risk stated qualitatively. "Low risk" gives the decision room nothing; a failure mode, a probability and an affected population gives it a decision.
Mitigations not identified. Many silicon risks can be screened at test or worked around in software, and the option is worth knowing before the gate.
Test and package items excluded. Risk consolidation that covers only design misses the categories that most often cause a late problem.
Acceptance without an owner. An accepted risk with no name against it has nobody watching for it at bring-up.
TO-04.fn: Step 3 is what gives the Go / No-Go meeting something to decide. An item with a mitigation—a test screen, a software workaround, a bin split—is a different decision from one without, and identifying which is which is this activity's contribution.

s: Present the decision pack — checklist, risks, readiness
Take the decision and capture conditions and dissent
Issue the minutes and assign the conditions
r: Go / No-Go decision minutes. The decision minutes are produced here, and the conditions attached are as important as the decision itself.
FEOL MTO release package. Mask data is not released before this decision, whatever the schedule pressure.
pu: Hold the Go / No-Go decision—the moment the program commits several million dollars of masks and a quarter of schedule to the design as it stands.

Half a week of activity and one man-month, preceded by three weeks of preparation. That ratio is correct: a gate argued in the room rather than before it is a gate whose outcome depends on who attended. The meeting exists to take a decision, record its conditions and name who owns them.
en: Checklist complete with signatures from TO-03
Risk acceptance record available from TO-04
ex: Decision recorded with conditions and their owners
Dissent captured in the minutes
Conditions assigned before mask data is released
rk: Decision taken because the date arrived. A gate that cannot say no is not a gate, and the organization learns that quickly.
Conditions accepted verbally. A Go granted "subject to" something unrecorded is an unconditional Go.
Wrong people in the room. The decision needs someone who can say no and someone who owns the consequence, and both have to attend.
Dissent unrecorded. It is the cheapest insurance available and it is routinely omitted.
Material presented for the first time in the room. A pack circulated on the day produces a decision based on whoever speaks most confidently.
TO-05.fn: Step 2 captures dissent deliberately. The objection nobody minuted is the one that resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at, and recording it costs a line.

TO-06.t: FEOL Layer Data Preparation and MTO Release
s: Select the FEOL layers and prepare the data
Hand off mask data preparation — fracture, OPC scope
Submit to the foundry and confirm acceptance
r: FEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The FEOL release package and submission record are produced here, and they are what start the mask and fab clock.
Released GDSII / OASIS database. The FEOL release is a subset of it, and the two must be traceable to the same checksum.
pu: Prepare and release the front-end layer data to the mask shop—the first of the two mask tapeouts, and the one that starts the fab clock.

FEOL goes first because it is the longest lead item and the least likely to change. Releasing it now starts mask writing while the back-end layers are still absorbing late fixes, which is the entire reason the two releases are separated.
en: Go / No-Go decision taken in TO-05
ex: Layer split matches the FEOL/BEOL plan exactly
Submission acknowledged by the foundry in writing
Released layers traceable to the database checksum
rk: Layer split wrong. A layer released as FEOL that later needs a fix cannot use the BEOL window, and the fix costs a new mask.
Released before the Go / No-Go. Schedule pressure makes this tempting and it removes the gate's authority entirely.
MDP requirements misunderstood. Fracture and OPC expectations differ per foundry, and a non-compliant submission is rejected.
Submission not acknowledged. A release nobody confirmed received is a release that may not have started the clock.
Traceability lost between database and submission. The submitted layers have to be provably from the checksummed database.
TO-06.fn: Step 1's layer selection has to be exact. A layer released with FEOL that later needs a fix cannot be fixed in the BEOL window, and a layer held back that the mask shop needed delays the whole set.

TO-07.t: FEOL Mask Order Confirmation and Mask Shop Scheduling
s: Confirm the mask order and purchase authorization
Confirm the mask shop schedule
Communicate the delivery date to the program
p: Mask shop schedule with completion date
Delivery date communication to the program
r: FEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The order confirmation half of the release record—the confirmed order, schedule and delivery date that make the FEOL release actionable.
Full mask set completion record. FEOL completion is the first half of the set; the completion date confirmed here is what wafer start is planned against.
pu: Confirm the FEOL mask order and get a mask shop schedule the program can plan wafer start against.

One man-month of administration that fixes a date the whole downstream schedule hangs on. Mask writing takes weeks, and knowing when the FEOL set will be ready is what tells FAB-02 when wafers can start.
en: FEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-06
ex: Order confirmed against the exact submitted layer set
Mask completion date received and communicated
Escalation contact identified
rk: Order placed without confirmed pricing. Mask cost is a large line item and an unconfirmed order produces an invoice nobody budgeted.
Mask shop schedule assumed. Mask writing capacity is shared, and the completion date is the shop's to give rather than the program's to assume.
Completion date not communicated. Wafer start planning depends on it, and a date held by one person is a date the program does not have.
No escalation path. Mask shop delays happen, and knowing who to call is worth arranging before it is needed.
Order and submission mismatched. The order has to name the exact layer set that was submitted.
TO-07.fn: Step 3 sounds trivial and is where schedules break. A mask completion date known only to the person who confirmed it is a date the rest of the program plans without.

TO-08.t: BEOL Fix Window for Metal-Layer ECOs
s: Set the fix window scope and admission rules
Implement the metal-layer ECOs
Prioritize the fixes and assess their risk
Verify each ECO
Run equivalence and consistency checks per fix
Close the window and freeze the BEOL database
p: Fix window scope and admission rules
r: BEOL ECO log covering the fix window. The ECO log covering the window is produced here, and the log is what makes the BEOL database traceable.
BEOL MTO release package. The database released to BEOL is the FEOL database plus this window's fixes.
pu: Use the four weeks between the two mask releases to make metal-layer fixes—the last window in which a design change is possible without a new front-end mask set.

This window is the reason the releases are split. FEOL masks are being cut and cannot change; BEOL is still open, and any fix implementable in metal can still be made. It is a genuine and finite opportunity, and it closes on a date.
en: Admission rules agreed before the window opens
Spare cell capacity available from PD-14
ex: Every fix implementable in metal, none requiring base layers
Combined database verified, not only individual fixes
Window closed on its date, not extended
rk: Window used as general contingency. Fixes admitted without rules accumulate into a database that differs from the verified one in ways nobody assessed as a whole.
Fix requiring base layers. If PD-14's spare cell strategy was not put in place, the fix cannot be made in metal and the window is useless.
Verification per fix but not in combination. Individually correct changes can interact, and the combined database needs a check of its own.
Window extended. BEOL mask release has a date; extending the window pushes the whole mask set and with it wafer start.
Equivalence skipped for speed. A metal ECO can change function, and the only detector is an equivalence run.
TO-08.fn: Step 1 has to be strict. Every late fix carries risk, and a window with no admission rules fills with changes that individually look safe and collectively make the BEOL database something nobody has verified as a whole.

TO-09.t: BEOL DRC, LVS, Antenna, and Density Re-Verification
s: Decide the re-verification scope from what the fixes touched
Verify DRC and antenna on the metal stack
Confirm the timing impact of the applied fixes
Re-check LVS and density
p: DRC and antenna results on the metal stack
r: BEOL MTO release package. The release is only defensible if the changed layers were re-verified.
BEOL ECO log. The log and the re-verification results are read together—what changed, and what was checked afterwards.
pu: Re-verify the metal stack after the fix window—DRC, LVS, antenna, density on the changed layers—before the back-end data is released.

The BEOL database is not the one that was signed off. It carries the fix window's changes, and every one of them touched routing. This re-verification is what makes the BEOL release as trustworthy as the FEOL one, and it has to fit inside the window's tail.
ex: Scope justified against what the fixes touched
Timing re-confirmed for every applied fix
Results complete before BEOL data is released
rk: Scope too narrow. A targeted re-run that misses an interaction between two fixes releases a violation into the mask set.
Timing not re-confirmed. Metal ECOs change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has replaced one problem with another.
Re-verification not fitting the window. Full-chip runs take days, and a window planned without them cannot accommodate them.
LVS skipped because the change was metal-only. Metal changes connectivity, which is exactly what LVS checks.
Results arriving after the release. Verifying after submission is verifying something already committed to masks.
TO-09.fn: Step 1 decides between a targeted re-run and a full one. Targeted is faster and risks missing an interaction; full is safe and may not fit the window. The scope decision has to be made on what the fixes actually touched.

TO-10.t: BEOL Layer Data Preparation and MTO Release
s: Prepare the BEOL layer data from the re-verified database
Hand off mask data preparation
Submit to the foundry and confirm acceptance
r: BEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The BEOL release package is produced here, and it carries the milestone the stage exists for—Tapeout.
BEOL ECO log. The released database is the FEOL one plus the logged fixes, and the two travel together.
pu: Prepare and release the back-end layer data—the second mask tapeout, and the moment the design is fully committed to silicon.

BEOL release is the real tapeout. After it nothing about the design can change without a new mask set, and the milestone the program has been working toward for eighty weeks is this submission being accepted.
en: FEOL layer split known from TO-06
ex: Layer set exactly complementary to the FEOL release
Submission acknowledged in writing
Database difference from the original traced to the ECO log
rk: Layer set not complementary to FEOL. A layer released twice or omitted produces an incomplete or contradictory mask set.
Released before re-verification completes. The fix window's changes are then committed unchecked.
Submission rejected on format. BEOL layers have their own OPC and fracture requirements, and a rejection costs days against a running FEOL clock.
No acceptance confirmation. An unconfirmed release may not have started the second mask clock.
Traceability broken. The BEOL database differs from the checksummed original, and the difference has to be exactly the ECO log.
TO-10.fn: The layer set here has to be exactly the complement of what TO-06 released. A layer released twice or not at all produces a mask set that is either wrong or incomplete, and the mask shop will not necessarily notice.

TO-11.t: BEOL Mask Order Confirmation and Full Mask Set Completion Tracking
s: Confirm the BEOL mask order
Track the full mask set to completion
Communicate mask availability to fabrication
r: Full mask set completion record. The completion record is produced here, and it is what confirms the split schedule held.
BEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The order half of the BEOL release record—the confirmed order against the exact submitted layer set.
pu: Confirm the BEOL order and track the mask set to completion, so that FAB-05 knows when back-end layers will be available and the line does not stall mid-lot.
The BEOL masks are needed several weeks into wafer processing, not at wafer start. Tracking them to completion is what confirms that the parallel schedule the FEOL/BEOL split assumed actually holds.
en: BEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-10
Mask order framework established in TO-07
Wafer processing plan available from FAB-04
ex: Order confirmed against the submitted layer set
Set completion tracked to the last layer
Availability communicated to fabrication against the line schedule
rk: BEOL masks late against the wafer schedule. Wafers reach the metallization steps and stop, which is worse than starting late.
Completion tracked per layer rather than per set. The set is usable when the last layer is done, and per-layer optimism hides that.
Availability not communicated to fabrication. The line plans against the date, and a date nobody passed on is a date the line does not have.
Order mismatched to submission. The order has to name exactly the layers submitted, and BEOL sets are large.
No contingency for a mask defect. Masks fail inspection sometimes, and a remake takes weeks.
TO-11.fn: Step 2 tracks the whole set rather than the second half. A mask set is only usable when every layer is complete, and the last layer to finish is the one that decides.

FAB-01.t: FEOL Mask Set Fabrication, Inspection, and Qualification
s: Confirm mask data acceptance and mask data preparation
Track FEOL mask writing
Prepare pellicles and handling
Review mask inspection and defect repair results
Disposition mask defects and take remake decisions
Qualify the mask set and release it to the line
p: Qualified mask set released to the line
r: FEOL and BEOL mask sets with qualification reports. The front-end half of the deliverable: the written, inspected and qualified FEOL mask set with its inspection and disposition record.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. Mask completion is the first date the wafer-out forecast is built on.
pu: Get the front-end mask set written, inspected and qualified—seven weeks of the mask shop's calendar that the program can watch but not accelerate.

EUV mask sets at this node are slow and expensive to produce, and a single mask failing inspection means a remake measured in weeks. The program's role is oversight rather than execution: confirm the data was accepted, review inspection results and escalate when a layer slips.
en: FEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-06
Inspection and disposition process agreed with the foundry
ex: Every mask inspected and dispositioned, not only written
Set qualified and released to the line
Completion date communicated against the wafer start plan
rk: Mask defect requiring a remake. Weeks of schedule, and the program has no way to accelerate the replacement.
Inspection criteria not understood. Whether a defect is printing depends on layer and position, and the disposition needs design input the foundry does not have.
Critical layers not prioritized. Mask shops write in a sequence, and the layers on the critical path can sometimes be pulled forward if anyone asks.
Data preparation rejected late. MDP problems surface days after submission and consume the schedule silently.
No visibility into progress. A seven-week activity with no status reporting means the first news is either completion or a delay.
FAB-01.fn: Step 5 is where a schedule is saved or lost. A mask defect can sometimes be repaired, sometimes waived as non-printing, and sometimes requires a remake—and the three outcomes differ by weeks.

FAB-02.t: Wafer Start on FEOL Mask Availability
s: Authorize wafer start and define the lots
Decide the starting material and lot split strategy
Confirm the start and communicate the schedule
r: Processed engineering-lot wafers. The lot definition here determines what comes out at the end.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. Wafer start is the point from which the forecast is measured.
pu: Start wafers the moment the front-end masks are qualified—lot definition, starting material, split strategy—because every day of delay here is a day at the far end of the program.

A single week of activity that gates the remaining eleven. The decisions it carries are small and consequential: how many wafers, what splits, which lots are hot, and whether any material is held back for a second attempt.
en: Capacity and hot-lot terms confirmed in TECH-05
Wafer quantity agreed against downstream needs
ex: Wafers started within days of mask qualification
Quantity sufficient for bring-up, qual and samples
Hot-lot priority invoked where it was negotiated
rk: Start delayed after masks are ready. Every day is a day at the far end of a schedule with no recovery mechanism.
Wafer quantity too small. Bring-up, characterization, qualification and customer samples all draw from this lot, and running short means a second lot and a quarter.
No process splits. A single condition gives one data point; splits reveal process sensitivity while there is still time to act on it.
Hot-lot status not invoked. The priority negotiated in TECH-05 has to be requested at start, not assumed.
Starting material not specified. Substrate type and specification affect device behavior, and defaulting is how an unexpected variable enters.
FAB-02.fn: Step 2 decides the split strategy—whether all wafers run the same process conditions or some are deliberately skewed. Splits cost wafers and buy information about process sensitivity that no simulation can provide.

FAB-03.t: BEOL Mask Set Fabrication, Inspection, and Qualification
s: Confirm BEOL mask data acceptance and preparation
Track BEOL mask writing
Disposition defects on the inspected layers
Track inspection and qualification
Release the masks to the line ahead of metallization
p: BEOL mask inspection and qualification results
BEOL masks released to the line
r: FEOL and BEOL mask sets with qualification reports. The back-end half of the deliverable: the BEOL mask set qualified and released to the line ahead of metallization.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. A BEOL mask delay stops lots mid-process, which the forecast has to reflect.
pu: Write and qualify the back-end mask set while front-end processing runs—the parallelism the FEOL/BEOL split was designed to create.

This activity is the payoff of the two-stage release. BEOL masks are written during the weeks the wafers spend in front-end processing, so the fix window cost the program nothing in schedule as long as these masks are ready when the lots reach metallization.
en: BEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-10
ex: Masks qualified before lots reach metallization
Progress tracked against the front-end schedule, not in isolation
First metal layers prioritized in the writing sequence
rk: Masks late against metallization. Lots stop mid-process, which wastes fab capacity and is harder to recover from than a late start.
Parallelism assumed rather than tracked. The split only pays off if the BEOL schedule is actively compared against the front-end progress.
Defect disposition slower on BEOL layers. There are more of them, and a per-layer process that worked for FEOL can bottleneck here.
Metallization start estimate stale. The masks are needed against a moving date, and planning against the original estimate is planning against fiction.
No priority on the first metal layers. They are needed first and can often be written first if anyone asks.
FAB-03.fn: Step 5's date is the one that matters. The masks do not need to exist at wafer start; they need to exist before the lots reach the first metal layer, and that is several weeks of margin the split created deliberately.

s: Confirm lot release and front-end entry
Track the wafers through transistor formation
Monitor inline data at the front-end critical steps
Track the wafers through contact and local interconnect
Respond to excursions and disposition the lots
Confirm front-end exit and hand off to the back end
p: Lot release and front-end entry confirmation
Inline monitoring findings at critical steps
Wafers through contact and local interconnect
r: Processed engineering-lot wafers. Front-end processing is where the transistors are actually made.
Inline, PCM and WAT data package. Front-end inline data is the earliest indication of how the lot is running.
pu: Watch the wafers through front-end processing—transistor formation, contacts, local interconnect—and respond when the line reports something unexpected.

Eight weeks in which the program does almost nothing and cannot afford to do nothing. The lots are the foundry's to run; what belongs to the program is understanding the inline data, recognizing an excursion early and deciding what to do about it.
en: Inline monitoring plan running from FAB-06
ex: Every excursion dispositioned against a framework, not improvised
Inline data reviewed by the design team, not only the foundry
Hot-lot priority maintained through the flow
rk: Excursion response improvised. Without a framework the decision defaults to whatever is least disruptive rather than what is best for the lot.
Inline data not reviewed by the program. The foundry monitors its process; only the design team can say whether a deviation matters for this device.
Hot-lot priority lost mid-flow. Priority granted at start can quietly lapse, and nobody notices until the cycle time slips.
Scrap decision taken too late. A lot continuing through eight weeks of processing after a fatal excursion wastes capacity that a second lot needed.
No second lot in reserve. If the first lot is lost, having no material started means restarting the whole cycle.
FAB-04.fn: Step 5 needs a standing decision framework. When a lot goes out of control limits the choices are scrap, rework, continue at risk or split—and making that decision in the moment, without a framework, tends to produce whichever answer is least disruptive rather than best.

s: Confirm back-end entry and BEOL mask availability
Track the wafers through metallization and via formation
Monitor back-end inline data
Track the wafers through top metal and passivation
Confirm wafer completion and lot exit
p: Back-end entry and mask availability confirmation
Wafers through metallization and via formation
Wafers through top metal and passivation
Wafer count confirmation against the downstream requirement
r: Processed engineering-lot wafers. The wafers are finished here—the deliverable the whole stage exists to produce.
Inline, PCM and WAT data package. Back-end inline data completes the process record for the lot.
pu: Complete the wafers through back-end-of-line processing—metallization, vias, top metal, passivation—and finish the lot.

The back end is where the design's routing becomes physical. It is also where the BEOL masks are consumed, which makes it the point at which the FEOL/BEOL split either paid off invisibly or produces a stall that everyone notices.
en: BEOL masks qualified and released by FAB-03
ex: Wafers completed without a mask-driven stall
Split traceability maintained to lot exit
Wafer count confirmed against the downstream requirement
rk: BEOL masks not ready at back-end entry. Lots stall mid-process, consuming fab capacity and adding cycle time nobody planned.
Metallization defects detected late. Back-end defects affect yield directly, and inline detection is what allows a response.
Passivation and top metal treated as routine. They affect bump attachment and package assembly, and problems here surface at ASSY-03.
Lot completion not confirmed against quantity. Wafers lost during processing reduce the number available downstream, and the count has to be checked rather than assumed.
Process changes between split lots not tracked. If splits were run, which wafer had which condition has to be traceable to the end.
FAB-05.fn: Step 1 is a confirmation with real consequences. If FAB-03 has not delivered qualified masks by this point the lots wait in the line, and waiting mid-process is more expensive than waiting at the start.

FAB-06.t: Inline Metrology and Defect Inspection Monitoring
s: Build the monitoring plan and select the critical steps
Review the inline metrology data
Detect excursions and escalate them
Review and classify the defect inspection results
Build the defect Pareto and attribute sources
Monitor continuously across the lot
p: Monitoring plan with critical step selection
Reviewed and classified defect inspection results
Inline monitoring log across the lot
r: Inline, PCM and WAT data package. The inline half of the deliverable, and the earliest signal the program gets.
Wafer acceptance disposition record. Inline findings inform the acceptance decision rather than being separate from it.
pu: Watch the inline metrology and defect inspection data across the whole run, so an excursion is caught while the lot can still be saved rather than at final test.

The foundry monitors its process against its own control limits; the program needs to know whether a deviation matters for this device. A defect density excursion on a layer the design uses heavily is a different event from one on a layer it barely touches, and only the design team can tell the difference.
en: Data access agreed with the foundry
ex: Monitoring focused on the design's actual sensitivities
Excursions escalated while the lot can still be acted on
Defects attributed to a source, not only counted
rk: Monitoring every step equally. Attention spread evenly finds nothing; the design's sensitivities decide where to look.
Data reviewed only by the foundry. Process control answers whether the line is in control, not whether this device is affected.
Excursions detected after the affected step. Once the lot has moved on, the response options narrow sharply.
Defects classified but not attributed. Knowing the count without the source gives no basis for a corrective action.
Monitoring stopping at front-end exit. Back-end defects affect yield as much and are often less well monitored.
FAB-06.fn: Step 1 chooses where to look. Monitoring every step equally wastes attention; selecting the layers and dimensions this design is most sensitive to—minimum-pitch metal, critical gate dimensions, via layers—is what makes the monitoring informative.

s: Confirm the PCM structure and parameter list
Collect and review the e-test data
Analyze across-wafer and lot-to-lot variability
Compare the parameters against target and model
p: Parameter comparison against model and target
r: Inline, PCM and WAT data package. The PCM half of the deliverable, and the earliest device-level data available.
Wafer acceptance disposition record. Parameter deviations are part of what acceptance is decided on.
pu: Read the e-test and PCM data—device parameters measured on structures in the scribe line—and compare them against what the models predicted.

PCM data arrives before packaged parts and answers process questions weeks earlier than the lab can. Threshold voltages, resistances, capacitances and ring oscillator frequencies measured on real silicon are the first hard evidence of whether the design's assumptions about the process were right.
en: Split lot definitions known from FAB-02
ex: Parameters compared against models, not only against targets
Split lots analyzed separately
Findings communicated before packaged parts arrive
rk: PCM data not reviewed until parts arrive. It answers process questions weeks earlier and costs nothing extra to read.
Comparison against target only. The design was built against models; comparing against the model is what predicts silicon behavior.
Variability ignored. Across-wafer parameter spread predicts the bin distribution, and the mean alone does not.
Split lots analyzed together. If splits were run, aggregating them averages away exactly the information the splits were for.
No link to the test chip results. TC-07 correlated models against silicon; this data either confirms that correlation or contradicts it.
FAB-07.fn: Step 4 is where the value is. A threshold voltage 30 mV from target changes timing across the whole design, and knowing that before parts arrive lets bring-up be planned around it rather than surprised by it.

FAB-08.t: Wafer Acceptance Test and Lot Disposition
s: Confirm the acceptance criteria with the foundry
Execute WAT and review the data
Escalate out-of-specification results with the foundry
Take the lot disposition and release decision
r: Wafer acceptance disposition record. The disposition record is produced here, and it is what a later yield discussion refers back to.
Processed engineering-lot wafers. Wafers are not released downstream until this decision is taken.
pu: Run wafer acceptance testing and decide whether the lot is accepted—the formal gate between the fab and everything downstream.

WAT is the contractual boundary. Parameters within specification mean the foundry delivered what was agreed; parameters outside mean a conversation about disposition, rework or credit. Either way the decision has to be taken deliberately rather than by default.
en: Acceptance criteria agreed with the foundry
ex: Disposition decided deliberately and recorded
Deviations documented and communicated to bring-up
Decision taken without holding the lot unnecessarily
rk: Acceptance by default. A lot released without a decision has been accepted by nobody, and the deviation is discovered later with no record.
Criteria not agreed in advance. Negotiating acceptance criteria after the data exists favors whoever is more motivated.
Marginal lot rejected on principle. On an engineering lot, silicon in the lab is usually worth more than a lot within every limit.
Deviations not documented. A parameter out of specification affects bring-up interpretation, and the bring-up team has to know.
Disposition delayed. Every day the lot sits undispositioned is a day of bring-up not happening.
FAB-08.fn: Step 4 can accept a lot that is out of specification. On an engineering lot the priority is usually silicon in the lab rather than perfect silicon, and accepting a marginal lot with the deviation documented is often the right call—but it must be a call.

s: Set up WIP tracking and the reporting cadence
Manage the hot-lot priority
Escalate schedule deviations
Maintain the wafer-out forecast
Communicate the forecast to downstream stages
Track continuously across the run
p: WIP tracking log across the run
r: Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. The forecast-versus-actual log is maintained here, and its value is in being current rather than in being right the first time.
First Silicon availability notice. The notice is the forecast's final form—the last wafer-out date this activity maintained becomes the availability the program declares.
pu: Track the lots and maintain an honest wafer-out forecast, because ten downstream activities are planning against a date this activity owns.

Assembly, test, bring-up and qualification all schedule against wafer-out. The forecast will move—fab schedules do—and the program's exposure is not the movement but the surprise. Four man-months across eighteen weeks buys a date everyone can plan against and early warning when it changes.
en: WIP data access agreed with the foundry
ex: Forecast updated at every status change, not monthly
Hot-lot priority actively maintained
Downstream stages replanning against the current date
rk: Forecast not updated. Downstream stages plan against a stale date and discover the change when the parts do not arrive.
Hot-lot priority lapsing. Priority is maintained by attention, and a lot that quietly loses it takes standard cycle time.
Deviations not escalated. A slip identified and not raised becomes a slip everyone discovers at the same time, too late to replan.
Forecast presented without confidence. A date with no stated uncertainty invites downstream teams to plan to the day.
Tracking limited to the fab. Wafer-out is not the same as parts available; sort, logistics and assembly all sit between.
FAB-09.fn: Step 5 is the reason this activity exists. A forecast held by the fab liaison and not distributed leaves ASSY, TEST and BU planning against the last number they heard, which is usually the original one.

FAB-10.t: Wafer Shipment and Logistics to Sort and Assembly
s: Plan the shipment and prepare the documentation
Handle customs and export control
Deliver to sort and assembly and declare First Silicon
p: Delivery confirmation to sort and assembly
r: First Silicon availability notice. The availability notice is issued here, and it carries the stage's milestone—First Silicon.
Processed engineering-lot wafers. Wafers become useful when they arrive, not when they are finished.
pu: Move the wafers from the fab to sort and assembly—shipment, customs, documentation—and confirm First Silicon is actually available.

Wafers finished in a fab on another continent are not parts in a lab. Shipment, export documentation and customs sit between wafer-out and anyone touching silicon, and they are the part of the schedule most often left out of the plan entirely.
ex: Documentation prepared before wafer-out, not after
Delivery confirmed at the destination
First Silicon declared on delivery, not on wafer-out
rk: Customs paperwork started at wafer-out. It can be prepared during processing and takes a week if it is not.
Export classification unresolved. Advanced semiconductors carry export controls, and an unclassified shipment does not move.
Destination not ready. Wafers arriving at a sort facility with no probe card or no capacity wait there instead of in the fab.
Shipment split without tracking. Lots split across shipments for risk are useful only if which wafers went where is traceable.
Milestone declared at wafer-out rather than at delivery. First Silicon means silicon someone can touch, and declaring it early hides a week of transit.
FAB-10.fn: Step 2 is where a week can vanish. Export control classification and customs paperwork for engineering samples crossing borders is a real process, and starting it when the wafers are ready rather than while they are in the line is what makes it a delay.

s: Consolidate the package requirements — die size, power, interfaces, thermal
Define the architecture options — interposer, bridge, organic
Screen capability and capacity per option
Study substrate construction and layer count
Compare cost per option with the DEF-04 model
Select the architecture and issue its specification
r: Package architecture specification. The architecture specification is produced here, and it is a supply chain commitment as much as a technical one.
Substrate and interposer PO with committed lead time. The architecture decides which supplier queue the program is standing in.
pu: Choose the package architecture—interposer type, substrate construction, layer count, body size—and commit to it, because everything from bump pitch to assembly capacity follows.

This decision has the same character as the monolithic-versus-chiplet call in ARCH-02: it looks like an engineering choice and it is a supply chain commitment. A 2.5D silicon interposer is a different supplier, a different capacity queue and a different cost structure from an organic bridge, and switching later is not practical.
en: Partitioning and die count known from ARCH-02
Backend supply chain findings available from TECH-09
Bandwidth and HBM requirements from DEF-05
ex: Architecture selected with capacity indicated, not assumed
At least two options evaluated and costed end to end
Specification issued before bump planning starts
rk: Architecture chosen without capacity. Advanced packaging capacity is scarce and allocated far ahead; a technically ideal option with no allocation is not an option.
Decision taken after the bump map. Package architecture constrains bump pitch and field, and deciding afterwards means renegotiating the die.
Cost compared on the package alone. Interposer, substrate, assembly yield and test all differ per architecture, and comparing one line misleads.
Thermal requirement not in the selection. Package thermal resistance is architecture-dependent and sets the achievable power envelope.
Single option evaluated. Without an alternative the program has no negotiating position and no fallback if capacity is refused.
PKGD-01.fn: Step 3 can eliminate an option outright. Advanced interposer capacity is allocated quarters ahead to a small number of customers, and an architecture the program cannot get capacity for is not an option however good it looks technically.

PKGD-02.t: Bump Map, Pitch, and Power-Ground Planning with Physical Design
s: Define the bump pitch and field against the architecture
Derive the power-to-signal ratio from the power envelope
Assign signal bumps per interface
Check escape feasibility against the substrate
Iterate die-side placement with physical design
Converge the bump map and hand it off
r: Bump map and interposer / RDL database. The bump map half of the deliverable; PKGD-03 supplies the interposer routing.
Package electrical design intent. Bump assignment determines channel quality before any routing is drawn.
pu: Negotiate the bump map with physical design—pitch, count, power-to-signal ratio, position—until both the die and the package can build what the other needs.

The bump field is where two design teams share one constraint. The die wants bumps where its logic is; the package wants them where its escape routing can reach; and the power delivery requirement takes most of the field regardless. Convergence takes iteration, and the iteration has to finish before PD-04 freezes.
en: Power delivery requirement known from PD-03
ex: Escape feasibility confirmed on the substrate, not only on the die
Power-to-signal ratio meets the delivery requirement
Map converged before the PD-04 freeze date
rk: Bump map converged on the die side only. A map that cannot escape on the substrate has to be redone, and by then the die may be placed around it.
Power bumps reduced to fit signals. The interfaces then work and the die cannot be fed, which SIPI-04 finds much later.
Pitch chosen from the previous program. Pitch depends on the interposer technology and the assembly process, both of which may have changed.
Signal assignment ignoring channel quality. Which bump a high-speed signal uses affects its escape path and its crosstalk exposure.
Iteration continuing past the freeze date. PD-04 and the substrate order both depend on this closing on time.
PKGD-02.fn: Step 4 is the check that usually forces the iteration. A bump assignment that works on the die can require escape routing the substrate cannot provide at its layer count, and finding that early is what keeps the map from being redone after freeze.

s: Plan the interposer layer stack and routing resource
Route the HBM channels with length management
Route the die-to-die and remaining signals
Design the power and ground distribution on the interposer
Route the RDL and plan the vias
Run interposer DRC and manufacturability checks
Release the interposer database
p: Interposer layer stack and routing plan
Routed HBM channels with length management
r: Bump map and interposer / RDL database. The interposer half of the deliverable—the routed silicon layer itself.
Package electrical design intent. Interposer routing is the highest-performance part of the package's electrical behavior.
pu: Route the interposer and its redistribution layers—the silicon layer that carries the die-to-HBM channels and everything else the substrate cannot.

On a 2.5D part the interposer carries the highest-density and highest-performance connections in the package. HBM channels alone run to thousands of nets at fine pitch, and their routing quality decides whether the memory interface trains at speed.
en: Interposer technology rules available from the supplier
ex: HBM channel lengths matched within the training budget
Reference planes continuous under high-speed channels
Interposer DRC clean against supplier rules
rk: HBM channel lengths unmatched. Skew across a wide parallel interface eats the training margin, and the failure appears at bring-up as a memory that will not train at speed.
Reference plane discontinuities. A channel crossing a plane split has an impedance discontinuity, and on HBM there are thousands of channels to get right.
Interposer power distribution underprovisioned. Current for two HBM stacks and the die passes through the interposer, and its resistance is part of the IR budget.
Manufacturability checked late. Interposer rules differ from die rules, and a design that violates them is a supplier rejection rather than a warning.
Routing started before the bump map converges. Every bump change is an interposer rework, and the rework is expensive at this density.
PKGD-03.fn: Step 2 dominates because HBM channels are numerous, fine-pitch and length-sensitive at once. Getting them routed with matched lengths and clean references is most of the interposer's difficulty and most of its schedule.

PKGD-04.t: Substrate Stack-Up, Escape Routing, and Package DRC
s: Define the stack-up and decide the layer count
Route the escape from the interposer footprint
Design the power and ground planes
Assign the board-side balls and breakout
Plan the via structures and drills
Run package DRC against the supplier rules
Release the substrate database
p: Package DRC results against supplier rules
r: Substrate design files (Gerber / ODB++) and stack-up. The substrate design files and stack-up are produced here, and they are what the supplier manufactures from.
Substrate and interposer PO with committed lead time. The order cannot be placed against a design that is not finished.
pu: Design the substrate—stack-up, escape routing, power planes, package DRC—the organic carrier that connects the interposer to the board.

The substrate is the part with the longest lead time and the least flexibility once ordered. Its layer count is fixed by escape routing needs and its cost scales with it, so the design converges on the smallest stack-up that can carry the escape—a trade made once and lived with.
en: Supplier design rules obtained via PKGD-09
ex: Layer count justified by an attempted escape, not assumed
Package DRC clean against the actual supplier's rules
Ball map agreed with the board design
rk: Layer count set before escape is attempted. A stack-up chosen for cost that cannot carry the escape has to be increased, and the cost model was built on the smaller number.
Supplier rules obtained late. Substrate rules vary by supplier and technology, and designing to generic rules produces a design one supplier can build.
Power planes fragmented by escape routing. Escape vias perforate the planes, and the resulting current path is what SIPI-03 will analyze.
Ball map not agreed with the board. The substrate's board-side interface is the board's problem too, and changing it late affects both.
Design released before DRC closes. A supplier rejection costs weeks against a twenty-week lead time.
PKGD-04.fn: Step 1 is the cost decision. Every substrate layer adds cost across the product's lifetime, and the layer count is set by whether the escape routing fits—which is not known until step 2 is attempted. The two steps iterate.

s: Allocate the channel budget to the package
Match lengths and control skew per interface
Design reference plane continuity and return paths
Design the via structures and manage the stubs
Separate and shield against crosstalk
Review the routing against the SI requirements
p: Channel budget allocation to the package
r: Package electrical design intent and model handoff to co-verification. The signal half of the deliverable—the design intent SIPI then verifies.
Substrate design files and stack-up. SI-driven routing is part of what the substrate files contain.
pu: Route the package for signal integrity—length matching, reference continuity, via design, crosstalk separation—so the channels can carry what the interfaces need.

Package routing is where high-speed channels are made or ruined. A via with a long stub, a trace crossing a plane split, or a differential pair routed without its partner all cost margin that the PHY then has to make up. SIPI-07 will measure the result; this activity is what determines it.
ex: Channel budget explicitly allocated between die, package and board
Via stubs managed rather than accepted
Routing reviewed against SI requirements before substrate release
rk: Via stubs unmanaged. They resonate in band for the fastest interfaces, and the remedy—back-drilling or blind vias—is a substrate cost decision made too late.
Length matching without reference continuity. Matched traces over a split plane have matched delay and mismatched impedance.
Channel budget not allocated. Die, package and board each consume part of the loss budget, and without allocation each assumes the others left room.
Crosstalk managed by spacing alone. On a dense substrate there is no spare space, and the answer is usually reference and via design instead.
Review after the substrate is released. SI findings then have nowhere to go except into the PHY's margin.
PKGD-05.fn: Step 4 is the one most often underestimated. Via stubs resonate at frequencies that matter for the fastest interfaces, and back-drilling or blind via structures are decisions with cost implications that belong to the substrate design rather than to routing.

PKGD-06.t: Package PDN and Decap Footprint Design
s: Define the package PDN topology and plane allocation
Design the power via arrays and current capability
Place the decoupling capacitor footprints
Analyze plane perforation and manage the current paths
Design the interposer-to-substrate power transition
Hand the PDN design intent to co-verification
p: Package PDN topology and plane allocation
Plane perforation and current path analysis
Interposer to substrate power transition design
r: Package electrical design intent and model handoff to co-verification. The power half of the deliverable, handed to SIPI for closure.
Substrate design files and stack-up. Plane allocation, via arrays and decap footprints are substrate content, so this design lands in the files the supplier manufactures from.
pu: Design the package power delivery—plane structure, via arrays, decoupling footprints—knowing that its electrical closure belongs to SIPI rather than to this activity.

The package sits between the die's instantaneous current demand and the board's slower supply. Its planes, vias and decoupling determine the impedance in the mid-frequency band where neither the die's on-chip decap nor the board's bulk capacitors help. Designing it is here; proving it works is co-verification.
en: Power delivery requirement known from PD-03
ex: Decoupling footprints placed for loop inductance, not convenience
Plane perforation analyzed rather than assumed away
Design intent handed over in a form SIPI can analyze
rk: Decoupling footprints too far from the current draw. Mounting position determines the loop inductance, and a capacitor mounted far away is a capacitor that does not help.
Plane perforation ignored. Escape vias perforate power planes, and the remaining current path can be far worse than the plane suggests.
Via array sized for DC only. Transient current is what the package has to supply, and DC sizing understates the requirement.
Closure assumed to be someone else's problem. If the design intent is not analysable, SIPI cannot close it and the iteration comes back here.
Interposer to substrate transition overlooked. The power path crosses two interfaces, and the transition is where its resistance concentrates.
PKGD-06.fn: Step 3 places footprints rather than choosing values. Which capacitors go where is decided by SIPI-05 against the impedance target; the package's job is to provide mounting positions close enough to the current draw for those choices to be available.

s: Build the thermal model — die, interposer, substrate, lid
Run steady-state thermal simulation and estimate Rjc
Analyze hotspots and transient thermal behavior
Select the TIM and study interface resistance
Simulate warpage across the reflow profile
Analyze mechanical stress and co-planarity
Issue the thermal and mechanical design recommendations
p: Thermal model of the package stack
Steady-state thermal results and Rjc estimate
r: Thermal and mechanical (warpage) simulation reports. The simulation reports are produced here, and PTV is what validates them.
Test vehicle requirement specification for PTV. The simulations decide which mechanical and thermal risks the vehicles must measure.
pu: Simulate the thermal and mechanical behavior of the package—heat path, warpage, co-planarity, TIM and lid—before any of it is built.

A package at this power dissipates hundreds of watts through a stack of materials with different expansion coefficients. The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope; the mechanical behavior decides whether the assembly survives reflow. Both are simulated here and measured on real vehicles in PTV.
ex: Thermal simulated against the real power map, not uniform power
Warpage simulated across the full reflow profile
Findings handed to PTV as vehicle requirements
rk: Thermal simulated at uniform power. An accelerator's power is concentrated in the compute clusters, and uniform assumptions understate the hotspot badly.
Warpage simulated at room temperature only. The failure happens at reflow peak, and the room-temperature number says nothing about it.
TIM performance taken from the datasheet. Interface resistance depends on bond line thickness and pressure, both of which are assembly properties.
Material properties assumed. Substrate and underfill properties vary by supplier and lot, and simulation is only as good as the inputs.
Results not fed into the vehicle plan. Simulation identifies which risks to measure, and a vehicle plan built independently measures the wrong things.
PKGD-07.fn: Step 5 predicts what PTV-07 will measure. Warpage across the reflow profile is the mechanism behind most 2.5D assembly failures, and simulating it before the vehicles are built is what makes the vehicle results interpretable rather than merely surprising.

PKGD-08.t: Test Vehicle Requirement Definition and Handoff to PTV
s: Identify the package risks the vehicles must cover
Define the vehicle type requirements — mechanical, thermal, electrical
Specify the measurement conditions and structures
Hand off the requirements and review the PTV plan
p: Package risk list for vehicle coverage
r: Test vehicle requirement specification for PTV. The requirement specification is written and handed off here, and its timing matters as much as its content.
Thermal and mechanical simulation reports. The vehicles measure what the simulations predicted, so the two are specified together.
pu: Tell PTV what the vehicles have to measure—which risks, which structures, which conditions—early enough that the vehicles can be designed, built and stressed before wafer-out.

The test vehicle program has a fifty-two week window and a hard gate at product wafer-out. Its requirements have to arrive while there is time to act on them, which is why this activity sits at week ten of a fifty-two week stage rather than after the package design is finished.
en: First thermal and warpage predictions available
Assembly process direction known from PKGD-10
ex: Requirements issued with time for the vehicle program to finish before wafer-out
Risks drawn from experience as well as from the design
Feedback mechanism into package design agreed
rk: Requirements issued after the package design completes. The vehicle program then cannot finish before wafer-out, and the gate is missed.
Risks identified from the design rather than from experience. The failures that matter are the ones previous programs hit, and they are rarely visible in a design review.
Electrical vehicle omitted. Daisy-chain continuity and assembly yield are as important as thermal and mechanical, and they need their own vehicle.
Conditions unspecified. A vehicle measured at the wrong temperature or reflow profile answers a question nobody asked.
No feedback loop defined. The vehicle results have to change something, and the mechanism for that has to be agreed up front.
PKGD-08.fn: Step 1 has to be done on an incomplete package design, which is uncomfortable and necessary. The architecture is known, the materials are known and the assembly process is broadly known—enough to say what will be risky, which is all the vehicle plan needs.

PKGD-09.t: Substrate and Interposer Supplier Selection and Lead-Time Booking
s: Screen the supplier long-list for capability
Assess design rule and technology fit
Confirm capacity and lead time
Negotiate the commercial terms and pricing
Select the supplier and set the qualification plan
Place the purchase order and book the lead time
p: Design rule and technology fit assessment
Purchase order with committed lead time
r: Substrate and interposer PO with committed lead time. The purchase order and its committed lead time are produced here, and the committed date is what wafer-out has to be planned against.
Substrate design files and stack-up. Supplier rules determine what the substrate design can contain.
pu: Select the substrate and interposer suppliers and book their lead time—a twenty-week commitment that sets the date the package can be built.

Substrate lead time is the longest single external dependency in the back half of the program, and it is ordered against a design that is not finished. Selecting the supplier early, understanding their rules and booking capacity is what makes the order placeable the moment the design freezes.
ex: Lead time committed in writing, not indicative
Supplier rules available before substrate design completes
Order placeable the week the design freezes
rk: Order placed after wafer-out is committed. A twenty-week substrate against a fixed wafer-out date means wafers waiting for a package.
Supplier rules obtained after design starts. A substrate designed to generic rules may be unbuildable by the chosen supplier.
Capacity assumed. Advanced substrate capacity is constrained, and a supplier who can build it may not be able to build it when needed.
Single supplier with no alternative. A supply disruption then has no mitigation, and substrates are not quickly re-sourced.
Lead time quoted without a commitment. An indicative lead time is not a date, and the difference appears when the schedule depends on it.
PKGD-09.fn: Step 6 takes four weeks because the order cannot be placed until the design is frozen, and the freeze is in PKGD-11. Everything before it exists so that the order can be placed the same week the design is released rather than a month later.

PKGD-10.t: OSAT Selection and Assembly Process Definition
s: Screen OSAT capability for the package architecture
Define the assembly process flow
Specify the bonding, underfill and molding parameters
Agree the known-good-die handoff and responsibility model
Select the OSAT and commit the capacity
Close the assembly agreement and process freeze plan
r: OSAT assembly process flow and agreement. The process flow and assembly agreement are produced here, and the agreement includes the responsibility model.
Thermal and mechanical simulation reports. The reflow profile the simulations use comes from the assembly process defined here.
pu: Select the OSAT and define the assembly process—bonding, underfill, molding, lid attach—because the process determines what the package design has to accommodate.

Assembly is not a service the package is handed to; it is a set of constraints the package is designed within. Bond force, reflow profile, underfill flow and lid attach all impose requirements, and choosing the OSAT late means designing a package that has to be adapted to whoever ends up building it.
ex: OSAT selected with committed capacity
Process parameters known to the package design, not assumed
Known-good-die responsibility agreed in writing
rk: OSAT selected after the package is designed. The design then has to be adapted to the assembler's process rather than developed with it.
Advanced packaging capacity not committed. The same constraint as the interposer, and it applies to assembly capacity independently.
Known-good-die responsibility undefined. The first failed lot is the wrong moment to discover nobody agreed who owns the die.
Process parameters left to the OSAT. Bond force and reflow profile affect warpage and CPI, and the package design has to know them.
Process frozen without vehicle data. PTV-12 freezes the process window on evidence; freezing earlier means freezing on assumption.
PKGD-10.fn: Step 4 settles a question that becomes expensive later. When an assembled unit fails, whether the die or the assembly is responsible determines who bears the cost, and agreeing it while nobody has lost money is far easier than afterwards.

PKGD-11.t: Package Design Freeze, DRC, and Tooling Release
s: Review design completeness across interposer and substrate
Run final package DRC and supplier rule compliance
Confirm the electrical intent against the SIPI findings
Release the tooling and manufacturing data
Run the supplier design review and obtain acceptance
Declare the design freeze and release the order
r: Package Design Freeze package. The freeze package is assembled and declared here, and it carries the stage's milestone.
Substrate and interposer PO with committed lead time. The order is released on this freeze; nothing before it starts the lead time.
pu: Freeze the package design, close its DRC, release the tooling—and start the twenty-week substrate lead time that everything downstream waits on.

The freeze is a schedule event more than a design one. The substrate order cannot be placed against a moving design, and the lead time that follows is what sets when packages can be built. Every week of delay here is a week at the far end, after wafer-out, where it is most visible and least recoverable.
ex: Supplier has accepted the design, not only received it
Order released the same week as the freeze
Co-verification findings incorporated before freeze, not after
rk: Freeze slipping. Twenty weeks of substrate lead time follow it, and the delay lands after wafer-out where nothing can absorb it.
Frozen before co-verification completes. A SIPI finding after freeze is a package change against an order already placed.
Supplier acceptance assumed. A design frozen internally and rejected on manufacturability has not frozen anything except the schedule.
Tooling data incomplete. Manufacturing data is more than the design files, and a missing item stalls the order after it is placed.
Late bump map change from the die side. PD-04 has to be frozen first, and a die-side change after this point is extremely expensive.
PKGD-11.fn: Step 5 runs in parallel and can send the design back. Suppliers review for manufacturability against their own process, and their acceptance is what makes the order placeable—a design frozen internally and rejected by the supplier has not frozen anything.

PTV-01.t: Test Vehicle Strategy and Risk Coverage Definition
s: Take in the risks from package design and previous programs
Prioritize the risks against product impact
Define the evidence that would retire each risk
Allocate a vehicle type to each risk
Check schedule feasibility against the wafer-out gate
Write the vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix
p: Risk intake from package design and previous programs
Package risk list with product impact
Test vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix
r: Test vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix. The vehicle plan and risk coverage matrix are written here, and the matrix is what every later result is reported against.
Package validation complete record. Validation is complete when the matrix's risks are retired, which is why the matrix has to be right.
pu: Decide which package risks the vehicles will actually retire—chip-package interaction, warpage, thermal, assembly yield—and what evidence would count as retiring them.

The vehicle program has one shot and a hard gate at product wafer-out. Its value depends entirely on measuring the risks that would otherwise be discovered on real dies, and a vehicle plan built from what is easy to measure rather than from what is risky produces reassurance instead of information.
ex: Every carried risk has defined retiring evidence
Programme schedule closes before the wafer-out gate
Plan reflects prioritized risk rather than measurement convenience
rk: Plan built from what is measurable. Easy measurements produce data; the risk list produces information, and the two are not the same set.
Schedule not checked against the gate. A fifty-two week program that finishes after wafer-out has validated nothing in time to matter.
Evidence undefined. Without agreeing in advance what would retire a risk, the results become an argument rather than a conclusion.
Previous-program failures not consulted. The package failure modes that recur are known, and they are the ones worth measuring.
Vehicle count driven by budget rather than by risk. Fewer vehicles means fewer risks retired, and the trade should be explicit.
PTV-01.fn: Step 5 checks the whole program against one date. Fifty-two weeks of vehicle work has to finish before product wafers come out at week 98, and if the arithmetic does not close then the plan has to shrink rather than the gate move.

s: Define the mechanical representativeness requirements
Design the dummy die and die stack
Design a bump array representative of the product
Design the interposer and substrate coupons
Integrate the measurement features — strain, reference marks
Release the MTV design
r: MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs. The mechanical vehicle of the three—the dummy die stack, representative bump array and coupon design that carry the package's mechanical behavior.

Warpage and co-planarity data across the reflow profile. What the MTV measures is bounded by how it was designed: the reference marks and strain features integrated here are what the warpage measurement reads.
pu: Design the mechanical test vehicle—dummy die stack, representative bump array, substrate coupon—that carries the package's mechanical behavior without any of its electronics.

The MTV exists to be stressed. Its die are blank, its interposer is representative and its purpose is to reproduce the mechanical stack faithfully enough that warpage, co-planarity and CPI measured on it predict what the product will do.
en: Die thickness and bump specification available from PD-04
ex: Mechanically representative in the dimensions that drive warpage
Measurement features integrated, not added externally
Released against a settled product stack
rk: Vehicle not mechanically representative. Different die thickness or underfill produces warpage that does not predict the product's.
Measurement features omitted. A vehicle with no reference marks or strain features can be measured externally and not internally.
Bump array simplified. Bump density and distribution drive local stress, and a uniform array does not reproduce the product's concentrations.
Design released before the product's stack is settled. A vehicle built on an assumption that changes measures the wrong package.
Coupon size unrepresentative. Warpage scales with body size, and a smaller coupon understates it.
PTV-02.fn: Step 1 defines what "representative" means for mechanics, which is narrower than it sounds. Die thickness, bump metallurgy, underfill and substrate construction matter; the circuitry does not. Getting that distinction right is what makes the MTV cheap.

s: Translate the power map into heater zones
Design the heater array and its drive requirements
Place the RTD and temperature sensors
Integrate the TTV die with the interposer
Define the sensor calibration approach
Release the TTV design
p: Heater zone map from the power distribution
Heater array design and drive requirements
r: MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs. The thermal vehicle of the three—the heater array matched to the product's power map and the sensor placement that makes gradients measurable.
Thermal characterization report with model correlation. What the TTV can measure bounds what the correlation can claim.
pu: Design the thermal test vehicle—embedded heaters and temperature sensors laid out to match the product's power map—so the package's thermal path can be measured rather than simulated.

A TTV is a die that only makes heat, in the pattern the real die will make it. Uniform heaters measure an average the product will never experience; heaters matched to the compute cluster distribution measure the hotspot that decides the achievable power envelope.
ex: Heater zones match the product's real power distribution
Sensors placed to see gradients, not only a peak
Calibration approach defined before build
rk: Uniform heaters. They measure an average power distribution the product will never have, and the hotspot goes unmeasured.
Sensors too few or badly placed. Thermal gradients are what matter, and a single center sensor cannot see one.
Sensor calibration not planned. An uncalibrated RTD gives a relative number, and thermal resistance needs an absolute one.
Heater drive capability underspecified. Reproducing hundreds of watts through a test vehicle needs real power delivery, and the setup has to supply it.
Power map taken from an early estimate. The distribution changes through implementation, and a TTV built on the architecture-era map measures the wrong hotspot.
PTV-03.fn: Step 3 decides what the vehicle can see. Sensors placed only at the die center measure a number the datasheet can quote; sensors distributed across the zones measure the gradient that determines whether the hotspot is survivable.

s: Inventory the interconnect levels — bump, TSV, via, ball
Design the daisy chain topology and segmentation
Design Kelvin structures for resistance measurement
Map each chain to its physical location for defect localization
Design the probe and measurement access
Release the daisy-chain vehicle design
r: MTV, TTV and daisy-chain vehicle designs. The electrical vehicle of the three—segmented daisy chains, Kelvin structures and chain-to-location mapping that make assembly yield measurable and attributable.
Built vehicle lots with assembly travelers. The daisy-chain vehicle is what makes the build's quality measurable.
pu: Design the daisy-chain electrical vehicle—continuity structures through every interconnect level—so assembly yield and interconnect integrity can be measured electrically.

Daisy chains turn assembly quality into a resistance measurement. Every bump, every via and every ball becomes part of a chain that either conducts or does not, which makes an otherwise invisible assembly process observable and quantifiable.
en: Interconnect structure known from PKGD-02 and PKGD-03
ex: Chains segmented finely enough to localize a failure
Every interconnect level covered by at least one structure
Measurement possible with equipment the OSAT actually has
rk: Chains too long. A single break makes the whole chain open, and the yield number carries no information about where or why.
No Kelvin structures. Two-wire resistance includes the probe path, and marginal interconnects are exactly where the difference matters.
Chain-to-location mapping omitted. A failing chain that cannot be located gives no basis for a process change.
Not all interconnect levels covered. Bump, TSV, via and ball each fail differently, and a vehicle covering only bumps misses the rest.
Measurement access not planned. A vehicle that can only be measured with equipment the OSAT does not have is a vehicle that is not measured.
PTV-04.fn: Step 2's segmentation decides the diagnostic resolution. One long chain says whether the assembly worked; many short segments say where it failed, and the difference is what turns a yield number into a corrective action.

PTV-05.t: TV Die Fabrication and Interposer / Substrate Vehicle Build
s: Plan the vehicle build and define the quantities
Fabricate the TV die — dummy, TTV and daisy-chain
Build the interposer vehicles
Build the substrate vehicles
Run incoming inspection and qualify the materials
Confirm material readiness for assembly
r: Built vehicle lots with assembly travelers. The material half of the deliverable; PTV-06 assembles them.
Package validation complete record. Nothing can be validated before the vehicles exist, and building them through the product's own suppliers is what makes the results transferable.
pu: Build the vehicle hardware—TV die, interposers, substrates—through the same suppliers and processes the product will use.

Sixteen weeks and six man-months: mostly waiting, on the same supplier queues the product will stand in. Using the real suppliers and the real processes is the point—a vehicle built through a different route measures a package the product will never have.
en: Vehicle designs released from PTV-02, PTV-03 and PTV-04
DOE quantity requirement known from PTV-06
ex: Vehicles built through the product's own suppliers and processes
Quantity sufficient for the assembly DOE
Materials inspected before assembly, not after
rk: Vehicles built through a different process. A package assembled from materials the product will not use measures a package that will not exist.
Vehicle builds competing with product builds. Same suppliers, same queue; without sequencing one delays the other.
Quantity too small for the DOE. The process window study needs enough units to vary conditions, and a build sized for a single condition cannot support it.
