Incoming inspection skipped. A vehicle built from out-of-specification material produces results that describe the material rather than the package.
Build schedule not tracked against the gate. Sixteen weeks of build inside a fifty-two week program leaves limited room for a slip.
PTV-05.fn: Step 4 sits on the same substrate queue as the product, which is why it needs planning rather than ordering. Vehicle substrates competing with product substrates for the same capacity is a scheduling problem the program creates for itself if nobody sequences them.

PTV-06.t: OSAT Vehicle Assembly with Process Window DOE
s: Design the DOE across the assembly parameters
Bond and die-attach across the conditions
Underfill and cure across the conditions
Mold and attach lids and TIM
Inspect inline during assembly — X-ray, CSAM
Maintain assembly travelers with condition traceability
Release the assembled lots to characterization
r: Built vehicle lots with assembly travelers. The assembly half of the deliverable, with the condition traceability that makes it useful.
Frozen assembly process window definition. The window is derived from this DOE, so its design determines what can be known.
pu: Assemble the vehicles at the OSAT across a designed experiment—bond force, reflow profile, underfill, cure—so the assembly process window is measured rather than assumed.

The process window is what ASSY will run to. Establishing it needs deliberate variation: units assembled at the edges of each parameter, not just at nominal, so that the window's boundaries are known rather than the center being confirmed.
ex: Units assembled across the parameter ranges, not only at nominal
Every unit traceable to its assembly conditions
Inline inspection performed during assembly, not after
rk: Assembly at nominal only. That confirms the center and says nothing about the boundaries, which is where production will occasionally operate.
Condition traceability lost. Units that cannot be attributed to their assembly conditions turn the DOE into an expensive single build.
DOE too large for the unit count. Varying every parameter needs units the build did not produce, and an under-powered DOE gives ambiguous results.
Inline inspection omitted. Assembly defects found only at final characterization cannot be attributed to a process step.
OSAT running its standard process. The point is deliberate variation, and an assembler defaulting to its recipe produces no window information.
PTV-06.fn: Step 6 is what makes the DOE usable. Every unit has to be traceable to the exact conditions it was assembled under, and an assembly traveler that records the lot but not the condition turns a designed experiment back into a single build.

PTV-07.t: Warpage and Co-Planarity Measurement Across the Reflow Profile
s: Set up the measurement — shadow moiré or equivalent
Measure the room-temperature baseline across units
Measure warpage across the reflow profile
Measure co-planarity and ball flatness
Correlate condition to warpage from the DOE
Compare the results against the PKGD-07 simulation
r: Warpage and co-planarity data across the reflow profile. The warpage and co-planarity data set is measured here, and the reflow-profile coverage is what distinguishes it from a room-temperature check.
Frozen assembly process window definition. Warpage against condition is one of the window's defining constraints.
pu: Measure warpage and co-planarity across the reflow profile—not at room temperature, but at every point in the thermal cycle where the package deforms.

Warpage is the mechanism behind most 2.5D assembly failures. A package flat at room temperature can bow by more than a hundred microns at reflow peak, opening joints that then re-close as it cools—leaving a unit that looks fine and has intermittent connections.
ex: Warpage measured across the full reflow profile
Simulation correlated against measurement
Results attributed to assembly conditions
rk: Measured only at room temperature. The failure occurs at reflow peak, and the room-temperature number is not predictive of it.
Simulation comparison skipped. Without correlation the model stays unvalidated, and the next package has to be measured from scratch.
Co-planarity ignored. Ball flatness determines whether the package mounts to the board reliably, and it is a separate property from warpage.
Too few units to see condition effects. Warpage varies unit to unit, and distinguishing a condition effect from noise needs population.
Results not linked to assembly conditions. Knowing the warpage without knowing which condition produced it gives no basis for a window.
PTV-07.fn: Step 6 is what makes the measurement reusable. A warpage number is one package; a validated simulation model predicts the next one, and correlating the two is what turns a measurement into a capability.

s: Plan the CPI stress evaluation and select the structures
Apply the thermal cycling stress
Inspect bump and BEOL integrity
Detect low-k and ULK cracks
Cross-section and analyze the affected units
Compile the CPI assessment with its design implications
p: CPI evaluation plan and structure selection
r: CPI stress assessment report—ULK, bump and BEOL integrity. The CPI stress assessment is produced here, and it is the most consequential result the vehicle program produces.
Package validation complete record. CPI is usually the risk the gate most depends on, and this assessment is the evidence that retires it or names it unretired.
pu: Evaluate chip-package interaction—the stress the package puts into the die's low-k dielectric stack, and whether the bumps and back-end metal survive it.

CPI is the failure mode that makes 2.5D packaging risky at advanced nodes. Ultra-low-k dielectrics are mechanically weak, the package expands differently from the silicon, and the resulting stress concentrates exactly where the bumps meet the top metal. It cracks or it does not, and simulation alone is not enough to know.
en: Die stack information available from TECH-03
Thermal cycling and FA capability available
ex: Stress applied to a cycle count that would reveal accumulation
Failures cross-sectioned and localized, not only detected
Findings delivered before the package design freeze
rk: CPI evaluated by simulation alone. Material behavior at these dimensions is not predictable to the accuracy the decision needs.
Insufficient thermal cycles. CPI failures accumulate; a short cycle count shows nothing and reassures wrongly.
Cross-sectioning skipped. Detection without localization gives no design implication, and the implication is the output that matters.
Only nominal units stressed. The DOE's edge conditions are where CPI is most likely, and testing only the center misses it.
Findings arriving after package design freezes. A CPI problem needs an underfill, bump or design change, none of which are available after PKGD-11.
PTV-08.fn: Step 5 is destructive and necessary. Electrical and acoustic methods say something is wrong; only cross-sectioning shows what failed and where, and the design implication depends entirely on which layer cracked.

s: Set up the thermal measurement and calibrate the sensors
Measure steady-state Rjc and Rja
Map hotspots across the heater zones
Study TIM performance and bond line
Measure the transient thermal response
Correlate the results against the PKGD-07 thermal model
p: TIM performance and bond line results
r: Thermal characterization report with model correlation. The characterization report with its model correlation is produced here, and the correlation is what makes the model reusable.
Frozen assembly process window definition. TIM bond line is an assembly parameter, and its thermal effect is measured here.
pu: Characterize the package's thermal performance—junction-to-case and junction-to-ambient resistance, TIM behavior, hotspot mapping—and correlate it against the simulation.

The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope, and the product is sold on that envelope. Measuring it on a TTV that reproduces the real power distribution is what turns a simulated Rjc into a number the datasheet can carry.
en: Assembled TTV units available from PTV-06
Sensors calibrated per the PTV-03 approach
ex: TIM performance measured as assembled, not as specified
Hotspot mapped rather than averaged
Thermal model correlated and updated
rk: TIM performance taken from the datasheet. Bond line thickness and pressure are assembly parameters, and the achieved performance differs from the specification.
Hotspot not measured. The average junction temperature is not what limits the part; the hottest zone is.
Simulation not correlated. The model then remains unvalidated, and every future thermal question needs another vehicle.
Transient response ignored. An accelerator's power is bursty, and the transient behavior determines whether the package can absorb a workload spike.
Measured at a single ambient condition. Rja depends on airflow and ambient, and one condition does not characterize the range the product will see.
PTV-09.fn: Step 4 measures the interface nobody can simulate reliably. TIM performance depends on bond line thickness, pressure and pump-out over time, and the datasheet value is a starting point rather than an answer.

s: Plan the board-level tests and design the coupon boards
Fabricate the coupon boards and mount the vehicles
Run temperature cycling to failure
Run drop and shock testing
Run bend and flex testing
Analyze the failure modes and establish characteristic life
p: Board-level test plan and coupon boards
Failure mode analysis and characteristic life
r: Board-level reliability data on vehicles. The board-level reliability data is produced here, and characteristic life is what customers will ask for.
Package validation complete record. Board-level survival is part of what "validated" has to mean.
pu: Stress the vehicles through board-level reliability—temperature cycling, drop, bend—because the package has to survive being mounted in a system, not only being assembled.

Board-level reliability is where the package meets the customer's manufacturing process. Solder joints crack under thermal cycling, boards flex during handling, and a package that passes component qualification and fails board-level testing is a package the customer cannot use.
en: Board-level standards and customer requirements known
ex: Testing run to failure, with characteristic life established
Coupon boards representative of customer mounting
Failure modes identified, not only counted
rk: Testing to a pass criterion rather than to failure. A pass tells the customer nothing about margin; characteristic life does.
Coupon board unrepresentative. Board thickness and pad design affect solder joint stress, and a test board unlike the customer's predicts poorly.
Started too late to finish. Temperature cycling to failure takes months, and it is the longest test in the vehicle program.
Failure modes not analyzed. Knowing units failed at a cycle count without knowing how gives no route to improvement.
Only one mounting condition. Different customers mount differently, and the package's sensitivity to that is worth knowing.
PTV-10.fn: Step 3 runs to failure rather than to a pass criterion. Characteristic life—the cycle count at which a defined fraction fails—is what a customer needs to assess the package in their system, and a pass at a fixed cycle count does not provide it.

PTV-11.t: Daisy-Chain Continuity Test and Assembly Yield Learning
s: Set up the continuity test and measurement plan
Measure chain continuity across the units
Measure Kelvin resistance on the interconnects
Localize failures from the chain segmentation
Correlate condition to yield from the DOE
Compile the yield learning and feed it back to the process
p: Assembly yield learning and process feedback
r: Built vehicle lots with assembly travelers. The travelers' condition data is what makes this analysis possible.
Frozen assembly process window definition. Yield against condition is the window's most direct evidence.
pu: Measure assembly yield electrically through the daisy chains, localize what failed, and turn that into process learning before the product is assembled.

Assembly yield on a 2.5D package with hundreds of thousands of interconnects is not guaranteed. The daisy chains make it measurable, and the segmentation makes it attributable—which is what lets the OSAT fix a process problem rather than accept a yield number.
en: Assembled daisy-chain units available from PTV-06
ex: Failures localized to interconnect level and position
Marginal joints identified by resistance, not only by continuity
Feedback delivered before the process window freezes
rk: Yield measured without localization. A number with no location gives the OSAT nothing to act on.
Marginal interconnects passing continuity. A high-resistance joint conducts and will fail in the field; Kelvin measurement is what distinguishes it.
Condition correlation not performed. The DOE's whole purpose is to link yield to parameters, and skipping the analysis wastes the build.
Feedback arriving after the process freezes. Learning that cannot change the process window is learning with no consequence.
Sample size too small for yield estimation. Assembly yield is a rate, and estimating it needs enough units for the rate to be meaningful.
PTV-11.fn: Step 5 is why the DOE was run. Yield varying with bond force or reflow profile identifies the parameter that matters, and that is the parameter the process window in PTV-12 will be built around.

PTV-12.t: Package Design Feedback and Assembly Process Window Freeze
s: Consolidate the results across all vehicle characterization
Assess risk retirement against the coverage matrix
Issue package design feedback and change requests
Define and freeze the assembly process window
Write the residual risk statement for unretired items
Declare package validation complete
p: Risk retirement assessment against the matrix
Package design feedback and change requests
r: Frozen assembly process window definition. The window ASSY will build the product to, derived from evidence rather than from the OSAT's standard recipe.

Package validation complete record—gate for product wafer-out. The validation-complete declaration—with every matrix risk marked retired or explicitly open—is issued here, and it is the gate product wafer-out waits on.
pu: Freeze the assembly process window, feed the findings back into package design, and declare package validation complete—the gate product wafer-out has to clear.

This is the activity the whole stage exists for. It converts a large body of measurement into two things: a process window ASSY will run to, and a statement that the package has been validated. Product wafers must not come out before it is issued, because the alternative is learning about the package on real dies.
en: Characterization complete from PTV-07 through PTV-11
ex: Every matrix risk marked retired or explicitly not retired
Process window frozen with boundaries that exclude observed failures
Window transferred to the OSAT as a specification, not a report
rk: Completion declared because the date arrived. The gate exists to be capable of holding wafer-out, and a declaration that cannot say no is not a gate.
Unretired risks not stated. A validation record that implies full coverage when some risks remain open misleads exactly the decision it informs.
Feedback arriving after PKGD-11. Package design changes are not available after the freeze, so vehicle findings have to land before it.
Process window frozen too wide. A window that accommodates every observed condition is not a window; the boundaries have to exclude what produced failures.
Window not transferred to the OSAT as a specification. A window that exists in a report and not in the assembly instructions will not be followed.
PTV-12.fn: Step 2 is the honest accounting. Some risks in the matrix will not have been retired—a vehicle failed, a measurement was inconclusive—and the declaration has to say which, rather than declaring completion because the date arrived.

SIPI-01.t: Chip Power Model (CPM/CPS) Extraction per Power Domain and Operating Mode
s: Define the model requirements with physical design
Select the switching scenarios from real workloads
Decompose by power domain and operating mode
Extract and assemble the CPM
Validate the model against die-level IR analysis
Release the model under version control
r: Chip power model (CPM/CPS) release per domain and mode. The model set is extracted, validated and released here, and everything else in the stage consumes it.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The model is the die-side input to every co-simulation; the scenario selection made here decides what the PDN analysis can see.
pu: Get a chip power model that represents the die's current demand honestly—per domain, per mode, under the switching the product actually produces.

Everything in this stage depends on this model. A CPM extracted under averaged activity understates the transient the package must supply, and every downstream conclusion inherits that error without any indication that it did.
ex: Model built on the worst realistic transient, not an average
Separate models per domain and mode
Validated against die-level IR before release
rk: Model built on averaged activity. The transient is what the package must supply, and averaging removes exactly the event of interest.
Single model for all modes. DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model represents none of them well.
Not validated against die-level IR. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own analysis is wrong somewhere, and nobody knows where.
Delivered late. The stage cannot start without it, and the stage gates mask release.
Version drift. Analysis run against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that has since changed.
SIPI-01.fn: Step 2 decides everything the stage can conclude. The worst realistic transient—a workload burst arriving after an idle period—is what the package has to absorb, and a model built on steady-state activity cannot represent it.

SIPI-02.t: Package and Board Electrical Model Extraction
s: Define the extraction scope and frequency range
Extract the interposer model
Extract the substrate model
Extract the board and socket models
Assemble the PDN network model
Validate and correlate the models
r: Extracted package and board electrical models. The extracted models are produced here, and they are what turn three design intents into one analysable circuit.
Channel compliance report per interface. Channel simulation runs on these models rather than on idealized transmission lines.
pu: Extract electrical models of the package and the board—3D field solution, S-parameters, RLC networks—so the system can be analyzed as one circuit rather than three assumptions.

Each of the three parties has been designing against a model of the other two. Extraction replaces those assumptions with a solved answer: what the interposer, substrate and board actually do electrically, at the frequencies the design cares about.
en: Interposer and substrate designs stable from PKGD-03 and PKGD-04
ex: Frequency range covers both PDN and channel needs
Board and socket included, not only die and package
Models validated rather than assumed correct
rk: Frequency range too narrow. A model extracted for PDN analysis cannot support channel simulation, and re-extraction is expensive.
Extraction on an unfinished design. Package routing changes invalidate the model, and re-extraction is measured in weeks.
Board model omitted. The board is part of the PDN and part of the channel, and excluding it makes the analysis die-and-package only.
Models not validated. A 3D extraction has convergence and meshing choices, and an unvalidated result can be confidently wrong.
Socket and connector effects ignored. The bring-up platform includes them, and channel margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.
SIPI-02.fn: Step 1's frequency range decides the extraction cost and its usefulness. PDN analysis needs DC to the switching harmonics; channel analysis needs far higher. Extracting once for both is efficient and extracting for the wrong range wastes the effort entirely.

s: Derive the impedance targets per domain
Assemble the combined die-package-board PDN
Analyze DC resistance and static drop
Analyze AC impedance across frequency
Identify and analyze the anti-resonances
Report the PDN findings and improvement recommendations
p: DC resistance and static drop results
r: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The impedance half of the deliverable; SIPI-04 supplies the dynamic IR half.
Decap budget and placement specification. The impedance profile is what the decap budget is designed to flatten.
pu: Simulate the die, package and board as one power delivery network and check its impedance against target across the frequency range that matters.

The three levels each cover a different band: on-die decap handles the highest frequencies, package decoupling the middle, board bulk capacitance the lowest. Analyzed separately each looks adequate; analyzed together the gaps between them appear, and those gaps are where the supply actually sags.
en: Chip power model released by SIPI-01
Package and board models extracted in SIPI-02
ex: Impedance analyzed across the full frequency range as one network
Anti-resonances identified and addressed
Findings carry recommendations naming which level to change
rk: Levels analyzed separately. Each looks adequate in isolation and the transitions between them are where the impedance peaks.
Anti-resonances missed. They occur at frequencies no single level would examine and can exceed target by a large factor.
Impedance target derived from a rule of thumb. The target follows from the current step and the allowable ripple, and a generic value is either wasteful or inadequate.
DC analysis only. Static drop is the easy half; the frequency-dependent behavior is where the problems are.
Findings without recommendations. An impedance plot that exceeds target tells the team there is a problem, not which level to fix.
SIPI-03.fn: Step 5 finds what separate analyses cannot. Anti-resonances form between the package's inductance and the die's capacitance, at frequencies neither level would identify alone, and they are where impedance peaks far above target.

SIPI-04.t: Dynamic Voltage-Drop Analysis with Package Inductance
s: Select the transient scenarios from the workload profiles
Run the combined transient simulation with package inductance
Analyze droop magnitude and duration per domain
Compare against the die-only IR results
Explore the worst-case scenarios
Assess the dynamic IR margin and report the findings
p: Droop magnitude and duration per domain
r: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The dynamic IR half of the deliverable, and the number signoff should be using.
Power-aware STA correlation report. Droop is what gets back-annotated into timing in SIPI-09.
pu: Analyze dynamic voltage droop with the package's inductance included, under the switching profiles the product actually produces—the number the die-only analysis is optimistic about.

Die-only dynamic IR excludes the package's series inductance, which is the dominant impedance at the frequencies a workload burst excites. The difference between the two numbers is real margin, and it is the reason this stage exists rather than trusting SO-04.
en: Chip power model and PDN model available
Die-only IR results available from PD-03
ex: Package inductance included in every result
Die-only and co-analysis numbers reconciled
Findings delivered before timing signoff closes
rk: Package inductance excluded. It dominates at the frequencies a burst excites, and excluding it produces a comfortable and wrong answer.
Transient scenario too gentle. The worst case is a burst after idle, and a scenario built from steady-state activity never reaches it.
Droop duration ignored. A deep short droop and a shallow long one have different timing consequences, and only the magnitude is usually reported.
Die-only comparison not made. Without it nobody knows whether SO-04's number is optimistic, and the two signoffs disagree silently.
Findings arriving after timing signoff. Droop consumes timing margin, and a late finding invalidates closure.
SIPI-04.fn: Step 4 is the comparison the program most needs. Where die-only analysis says 4.1% and the co-analysis says 5.0% against a 5% budget, the design has no margin—and the two numbers have to be reconciled before SO-04 signs off on the optimistic one.

SIPI-05.t: Decap Budget and Placement Optimization Across Die, Package, and Board
s: Allocate the frequency bands across the three levels
Set the on-die decap requirement and cost its area
Select the package capacitors and their mounting positions
Set the board bulk capacitance requirement
Verify the combined impedance with the allocation
Issue the decap specification and hand it to each level
p: On-die decap requirement with area cost
r: Decap budget and placement specification across die, package and board. The decap budget and placement specification is produced here, and it is the only place the three levels are allocated together.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The allocation is verified against the impedance target it was designed to meet.
pu: Allocate the decoupling budget across die, package and board—how much capacitance, of what type, mounted where—so the three levels cover the frequency range between them rather than overlapping.

Decoupling is a system-level allocation that is usually made three times independently. On-die capacitance is expensive in area, package capacitors are limited by mounting positions, and board bulk is cheap and slow. Optimizing them together is what covers the band; optimizing them separately leaves the middle uncovered.
en: Mounting and area constraints known from each level
ex: Bands allocated so the three levels cover the range without gaps
Package capacitors placed for loop inductance
Allocation verified against the impedance target before handoff
rk: Each level decoupled independently. The bands overlap in places and leave gaps in others, and the gaps are where the impedance peaks.
Package capacitors placed where there is room. Mounting position determines loop inductance, and a capacitor far from the current draw contributes little.
On-die decap area not costed. It is die area, and treating it as free produces a design that traded logic for decoupling without anyone deciding to.
Allocation not verified. A budget that has not been re-simulated against the impedance target is a proposal rather than a solution.
Specification not handed to each level. A system allocation that stays in a report is not implemented by anyone.
SIPI-05.fn: Step 2 carries a real cost. On-die decoupling consumes die area that could have been logic, and the trade between area and package capacitors is a system decision rather than a physical design one.

SIPI-06.t: Simultaneous-Switching Noise (SSN / SSO) Analysis at the IO Ring
s: Scope the SSN analysis — which interfaces switch together
Model the IO ring power and ground network
Simulate simultaneous switching per interface
Analyze ground bounce and reference shift
Assess mitigations — bump assignment, decoupling
Report the SSN findings and interface impact
p: IO ring power and ground models
Ground bounce and reference shift analysis
r: Channel compliance report per interface. SSN degrades the eye of the interface that causes it, so it belongs in the same compliance assessment.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. SSN is a local PDN problem and is reported alongside the global one.
pu: Analyze simultaneous switching noise at the IO ring—the supply disturbance many outputs switching together inject into their own reference.

SSN is a local problem with system consequences. When a wide interface switches together, the current through the shared return path moves the reference the receivers are measuring against, and the resulting noise appears as jitter and reduced eye margin on the very interface that caused it.
ex: Worst-case simultaneous switching simulated per interface
Reference shift included in the interface eye budget
Mitigations identified before the bump map freezes
rk: SSN analyzed per pin rather than per interface. The problem is simultaneity, and a single-pin analysis cannot see it.
Reference shift not included in the eye budget. Ground bounce moves the receiver's threshold, and excluding it overstates the margin.
Mitigation identified after bump map freeze. The most effective remedy is bump assignment, and it is unavailable after PKGD-02 closes.
Worst-case switching pattern not simulated. All outputs switching the same direction simultaneously is the worst case and is rarely the default pattern.
IO ring modelled as ideal. The ring's own power distribution is what carries the return current, and idealizing it removes the effect being analyzed.
SIPI-06.fn: Step 5 usually points back at the bump map. The most effective SSN mitigation is more or better-placed power and ground bumps for that interface, which is a PKGD-02 decision—and one that has to be made before the map freezes.

SIPI-07.t: High-Speed Channel Simulation with Extracted Package Models
s: Define the channel topology per interface
Assemble the end-to-end channels from the extracted models
Analyze insertion loss and return loss
Analyze near-end and far-end crosstalk
Analyze return paths and discontinuities
Characterize each channel against the PHY assumption
r: Channel compliance report per interface, with margins. The per-interface compliance report is produced here, and the margin is stated against the real channel.
Extracted package and board electrical models. Channel simulation is the primary consumer of the extraction.
pu: Simulate the high-speed channels end to end with extracted package models—insertion loss, crosstalk, return path, reflections—rather than against the idealized channel the PHY was designed to.

Every PHY closes its margin against an assumed channel. This activity produces the real one: interposer, substrate, board, socket, connectors and all their discontinuities. Where the real channel is worse than assumed, the margin the PHY reported never existed.
en: Package and board models extracted in SIPI-02
Package SI routing complete in PKGD-05
ex: Channels simulated end to end including socket and connectors
Real channel reconciled against the PHY's assumed budget
Findings delivered before the package design freeze
rk: Channel simulated on nominal models only. Manufacturing variation moves impedance and loss, and the compliance margin has to survive it.
PHY assumption not reconciled. The PHY closed against a budget; if the real channel is worse, the interface has no margin and nobody has noticed.
Crosstalk analyzed only at the near end. Far-end crosstalk on a long dense channel can dominate, and it behaves differently.
Socket and connector excluded. The bring-up platform includes them, and margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.
Findings after the package design freeze. Channel improvements are routing changes, and they are unavailable after PKGD-11.
SIPI-07.fn: Step 6 is the reconciliation that matters. The PHY in AMS-03 closed against a channel budget; this activity says what the channel actually is, and any gap between them is margin the interface does not have.

SIPI-08.t: Eye, Jitter, and BER Budget Closure per Interface
s: Structure the budget and allocate contributions per interface
Assemble the jitter budget — random, deterministic, correlated
Run statistical eye analysis with equalization
Estimate BER and margin against the mask
Analyze sensitivity to channel and process variation
Close the budget and sign off each interface
p: Stated margin per interface against its mask
r: Eye, jitter and BER budget closure record. The budget closure record is produced here—the statement that each interface will work.
Channel compliance report per interface. Compliance is a budget conclusion rather than a channel property alone.
pu: Close the eye, jitter and BER budget per interface—combining channel loss, crosstalk, SSN, PHY equalization and jitter into one number that either meets the compliance mask or does not.

This is where all the electrical work resolves into a pass or a fail. Every contribution—the channel from SIPI-07, the noise from SIPI-06, the PLL jitter from AMS-02 and the PHY's own equalization—lands in a single budget, and the interface either has margin or it is shipping on hope.
en: PHY and PLL contributions available from AMS-02 and AMS-03
ex: Every interface closed against its compliance mask with stated margin
Jitter combined correctly rather than summed
Budget holds across variation, not only at nominal
rk: Jitter contributions summed naively. Random and deterministic components combine differently, and getting it wrong produces a budget that is confidently wrong.
Equalization assumed at its maximum. A PHY closing only with full equalization has no adaptation range left for a worse-than-nominal channel.
Variation sensitivity ignored. The budget has to hold across manufacturing spread, not only at nominal.
SSN excluded from the budget. It is a real contribution and it degrades the interface that generates it.
Interface failing the mask with no route to fix. Late findings leave only channel changes, PHY changes or a rate reduction, and all three are expensive.
SIPI-08.fn: Step 2 is where interfaces are usually lost. Jitter contributions from the PLL, the PHY, the channel and the SSN do not add linearly, and a budget that sums them naively either over-designs or, more often, over-promises.

SIPI-09.t: Power-Aware STA Correlation with Back-Annotated Voltage Drop
s: Generate the droop map per region and mode
Set up voltage-aware timing analysis
Re-analyze timing with the back-annotated droop
Assess the margin impact per timing path group
Reconcile with the SO-02 signoff margin
Report the power-aware timing findings and recommendations
p: Droop map per region and mode
r: Power-aware STA correlation report. The correlation report is produced here, and it connects two signoffs that otherwise run independently.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The timing consequence is what makes the IR number actionable.
pu: Back-annotate the voltage droop into static timing analysis—because a design signed off at nominal voltage was signed off at a voltage the die does not see.

Timing and power are analyzed by different teams with different tools, and the connection between them is usually a margin someone assumed. This activity replaces the assumption: the droop map from SIPI-04 applied to the timing analysis, so that closure reflects the supply the logic actually has.
ex: Droop applied regionally rather than as a flat margin
Reconciled with the SO-02 signoff assumption
Recommendations targeted at the regions that need them
rk: Flat voltage margin used instead. Droop is regional, and a flat margin is simultaneously wasteful where droop is low and inadequate where it is high.
Analysis run after timing closure. Findings then require reopening closure, which is expensive at this point in the schedule.
Droop map too coarse. Region granularity determines whether the analysis can distinguish a hot spot from an average.
Reconciliation skipped. Two signoffs with different voltage assumptions produce a design that satisfies neither cleanly.
Recommendations global rather than regional. The remedy is usually local—more decoupling or a PDN change in one region—and a global response over-corrects.
SIPI-09.fn: Step 5 is the reconciliation. If timing signoff already carries a flat voltage margin and this analysis shows the droop is worse in some regions and better in others, the flat margin was both too generous and insufficient—and the recommendation is regional rather than global.

SIPI-10.t: Electro-Thermal Co-Analysis with the Package Thermal Model
s: Define the coupling methodology and iteration scheme
Integrate the thermal model with the package model
Model the leakage-temperature feedback
Iterate the coupled electro-thermal analysis to convergence
Assess the hotspots and gradients
Compare the findings against the isolated analyses
r: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. Temperature affects both resistance and leakage, and the coupled result is the honest one.
Power-aware STA correlation report. Temperature affects timing as well as voltage, and both belong in the same correlation.
pu: Couple the electrical and thermal analyses—because leakage rises with temperature, temperature rises with power, and the two feed each other until they settle somewhere the isolated analyses did not predict.

Electro-thermal coupling matters at this power density. A hotspot raises local leakage, which raises local power, which raises the hotspot. Analyzing power at a fixed temperature and temperature at a fixed power finds an equilibrium that is optimistic in exactly the region that matters.
en: Package thermal model available from PKGD-07
Chip power model available from SIPI-01
ex: Coupled analysis converged, or non-convergence investigated
Compared against the isolated analyses to quantify the difference
Gradients assessed alongside peak temperature
rk: Analyses run at fixed temperature and fixed power. The equilibrium the coupled analysis finds is worse, and it is the one that occurs.
Leakage-temperature model too coarse. The feedback is exponential, and a linear approximation understates the hotspot.
Non-convergence dismissed as a numerical issue. It can indicate a real thermal runaway risk and deserves investigation rather than a damping factor.
Package thermal model unvalidated. If PTV-09 has not correlated it, the coupled analysis inherits an unknown error.
Gradient ignored in favor of peak temperature. Gradients drive mechanical stress and timing variation across the die, and the peak alone does not capture them.
SIPI-10.fn: Step 4 iterates to convergence, and whether it converges is itself information. A design where the leakage-temperature loop does not settle is a design with a thermal runaway risk, which is a different and more serious finding than a high temperature.

SIPI-11.t: Co-Verification Signoff Review and Criteria Disposition
s: Confirm the exit criteria across all analyses
Consolidate the results and summarize the margins
Disposition open items with the die, package and board owners
Run the signoff review with the design and package teams
Write the residual risk statement
Declare the co-verification signoff
p: Signoff review record with design and package
r: Chip-package-system co-verification signoff—tapeout gate. The co-verification signoff is produced here, and it carries the stage's milestone.
Eye, jitter and BER budget closure record. An interface that has not closed its budget is an open item at this gate.
pu: Hold the co-verification signoff—every result reviewed against named exit criteria, dispositioned, and signed—because mask release depends on it.

This is the gate the stage exists to reach. Without a signoff with criteria, co-verification is a collection of analyses that each conclude something and together conclude nothing. The disposition here is what SO-06 reviews and what makes the MTO gate at week 78 meaningful.
en: Analyses complete from SIPI-03 through SIPI-10
Die, package and board owners available to disposition
ex: Every analysis assessed against a named exit criterion
Open items dispositioned by their owners, not by the analysis team
Signoff complete before the package design freeze and the MTO gate
rk: Signoff without exit criteria. The analyses each conclude something and together conclude nothing that can be signed.
Open items dispositioned without their owners. An item closed by the analysis team rather than by the die, package or board owner has not actually been closed.
Signoff after the package design freeze. Findings then have nowhere to go, and the freeze was taken without them.
Residual risk not stated. Some margin will be thin; saying which and how thin is what lets the tapeout decision be informed.
Declared to meet the date. The gate exists to be able to hold mask release, and one that cannot is not a gate.
SIPI-11.fn: Step 3 is a three-party disposition. Every open item belongs to the die, the package or the board, and closing it requires the owner in the room—which is why co-verification signoff is a joint review rather than a report circulated for comment.

s: Receive the wafers and set up sort on the probe station
Execute wafer sort against the KGD criteria
Disposition the marginal die
Select the known-good die and build the wafer maps
Release the die to assembly with traceability
p: Wafers received with sort setup complete
Die released to assembly with traceability
r: Assembled units. Everything assembled starts from a die this activity selected.
Assembly yield report and failure pareto. Assembly failures traceable to die quality belong against the sort coverage that let them through.
pu: Sort the wafers and pick the known-good die that will go into packages—because on a 2.5D part a bad die does not fail alone, it takes an interposer, two HBM stacks and an assembly with it.

Known-good-die screening is what makes multi-die packaging economically viable. The coverage achieved at sort determines how many assembled units fail for reasons that were detectable on the wafer, and each of those is a package's worth of material lost.
en: Sort program and probe card ready from TEST-03 and TEST-05
KGD criteria agreed with the OSAT
ex: Coverage sufficient for the assembled unit's economics
Marginal criteria set against package cost, not die cost
Every released die traceable to wafer and position
rk: KGD coverage below what the package economics need. Every escaped die costs an assembled unit, and the coverage target follows from that cost rather than from a test convention.
Marginal criteria set against die cost. On a 2.5D part the assembled unit is worth many times the die, and the reject threshold should reflect that.
Traceability lost between wafer and package. An assembly failure that cannot be traced back to a die and its wafer position cannot be attributed.
Sort program not ready. The probe card and program come from TEST, and a delay there stops assembly rather than delaying test.
Sorting only for function. Parametric marginality—leakage, Vmin—predicts field failure and is worth screening even when the die functions.
ASSY-01.fn: Step 3 is where the economics live. A marginal die is cheap to scrap and expensive to assemble; the criteria for rejecting one have to be set against the assembled unit's cost rather than against the die's.

ASSY-02.t: HBM Stack Procurement and Incoming Inspection
s: Confirm HBM procurement and take delivery
Run incoming inspection against the specification
Review the supplier test data
Qualify the stacks and release them to assembly
Maintain inventory and lot traceability
r: Assembled units. HBM is part of every assembled unit, and its quality is part of the unit's.
Package-level inspection and test data. Incoming HBM data belongs with the assembly's own inspection record.
pu: Procure and inspect the HBM stacks—bought components that go into the package alongside the program's own die, and that fail in ways the program does not control.

HBM is a purchased part with its own supply constraints and its own quality distribution. Incoming inspection matters because an HBM stack that fails after assembly costs the whole unit, and the supplier's outgoing quality is not the program's to verify after the fact.
ex: Every lot inspected and its supplier data reviewed
Stacks confirmed against the package specification
Lot traceability maintained into assembly
rk: HBM supply constrained. It is a scarce component with long lead times, and a shortage stops assembly regardless of how many die are ready.
Incoming inspection skipped. A marginal stack bonded into a unit costs the whole unit, and the fault is only visible afterwards.
Supplier data not reviewed. The distribution the lot came from predicts its behavior, and the data is provided at no cost.
Lot traceability not maintained. An HBM-related failure that cannot be traced to a supplier lot cannot be escalated usefully.
Specification mismatch discovered at assembly. Stack height, bump pitch and thermal characteristics all have to match the package design.
ASSY-02.fn: Step 3 costs almost nothing and catches a class of problem inspection cannot. Supplier test data shows the distribution the delivered lot came from, and a lot at the edge of specification is worth knowing about before it is bonded in.

ASSY-03.t: Die Attach and Micro-Bump Thermo-Compression Bonding
s: Set up the process to the frozen window
Prepare the micro-bumps and apply flux
Monitor the bond parameters during the run
Bond the die and stacks by thermo-compression
Inspect post-bond and record the travelers
p: Process setup record against the frozen window
r: Assembly travelers and process data. The traveler starts here, where the actual bond conditions are recorded per unit.
Assembled units. Bonding is the step that makes a set of components into a package.
pu: Bond the die and HBM stacks to the interposer—micro-bump preparation and thermo-compression bonding—inside the process window the vehicles established.

This is the step the whole PTV program existed to de-risk. Bond force, temperature and time were characterized on vehicles; here they are applied to real die, and the process window is either followed or the vehicle work was wasted.
ex: Every unit bonded inside the frozen window
Actual bond parameters recorded per unit
Post-bond inspection coverage sufficient to catch localized defects
rk: Running outside the frozen window. The PTV program established boundaries; operating outside them discards the evidence it produced.
Bond parameters not recorded per unit. A failed unit cannot be attributed to its conditions, and the yield analysis loses its most useful variable.
Bump preparation inconsistent. Flux and surface condition affect joint formation, and variability here shows up as scattered yield.
Post-bond inspection sampled too thinly. Bonding defects are localized, and a sample that misses them lets them through to underfill where they are unfixable.
Process drift across the run. Long runs drift, and without monitoring the drift is only visible in the yield trend afterwards.
ASSY-03.fn: Step 3 records what actually happened. The frozen window says what the parameters should be; monitoring says what they were, and a unit that failed can only be attributed if its actual bond conditions were captured.

s: Attach the interposer to the substrate
Dispense and flow the underfill
Inspect voids and fillet before cure
Cure the underfill and mold the assembly
Inspect post-mold
r: Assembled units. After molding the unit is mechanically complete—attach, underfill and mold quality here decide the robustness the finished unit carries.
Package-level inspection and test data. Void and fillet inspection results are part of the unit's quality record.
pu: Attach the interposer to the substrate and underfill and mold the assembly—the steps that make it mechanically robust and that lock in whatever went before.

Underfill is irreversible. Once it has flowed and cured, a bonding defect underneath is permanent and invisible to everything except acoustic imaging. The step's quality—void-free flow, complete fillet, correct cure—determines whether the mechanical stress the package will see is distributed or concentrated.
en: Substrates delivered against the PKGD-09 order
ex: Void and fillet inspected before cure, not after
Cure profile within the frozen window
Warpage during the process inside the validated range
rk: Underfill voids. They concentrate stress and are the mechanism behind delayed CPI failures, and they are invisible after cure without acoustic imaging.
Incomplete fillet. The fillet distributes stress at the die edge, and an incomplete one puts that stress into the die corner instead.
Cure profile deviation. Under-cured underfill has different mechanical properties, and the difference appears as reliability rather than as a visible defect.
Warpage during cure exceeding the window. The vehicle program measured it; running outside that window reintroduces the risk that was retired.
Inspection only after molding. Once molded the assembly cannot be examined usefully, and the inspection has to happen before.
ASSY-04.fn: Step 3 is the last chance to catch a bonding problem. Acoustic imaging before cure can still identify a void or an incomplete fill; after cure the unit is what it is, and the defect surfaces during thermal cycling months later.

ASSY-05.t: Lid / TIM Attach and Ball Attach
s: Apply the TIM and attach the lid
Attach the balls and reflow
Check lid flatness and co-planarity
Run final visual and dimensional inspection
r: Assembled units—bring-up, qualification and sample lots. A unit becomes a finished package here: TIM, lid and ball attach produce the units the bring-up, qualification and sample lots are drawn from.
Package-level inspection and test data. Dimensional and flatness data belongs with the unit's record.
pu: Finish the package—TIM, lid and ball attach—and produce units that can be mounted, cooled and tested.

These are the last steps and they determine two things the product is judged on: the thermal interface that decides the achievable power envelope, and the ball array that decides whether the package mounts reliably. Both were characterized on vehicles and both are executed here.
ex: TIM bond line within the characterized range
Lid flatness and ball co-planarity inside specification
Every unit inspected, not a sample
rk: TIM bond line thicker than characterized. Thermal resistance rises, and the power envelope the product was sold on shrinks.
Lid flatness out of specification. The cooling solution then contacts unevenly, which produces hotspots the thermal design did not predict.
Ball co-planarity outside the mounting window. The package does not mount reliably, and the customer discovers it during their assembly.
Dimensional drift from the specification. The package has to fit sockets, heatsinks and board footprints that were designed to the drawing.
Final inspection sampled rather than complete. On an engineering build every unit is precious, and a defect shipped to bring-up costs lab days.
ASSY-05.fn: Step 1 sets the thermal performance the product will actually have. Bond line thickness under the lid is a process parameter, and the difference between the characterized value and the achieved one is watts of headroom.

ASSY-06.t: X-Ray, CSAM, and Warpage Inline Inspection
s: Set the inspection plan and sampling strategy
X-ray the joints and voids
Classify and disposition the defects
Run acoustic imaging and warpage metrology
r: Package-level inspection and test data. The inspection record is produced here—the non-destructive record of what is inside each unit.
Assembly yield report and failure pareto. Inspection findings are the physical evidence behind the yield numbers.
pu: Inspect the assemblies without taking them apart—X-ray for joints, acoustic imaging for delamination and voids, metrology for warpage—because most assembly defects are invisible from outside.

A 2.5D package hides everything that matters. The joints are under the die, the underfill is under the interposer, and the only way to see any of it non-destructively is through imaging. What this activity catches is what does not reach bring-up as an unexplained failure.
en: Assemblies available at each process stage
Inspection criteria derived from PTV results
Imaging capability available at the OSAT
ex: Inspection at each process step, not only at the end
Defects classified against a consistent scheme
Findings fed back to the process that created them
rk: Sampling too thin on an engineering build. Full inspection is affordable at these quantities, and a defect reaching bring-up costs far more than the inspection would have.
Defects classified inconsistently. Without a scheme the same feature is a defect on Monday and acceptable on Tuesday, and the yield data becomes noise.
Inspection only at the end. Defects are cheapest to catch at the step that created them, and end-of-line inspection cannot attribute them.
Warpage limits not applied. The vehicle program set them; a unit outside them is a reliability risk regardless of whether it functions.
Findings not fed back to process. Inspection that produces a pass/fail and no process signal wastes most of its value.
ASSY-06.fn: Step 1's sampling strategy is a real decision on a small build. Full inspection is affordable at engineering-lot quantities and not at production volume, and starting with full coverage is what tells you what sampling would have missed.

ASSY-07.t: Assembly Yield Analysis and Process Tuning
s: Collect the yield data across process steps
Build the failure pareto by mode and process step
Compare against the PTV yield prediction
Run root cause analysis with the OSAT
Track the corrective actions
Tune the process inside the frozen window
r: Assembly yield report and failure pareto. The yield report and failure pareto are produced here, and the pareto is what the OSAT acts on.
Assembly travelers and process data. Yield attribution depends on the traveler data, and the analysis feeds back into what travelers should capture.
pu: Analyze the assembly yield, build the failure pareto, find the root causes with the OSAT and tune the process inside the window the vehicles defined.

First-build assembly yield on a 2.5D part is rarely what the cost model assumed. This activity turns the gap into a set of attributed causes and process adjustments—and compares the result against what the vehicle program predicted, which is how the vehicle work gets validated in turn.
en: Assembly running with data collection in place
Vehicle yield prediction available from PTV-11
ex: Failures attributed to process steps, not only counted
Tuning kept inside the validated window
Yield compared against the vehicle prediction
rk: Yield reported without attribution. A number tells the program it has a problem; a pareto by process step tells the OSAT what to change.
Tuning outside the validated window. It may improve yield and it discards the reliability evidence the vehicles produced.
Vehicle prediction not compared. The comparison is what validates or invalidates the whole PTV program, and it is cheap to make.
Root cause pursued without the OSAT. Process knowledge sits with the assembler, and analysis without them produces hypotheses rather than causes.
Corrective actions untracked. An agreed action that nobody follows up is an action that did not happen.
ASSY-07.fn: Step 6 stays inside the window deliberately. Tuning beyond the validated boundaries would abandon the evidence the vehicle program produced, and a yield improvement bought that way carries an unquantified reliability risk.

ASSY-08.t: Package-Level Open / Short and Continuity Test
s: Set up the test and continuity criteria
Execute the open and short tests
Screen for marginal resistance
Disposition the failures and release the units
p: Open and short results per unit
r: Package-level inspection and test data. The electrical half of the deliverable, alongside the imaging from ASSY-06.
Assembled units. A unit that fails continuity is not released to bring-up, however scarce units are.
pu: Test the assembled packages electrically for opens, shorts and marginal joints before they go anywhere—the cheapest possible screen on the most expensive units the program has.

A package-level continuity test costs minutes and catches assembly failures that would otherwise consume lab days at bring-up. On units this expensive, screening before shipping is not optional economics.
ex: Every unit screened before release
Marginal joints identified by resistance, not only continuity
Failures fed into the yield pareto
rk: Screening skipped because units are scarce. A failed unit consumed at bring-up costs more lab time than the whole screen would have.
Continuity only, no resistance. Marginal joints conduct and fail later, and only a resistance measurement distinguishes them.
Criteria not derived from vehicle data. PTV-11 measured what good and marginal look like, and the criteria should come from there.
Failures not fed to yield analysis. An electrical failure is yield data and belongs in the pareto.
Test fixture damaging units. On packages this expensive the fixture itself has to be qualified.
ASSY-08.fn: Step 3 separates working from reliably working. A joint that conducts with elevated resistance passes a continuity test and fails in the field, and screening for it here is far cheaper than a field return.

ASSY-09.t: Unit Build and Allocation for Bring-Up, Qualification, and Samples
s: Collect the allocation requirements from each consumer
Allocate and reserve the units
Resolve contention and escalate where needed
Build to the allocation across lots
Release with traceability per allocation
r: Unit allocation record across bring-up, qual and customers. The allocation record is produced here, and it settles a contention that would otherwise be settled by whoever asks loudest.
Assembled units—bring-up, qualification and sample lots. The units as allocated lots rather than as an undifferentiated build.
pu: Allocate the finished units—bring-up, qualification, customer samples—and build to that allocation, because the first build never has enough for everyone.

Three groups need units simultaneously and all of them are on the critical path of something. Bring-up needs them to start debugging, qualification needs them to start a months-long stress campaign, and customers were promised samples. The allocation is a program decision, not an assembly one.
en: Units screened and released from ASSY-08
Requirements collected from all three consumers
ex: Allocation decided at program level, not by request order
Qualification quantity sufficient to start its campaign
Every allocated unit traceable to its lot and conditions
rk: Allocation decided by whoever asks first. The three consumers have different downstream consequences, and the trade belongs to the program.
Qualification starved. Reliability stress runs for months; starting it late moves mass production directly.
Customer samples cut. They are frequently contractual, and missing them has commercial consequences the program may not see.
Build quantity below the sum of needs. Which is normal, and it means the shortfall has to be decided rather than discovered.
Traceability lost per allocation. A qualification failure has to be traceable to its lot and its assembly conditions.
ASSY-09.fn: Step 3 is a program decision escalated deliberately. Qualification starting late delays mass production; bring-up starting late delays everything; and customer samples are often contractual. Resolving that trade below the program level puts it in the wrong hands.

EVB-01.t: Validation Platform Requirements and Topology Definition
s: Collect validation requirements from bring-up, characterization and qual
Define the platform topology options — socketed, soldered, mezzanine
Assess reuse against existing platforms
Select the topology and record its trade-offs
Set the quantity and revision plan
Write the platform specification
r: Validation platform specification. The platform specification is written here, and everything the board team builds derives from it.
Fabricated and assembled boards. The quantity and revision plan decides how many boards exist and when.
pu: Decide what the silicon will be validated on—how many platforms, in what configuration, at what quantity—before anyone draws a schematic.

The board is the only way to touch the silicon, and its capability bounds everything bring-up and characterization can do. A platform that cannot reach a rail, cannot socket a part, or cannot be temperature-soaked closes off measurements that the qualification plan assumes are available.
en: Package pin map stable enough to plan against
ex: Requirements collected from all three consumers, not just bring-up
Socket-versus-solder decided and its consequences accepted
Quantity plan sized against parallel debug needs
rk: Requirements collected from bring-up only. Characterization and qualification also live on this platform, and their needs—soak capability, instrumented rails—differ.
Socket versus solder decided late. It changes the board, the mechanical design and the unit consumption, and reversing it costs a board revision.
Quantity underestimated. Boards are the constraint on parallel debug, and a second fabrication run costs two months.
Reuse not assessed. An adaptable existing platform is the cheapest schedule available and it is often never looked for.
Specification written after design started. The board then documents what was built rather than bounding what should be.
EVB-01.fn: Step 3 is where a schedule can be bought. An existing platform that carries 70% of the requirement, adapted, beats a new design by a quarter—and the assessment costs a week.

s: Draw the block diagram and partition the interfaces
Design the power tree and VRM schematic
Design the clocking and reference schematic
Design the host interface and connector schematic
Design the debug and instrumentation headers
Design the socket and DUT interface schematic
Build the BOM and check component sourcing
Review the schematic and release it to layout
p: Bill of materials with sourcing status
r: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The schematic half of the deliverable—the reviewed schematic and sourced BOM that layout is built from.
Validation platform specification. Schematic decisions feed back into what the specification can promise.
pu: Design the EVB schematic—power tree, host interface, socket, clocking, debug headers—and its bill of materials.

The schematic is where the platform's capability is fixed. A rail without a sense point cannot be measured, a debug header omitted cannot be added, and a component with a 40-week lead time turns a board schedule into a procurement schedule.
en: Package pin map frozen from PKGD-04
Power rail requirements available from PD-08
ex: Every rail instrumented with a sense point
BOM sourced with lead times confirmed against the schedule
Schematic reviewed by validation, not only by hardware
rk: Rails without sense points. A rail that cannot be measured cannot be characterized, and the omission is only discovered during bring-up.
Long-lead components found after layout. The substitution then costs a board revision instead of a schematic edit.
Debug headers designed for the debugger nobody uses. The tooling has to be agreed with validation rather than assumed.
Pin map changing after schematic release. The package pin map has to be frozen for the schematic to be worth reviewing.
Power tree sized without the real power envelope. A VRM sized to an early estimate cannot supply the silicon's actual transients.
EVB-02.fn: Step 7 runs alongside deliberately. Component lead times are discovered during sourcing, and a part found to be 40 weeks out while the schematic is still editable can be substituted; found after layout it cannot.

EVB-03.t: PCB Layout with High-Speed Channel SI/PI Simulation
s: Plan the stack-up and impedance
Place the components and floorplan the board
Simulate SI on the critical channels during routing
Route the high-speed channels
Simulate PI on the board PDN
Lay out the power planes and PDN
Apply the thermal and mechanical layout constraints
Run DRC, review and release to fabrication
p: SI simulation results on critical channels
PI simulation on the board PDN
DRC-clean layout database released to fabrication
r: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The layout half of the deliverable—what fabrication is built from.
Fabricated and assembled boards. Fabrication takes the released layout database directly; its DRC-clean release date is what starts the vendor cycle.
pu: Lay out the PCB with signal and power integrity simulated on the critical channels, because a validation board carrying PCIe Gen6 or CXL is itself a high-speed design.

The board is in series with every interface measurement bring-up will make. A channel with a marginal board contribution produces link failures that look like silicon problems, and separating the two costs weeks of debug time that the simulation would have avoided.
en: Channel and PDN budgets from SIPI-04 and SIPI-06
ex: Board channel contribution inside its share of the SIPI budget
SI and PI simulated during routing, not after
Mechanical and thermal constraints met without a revision
rk: Board channel contribution not budgeted. The SIPI channel budget covers package and board together, and a board that consumes more than its share leaves the silicon nothing.
SI simulated after routing. The result is a report rather than a design change, and fixing it costs a revision.
Board PDN inadequate for the transient. The silicon's di/dt is on the package model; a board PDN sized without it droops.
Stack-up chosen for cost before impedance. Controlled impedance on the high-speed layers is not negotiable, and a cheaper stack-up that misses it is not cheaper.
Mechanical constraints applied last. The cooling solution and socket need space, and finding that out after routing costs a revision.
EVB-03.fn: Steps 3 and 5 run against the routing rather than after it. A channel simulated after the board is routed produces a report; simulated during, it produces a routing change.

s: Select the fabrication vendor and release the data
Track PCB fabrication
Procure the components against their lead times
Assemble the boards
Run first article inspection
Run incoming inspection and accept the boards
p: Vendor selection and released fabrication data
r: Fabricated and assembled boards, rev A/B with quantity plan. The board fleet is fabricated, assembled and inspected here, delivered at the quantity the parallel-debug plan needs.
EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. Fabrication findings—DFM issues, substitutions—feed back into the database.
pu: Get the boards fabricated, assembled and inspected—an eight-week vendor cycle that is mostly waiting and entirely on the critical path to bring-up.

This is procurement work with an engineering tail. The board has to arrive before silicon does, its quantity has to match the parallel-debug plan, and every board that arrives faulty is a debug station that does not exist.
en: Components ordered against confirmed lead times
ex: Boards delivered before silicon arrives
First article inspected before the run completes
Controlled impedance verified by coupon
rk: Long-lead components blocking assembly. The board is fabricated and waiting on one part, which is the most common way this activity slips.
First article skipped. An assembly error is then replicated across the entire run and discovered at bring-up.
Quantity cut for cost. Boards are the constraint on parallel debug, and the saving is repaid in serialized lab time.
Boards arriving after silicon. Silicon waiting on a board is the worst schedule outcome the program can produce.
Controlled impedance not verified. The stack-up was designed for it; the fabricated board has to be coupon-tested to confirm it.
EVB-04.fn: Step 5 catches assembly problems on one board before they are replicated across the whole run. It costs a day and it is routinely skipped in the interest of speed, which is how twenty identically-wrong boards get built.

EVB-05.t: Power Delivery, VRM, and Telemetry Design and Bring-Up
s: Derive the power tree requirement from the die and package
Select and design the VRMs
Design the transient response against the SIPI budget
Design the telemetry and monitoring
Design the protection and sequencing
Bring up and validate the power subsystem on the board
r: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The power subsystem design is part of the schematic package.
Board bring-up report and known issues. Power bring-up results are the first part of the board's own bring-up record.
pu: Design and bring up the power delivery, VRM and telemetry on the platform—the rails the silicon runs on and the instrumentation that measures them.

Characterization is mostly a power measurement. Shmoo needs rails that can be swept, power validation needs rails that can be measured accurately, and both need protection that trips before an expensive part is destroyed rather than after.
ex: Rails sweepable across the full shmoo range
Protection validated before any real part is inserted
Telemetry accurate enough for characterization
rk: Rails not sweepable across the shmoo range. Characterization then cannot reach the corners the qualification plan requires.
Protection untested before a real part goes in. A sequencing fault destroys a first-silicon unit, and there are very few of them.
Telemetry accuracy insufficient. Power measurements at the resolution characterization needs demand real instrumentation, not a rough monitor.
Transient response inadequate. The die's di/dt is known from SIPI; a VRM that cannot follow it produces droop that looks like a silicon failure.
Sequencing not matching the silicon's requirement. The power-up order comes from the design, and getting it wrong is a common first-board fault.
EVB-05.fn: Step 5 is what protects the units. A sequencing error or an overcurrent event on a first-silicon part costs a package worth many thousands, and the protection has to be validated before a real part is ever inserted.

s: Collect the debug requirements from validation and DFT
Design the JTAG and trace pod interfaces
Design the logic analyser and scope access
Design the interposers and probe access
Integrate the software debug tooling
Validate the debug infrastructure and document it
r: Debug and trace access documentation. The access documentation is produced here, and it is what the bring-up team reads at 2am.
EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. Debug headers and access points are schematic and layout content.
pu: Build the debug access—JTAG and trace pods, interposers, probe points—because silicon debug is bounded by what can be observed.

When first silicon does something unexpected, the difference between a day and a month is whether the state that explains it can be read out. The DFT infrastructure provides the internal access; this activity provides the physical path to it.
en: DFT debug architecture available from DFT-08
ex: Debug access matching what DFT actually exposes
Trace bandwidth sufficient for the events being traced
Debug path validated before silicon, not during a crisis
rk: Debug access designed without DFT. The internal observability comes from DFT-08, and the board access has to match what it exposes.
Trace bandwidth insufficient. Trace is only useful if it can keep up with the events being traced, and the bandwidth is a board design parameter.
Probe points unreachable once the cooling solution is mounted. The thermal solution and the probe access compete for the same physical space.
Debug path unvalidated before silicon. It is then debugged during the emergency it exists to resolve.
Software tooling not integrated. A hardware debug path with no software to drive it is not a debug path.
EVB-06.fn: Step 6 validates the debug path before it is needed. A trace pod that does not work is discovered during the crisis it was meant to resolve, which is the worst possible moment.

EVB-07.t: Board Bring-Up with Socketed or Dummy Parts
s: Plan the bring-up and fit the dummy parts
Bring up the power tree and verify the rails
Validate the telemetry and protection
Validate the clocking and references
Check the thermal solution fit
Validate the interface loopbacks and signals
p: Bring-up plan and fitted dummy parts
Interface loopback and signal validation results
Board bring-up report and known issues
r: Board bring-up report and known issues. The bring-up report and known-issues list are produced here, and the known-issues list is what stops board faults being mistaken for silicon faults.
Fabricated and assembled boards. A board is not released to silicon bring-up until it has passed this.
pu: Bring the board itself up—with dummy parts or a socketed loopback—so that when silicon arrives, every failure is the silicon's.

This is the single highest-leverage activity in the stage. A board debugged before first silicon means bring-up starts on a known-good platform; a board debugged alongside first silicon means every anomaly has two possible causes and each takes days to separate.
en: Dummy parts or loopback fixtures available
ex: Board bring-up complete before silicon arrives
Known issues documented for the bring-up team
Every board in the fleet brought up, not just one
rk: Board bring-up deferred until silicon arrives. Every anomaly then has two candidate causes, and separating them costs days each.
Known issues not documented. The bring-up team then rediscovers each board quirk independently, once per engineer.
Dummy parts not representative. A loopback that does not load the rails or exercise the channels validates less than it appears to.
Only one board brought up. Board-to-board variation is real, and a fleet where only one is characterized is a fleet with unknown members.
Thermal fit checked after silicon insertion. A cooling solution that does not fit is discovered with an irreplaceable part underneath it.
EVB-07.fn: The whole activity is scheduled to complete before silicon arrives. Every hour spent here is an hour not spent, at ten times the cost, debugging a board while first silicon waits on the bench.

EVB-08.t: Thermal Solution and Cooling for the Lab Platform
s: Derive the thermal requirement from the package envelope
Select the cooling solution
Design the airflow and enclosure
Design the mounting and interfaces
Build in temperature control and soak capability
Validate the thermal solution on the platform
r: Validation platform specification. Thermal capability is part of what the platform can promise.
Board bring-up report and known issues. Thermal validation results belong in the platform's own record.
pu: Design and validate the cooling for the lab platform—which is not the product's thermal solution, but has to remove the same power.

A part that thermally throttles during characterization produces data about the cooling rather than about the silicon. The lab solution can be oversized and ugly in ways the product's cannot, and it should be, because measurement validity depends on it.
ex: No throttling at maximum power during characterization
Temperature held at set point, including the hot corner
Mounting compatible with debug probe access
rk: Cooling sized to the product's solution rather than to the lab's need. The lab platform can be oversized, and measurement validity is worth more than realism.
No temperature control, only cooling. Characterization needs the part held at a set point, including a hot one.
Throttling during characterization. The data then describes the cooling rather than the silicon, and it is often not noticed.
Mounting competing with probe access. The debug points and the heatsink want the same space, and the conflict has to be resolved in layout.
Thermal validated only at nominal power. The interesting measurements are at maximum power, which is where the solution is stressed.
EVB-08.fn: Step 5 is what makes qualification-adjacent measurement possible. Characterization needs the part held at a temperature, not merely kept cool, and a solution that only cools cannot produce a hot-corner shmoo.

EVB-09.t: Lab Instrumentation Reservation and Test Rack Build
s: Derive the instrument requirement from the characterization plan
Reserve and procure the instruments
Build the automation and control infrastructure
Build and cable the test racks
Provision the lab space and power
Integrate and calibrate the racks
p: Lab setup and instrument reservation plan
r: Lab setup and instrument reservation plan. The reservation plan and rack build come from here, and they are what stop bring-up queueing for a scope.
Board bring-up report and known issues. The lab setup is the context every bring-up measurement is made in.
pu: Reserve the instruments and build the lab racks—because characterization needs equipment that is expensive, shared and booked months ahead.

A high-speed oscilloscope or a BERT is a capital item with a queue in front of it. Discovering during bring-up that the scope with the right bandwidth is committed elsewhere for six weeks does not delay the measurement by six weeks—it delays everything downstream of it.
ex: Instruments reserved against the bring-up window, not requested during it
Automation working before bring-up starts
Racks calibrated and their calibration current
rk: Instruments booked too late. High-bandwidth equipment is shared and queued, and a six-week wait delays everything downstream.
Automation deferred to bring-up. It is then written under time pressure by people who should be debugging silicon.
Racks not calibrated. Measurements from an uncalibrated setup are unusable for characterization and often not questioned.
Lab power or space insufficient. A rack that cannot be powered is a rack that does not exist, and facilities lead times are long.
Instrument bandwidth below the signal rate. A scope that cannot resolve the edge produces a plausible and wrong measurement.
EVB-09.fn: Step 3 decides whether characterization is manual or automatic. A shmoo run by hand takes days per corner; the same shmoo automated runs overnight, and the automation is written here rather than improvised during bring-up.

s: Define the handoff boundary with the firmware team
Write the minimal boot and initialization software
Build the host driver stub and enumeration
Build the register access and diagnostic tooling
Build the logging and data capture
Validate the host enablement on the platform
r: Board bring-up report and known issues. Host enablement is validated as part of the platform and reported with it.
Debug and trace access documentation. The diagnostic tooling is how debug access is actually used.
pu: Provide the minimum host-side software needed to power on and talk to the part—boot, register access, enumeration, logging—without taking on the product's software stack.

SW/FW is outside this program's scope, but silicon cannot be brought up without something on the other end of the link. The boundary matters: this activity delivers exactly enough to reach first register read and no more, and where that line sits should be agreed rather than discovered.
ex: Boundary with firmware explicit and agreed
Register access validated against the current map
Enablement validated on the platform before silicon
rk: Boundary with firmware left implicit. Either the work is duplicated or nobody does it, and both are discovered at power-on.
Register map drifting from the RTL. A diagnostic tool built against a stale map reads the wrong addresses and reports plausible nonsense.
Scope creeping into the product stack. Minimal enablement becomes a driver project, and the validation team stops validating.
Logging insufficient for post-mortem. A failure that cannot be reconstructed from the log has to be reproduced, which on first silicon may not be possible.
Enablement unvalidated before silicon. Software bugs then present as silicon bugs during the most expensive week of the program.
EVB-10.fn: Step 1 is the activity's most valuable hour. Without an explicit boundary, hardware validation writes software the firmware team is also writing, and each assumes the other is doing it.

TEST-01.t: Test Plan and Coverage Strategy Definition
